FROM BLACK OF READING

The Duke of Edinburgh's new Harvard training plane gets the five-stars
insignia of Marshal of the Royal Air Force after delivery to White Waltham
(Berks) R.A.F. station.
Pictured here putting the finishing touches to the job is Fairey Aviation
mechanic Peter Barton of Gosbrook Road, Caversham, Reading. With him is
Sgt. James Murray, one of the ground staff who will service the plane.
Delivery of the 200-miles-an-hour American-built Harvard means that the
Duke's training has now progressed beyond the 120 m.p.h. Chipmunk in which
he received his initial flying lessons. When he masters the Harvard, he
will move on to jet planes - probably the 600-miles-an-hour Gloster Meteor.

PROGRESS ON THE ANGLO-
The great new oil refinery of the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company,
with a projected capacity of 4,000,000 tons a year, is taking
shape. It is due for completion in the summer of 1952,
but the Crude Oil Distillation Unit and its necessary
auxiliaries are expected to be in commission in a few months.
Situated at the Isle of Grain, on the Kent coast, the new
refinery will cost £40,000,000, and its output will be about
one-sixth of the Abadan refinery. It is being constructed
on reclaimed marshland on which a million tons of sand from
the sea bed off the Nore have been pumped in order to stop
the natural sinking of the land, and to prevent the sand
drifting, a mixture of grass and clover has been planted.
New jetties are under construction to accommodate the largest
of tankers, and there will be 160 storage tanks.
The picture shows:

1983-5286/51756

A view of the new refinery site looking south-east from
Cat. Cracker, showing combined blow down stack and tanks
in the foreground, Crude Distillation Unit (left centre),
No.1 Vacuum Unit (right centre), temporary construction
Offices, canteen, concrete batch plant, etc. Centre
background. River seen in far distance.

Indus, Oil Refineries, Isle of Grain.

Transcribed_Text:

        They Planned A City

Even while Nazi bombs were raining on London, experts with their eyes fixed
on the future, were planning a new London that shall do away with the
many blemishes that still mar the face of the Empire's capital. Now you are
introduced to some of the people who have been working for the future of
London in this article by CONNERY CHAPPELL

OHN HENRY FORSHAW, M.C., the ex-Royal
Engineers officer, who is the chief man behind
the London County Council's Plan for rebuild-
ing London, is forty-seven and earns £2,750 a year.
And while the Plan, to which he contributed more
than any one else has had more space and publicity
than any other single news item since the war started,
Forshaw himself has had practically none. Which is
how he prefers it.

The Plan, of course, has broken all records. It has
gone into a second edition as a book at 12s. 6d. More
than 1,500 people a day have seen models of it at the
County Hall—mostly housewives, service men on
leave and young people who wanted to see the world
of the future—there its exhibition has had to be ex-
tended. Editorial comment on it runs into hundreds
of columns.

In short, after taking two years to prepare, the Plan
is revealed as the biggest thing of its type ever at-
tempted.

It is a Plan, not of lines, but of lives, designed to
take the ugliness out of London, in the words of Lord
Latham, Leader of the Council.
The decision to produce it was taken more than two
years ago, during the big air raids. A special staff
was built up from people in the Town Planning Sec-
tion of the L.C.C.'s big architectural department at
County Hall.
Every one concerned with it carried on with their

normal Civil Defence and Home Guard duties, and
often with their departmental work as well. There were
no privileges, no special favours. It was an enormous
job, frequently done under bad conditions during air
raids.

As consultant, the L.C.C. engaged Leslie Patrick
Abercrombie, Professor of Town Planning at Uni-
versity College, London, who is accepted as Britain's
leading expert on the subject. Wesley Dougill, who
died in February, when the job was nearly done, was
Assistant Planning Officer, and did brilliant work.

The whole thing was produced on an informal con-
ference system, many meetings taking place in the
early hours of the morning during the hectic nights of
1941.

Professor Abercrombie, who was visiting County
Hall several times a week, frequently stayed over and
slept there, and Mr. Forshaw was usually on the spot—
for in addition to his position as deputy architect and
later architect to the council he was also in charge of
A.R.P. rescue work and debris disposal for London.

This involved spending many nights at headquarters
and it was during these sessions, waiting for air raid
alerts, that a lot of the early theoretical work was done.

Gradually, the staff sorted itself out; it never
exceeded thirty and averaged about twenty. It was
enthusiastic, and young, which was as well, for an
enormous amount of groundwork had to be cleared up
before the Plan could reach the drawing boards.

Transcribed_Text:
THE FUR STORAGE
VAULT
wavy.
By CALLISTHENES

The other day a charming customer
who brought to our Fur Department
several articles requiring immediate
attention told us of an experience which
may be common to many. Last Spring,
feeling very economical and imagining
that the trifling cost of fur storage might
be avoided, the lady purchased a moth-
proof bag, stored her furs therein and
put the bag away. The receptacle,
unfortunately, was not proof against
the tiny invader, for a carelessly folded
opening admitted the enemy, with the
result that the lady’s furs can only be
saved by the immediate attention we
are now giving them. For protection
is not so much a matter of only moth-
proof bags as the application of storage
conditions that make damage
impossible.

The Fur Storage Vault of ours is a
well-known and enormously patronised
department of this business. We believe
it to be one of the largest fur vaults
of its kind in the world. It is so arranged
that its temperature is maintained
continuously below freezing-point, so
that it becomes impossible for moth
eggs to germinate, even though they be
depply hidden in the fur. But this
precaution against germination is only
a single stage in a carefully planned
campaign against the insinuating moth.
Two or three times during the summer
months—for an entire 24 hours—the
temperature of the vault is allowed to
rise to that of the street. By this means
whatever eggs are left in the furs are
encouraged to hatch out. The trouble-
some insects are then submitted to the
freezing process and eliminated utterly.
It has been noted, by the way, that pelts
treated by this process recover their
original sheen, and seem rejuvenated
after their emergence from cold storage.
Carefully examined before they are
stowed away and no less carefully
re-examined before being handed over,
the pelts return with a newness and a
glossiness which is otherwise lost to
them. The cost of this work is so
small—a matter, really, of a few shillings
—as to represent the most profitable
outlay on one’s wardrobe needs.

We have now arrived at a period of the
year when many of these gems of the furrier's
art are being removed. Yet we feel that our
reference to this fascinating subject is timely,
if only for the moral it points. To incur
avoidable risk to precious furs in the hope
of saving a few shillings for storage is to be
“ penny wise, pound foolish ” in the widest
sense of the phrase.

Selfridge & Co., Ltd.

London: Mr. Charles Orr-Ewing, Conservative
Member of Parliament for Hendon, North, sits
in the camera chair when fourteen Conservative
members of Parliament to-day began a B.B.C.
television course, similar to one recently held
for television writers, at Alexandria Palace.

description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Housing ÃƒÆ’Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â» Post War ÃƒÆ’Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â» Houses - Miscellaneous Planning.
Transcribed_Text:
“MOTOpia. A study in
the Evolution of the
Urban Landscape,” by
G. A. Jellicoe. Studio
Books, 42s.

NOT so long ago nearly
everybody thought
that they knew the
answer to the traffic prob-
lem.

We had only to spend a
few hundred millions a year
on motorways, ring roads,
flyovers, road widenings and
multi-storey parking
garages, and Bob would (in
due course) be your uncle.
This innocent illusion, because
successive Governments have
refused to spend anything more
than small change on building
roads, and we were unable to
learn from experience (as the
Americans are now doing) that
the engineering solution opens a
bottomless financial pit, but

—the futuristic town

planned to make

the best of motors

by
Malcolm MacEwen

an official of the Royal Institute of British Architects

does not solve the traffic
problem.
Two cars in every Los
Angeles garage are a sign less
of American affluence than of
the catastrophic collapse of
public transport, of waste on a
vast scale, and of the dispersal
of the city far and wide over
the countryside.
“Motopia” is the name given

by G. A. Jellicoe, the landscape
architect, architect and town-
planner, to his theoretical
design for an ideal motorised
town.

Its great merit is that he
breaks through the fetters of
conventional thinking in an
effort to design a new kind of
town in which we can get the
best of both worlds — the
mobility of the motor car with-
out its dirt, noise, smells, con-
estion and danger.

Motopia consists of a rect-
angular grid of five-storey ter-
races, forming a series of great
own “squares.”

The first four storeys are flats
and maisonettes, some with gar-
lens; the fifth storey is a
“mews storey” for car parking
and vehicular access; and the
roads are on the roof, screened
by plants.

The entire space between the
buildings, and under them, is a
vast park of unending variety
and beauty, in which lie schools
and other public buildings, and
through which one can walk
everywhere in safety.

At the corner of each square
the buildings form a hollow
circle, containing local shops
and other facilities on the
ground floor, and a roundabout
for the rooftop road.

SHOPPING

At one side of the town is a
great multi-level, glassed-in
shopping centre, where people
meet for shopping and pleasure
after parking their cars on the
roof.

It is easy to criticise Mr. Jel-
licoe’s conception. It is a shot
in the dark because nobody has
yet done the basic studies on
traffic generation that would
enable us to discover the practi-
cal limits to the use of the motor
car in towns.

All we do know is that large
towns and cities, if they are to

“Helicopter-view” of
Motopia, showing how the
space that would normally
be taken up by congested
roads is given over to parks
and recreation grounds.

remain reasonably compact
groupings for social intercourse,
must depend largely on public
transport.
In Motopia, this is limited to
water buses on the lakes—
delightful, but of limited prac-
tical value.

To put the traffic on the roof
and the people on the ground is
obviously more difficult than the
opposite, and the widths of
roads and roundabouts are
limited by the width of the
buildings, and cannot easily be
related to the volume of traffic.

EXERCISE

To dismiss Motopia for these
reasons would, however, be to
miss its real point. For Motopia
is an exercise in the imagina-
tion, and opens our eyes to the
possibilities that have still to be
explored in landscape and town
design.

The greater part of the book
illustrates the historical devel-
opment of the urban landscape,
which Mr. Jellicoe wishes to
restore to the place it held in
the 18th century when town and
country were brought together
in the Bloomsbury squares.

We shall not find the answer
to the motor-car problem by
hacking the city to pieces to
make way for it in unlimited
numbers.

We must begin by designing
for people, by setting our archi-
tects and their professional col-
leagues to work to design a new
kind of town in which we can
live civilised lives, using the
motor-car without being en-
slaved by it.

If “Motopia,” which is richly

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION MONDAY IS EVENING JULY 18th 1949.
BRITAIN LEADS WORL IN MOTOR RUSTPROOFING TECHNIQUE.
JS 18.7.49.
Morris cars coming off the assembly lines at Cowley, Oxfordshire,
are now receiving a 100% anti-rust treatment from a special plant
known as the "Rotodip" which, operated in conjunction with one of
the most up-to-date paint plants, forms an engineering project in
which Britain leads the whole world. Until the advent of this new
technique the procedure for finishing car bodies was to first
to thoroughly clean down the body to remove all grease, and to
finally rinse by hand or automatic spray, followed by a drying
process, after which the primer and finish coats of paints were
added by spray gun. This method, however, did never give complete
protection because many important parts of the body were never
reached.
Now the bodies go through the plant which consists of a tunnel
some 20 feet square and 300 feet long, which they enter in the
plain steel, greasy state, and emerge some 12 houraw later having
been cleaned, rustproofed, and primer-painted inside and out.
entirely automatically.

bodies are mounted on a revolving spit with the bonnet, wings and
boot in position but spaced-inch from the body to allow free
circulation, and is then carried broadside through the length of
the plant on conveyor chains in such a way that the body revolves
on its own axis while passing through the machine. The process
is in two stages - first rustproofing by cleaning, rinsing and
proofing for which the bodies pass through six large tanks, and
secondly, primer-painting during which the body is dried in an
cooled down, and painted.

In their journey through the plant, the

aries of pictures illustrates the remarkable process which
rris engineers are confident will protect the bodies
at corrosion and paint flaking.

SIR HUGH CASSON took a sheet of paper
        from his conference documents and did
        a lightning sketch. There it is above—his idea
        of a seaside pier "for motorists only," where
        the whole family can spend a car-based day
        enjoying the ozone.
        Sir Hugh, the eminent architect, had just given his
        ideas about a new seaside, made-to-measure for the
        motorist, to the people most concerned—200 represen-
        tatives of British seaside resorts. They were meeting
        in London.
        They may have thought
        his ideas fanciful. But he is
        practised in making his
        dreams come true.
        He was chief architect of
        the Festival of Britain.
        "These car piers," he told his
        audience, "should be like the
        conventional seaside pier, out at
        sea on legs and reached by a
        causeway.
        Exciting and

        Expensive
        "They would have two- or
        three-storey viewing decks for
        cars only.
        "They need not look unsightly
        —on the contrary they could
        look most exciting. They would
        be expensive, or indeed an
        multi-storey garages on land,
        but at least there are no expen-
        sive site costs to meet.
        "If the pierhead amenities in-
        cluded such obvious facilities as
        cafes, souvenir shops, lavatories
        and the like then the motorist

        By FRANK
        DAWES

        would not grudge an ap-
        priate charge."
        He told me afterwards
        he picked up the idea
        Chicago, where a car pier is
        being built over the lake to solve
        the parking problem.
        He also suggested the two-
        storey promenade—one level for
        vehicles, the other for strollers.
        Sir Hugh agreed that the
        piers were perhaps suitable only
        for large resorts. He wanted a
        complete ban on motor-cars in
        the smaller resorts.
        Motor cars
        defined
        But before his piers get under
        way he asks for an immediate
        policy of charging for prome-
        nade parking at all resorts.
        After all to the car-borne

        holidaymaker the car is more
        than a vehicle, he said.
        "It is a home base—
        • The place to which the
        family returns for meals.
        • To put the baby down for its
        afternoon sleep.
        • For sun-bathing.
        • Where the children change
        in and out of bathing things.
        • Where Granny snoozes all
        day over her knitting.
        • Or of the pick-nick: a teenage
        daughter, tuned into Radio
        Luxembourg, sits daydreaming
        on her shoulder blades and
        brooding over the injustices of
        her life.
        And the men from Blackpool,
        Brighton, Bognor and Broad-
        stairs and all the resorts in the
        alphabet laughed and ap-
        plauded Sir Hugh's devastating
        description of a typical seaside
        town today.
        It rung bells. Here's an ex-
        cerpt about some place you may
        recognise.
        "The Old Town, cobbled,
        clamorous and smelly, locally
        referred to as the "haunt of
        artists", dominated by a fine
        parish church marooned like a
        stone schooner in a small sea of

        17th- and 18th-century cottages,
        some semi-derelict, a few still
        lived in, some "cutted up" as tea
        shops and junk shops.
        "To left and right, along the
        coast, small groups of regency
        terraces and squares, most of
        them come down in the world.
        minus balconies or cornices and
        looking like a group of elegant
        but shabby old ladies. perching
        upon the cliffs under the glaring
        eye of the local Grand Hotel—
        usually a magnificent Margaret
        Rutherford sort of building,
        mauve-faced, majestic and ex-
        travagantly behatted."

Transcribed_Text:
CHILDREN with flaming torches led a march
        of 2,000 homeless last night—a march
        which ended with a bishop describing the
        plight as "a disgrace to the nation."

        Among the women in the quarter-mile long proces-
        sion which wound slowly from St. Paul's Cathedral to
        Southwark were mothers with babies in their arms
        with toddlers in push-
        chairs.
        At the end of the "croco-
        dile," men bore a huge
        banner which said simply:
        "No room in the inn."
        The two bishops who organ-
        ised the march—Dr. Robert
        Stopford, Bishop of London, and
        Dr. Mervyn Stockwood, Bishop
        of Southwark—took part in it.
        And from his pulpit at South-
        wark Cathedral, hard-hitting
        Dr. Stockwood spoke passion-
        ately about the problem of Lon-
        don's homeless—an emergency,
        he said, as great as the war.
        The cathedral, which holds
        about 1,200 people, was
        packed, and Dr. Stockwood's
        words were relayed by loud-
        speakers to hundreds who
        stood outside in the gather-
        ing darkness.
        The bishop said there were
        80,000 families in London wait-
        ing for homes—families living
        in overcrowded rooms, with
        inadequate facilities and shock-
        ing sleeping accommodation.
        REMEDIES
        And he suggested these reme-
        dies:
        A national housing authority,
        of which housing is now
        by the Government.
        • Priorities based on need,
        and if it is used for offices and
        factory building, it cannot be
        building homes," he said.
        • Control of land. "Is it right
        to leave speculators to deter-
        mine its value?" he asked.
        • In times of war the Govern-
        ment assumes control. Isn't the
        present emergency as grave?
        Among his other suggestions
        were mobile homes in London
        parks and open spaces, and the
        requisitioning of empty houses.

        DESPERATE
        As the bishop finished his ser-
        mon, 28-year-old Mrs. Gwyneth
        Cleaver, mother of two children
        who is living in an LCC centre
        apart from her husband, said:
        "This is our last desper-
        ate hope—that this march
        will move someone's con-
        science. Christmas isn't
        going to be much fun for us."
        Later, Dr. Stockwood, said: "I
        don't want to make this an anti-
        landlord thing. It's a question of
        human cupidity. We're all guilty
        of that—all ready to make a bit
        of money where we can.
        "What really sticks in my gul-
        let is the fact that a single room
        in, say, Hampstead, without
        facilities—water or anything—
        can be offered for £5 a week to
        desperate people.
        "And they are forced to take
        these rooms. They live in war-
        ren-six rooms, and maybe 30
        people in them. It's scandalous."

                                                   It was all, of course, what has

                                                   Like countless coopers before

                                                 THE LAST

                                                 But because the trend is to-
                                                 barrelmaking craft is dying and

                                                 Truman, Hanbury and Bux-

                                                   William, who is nearly 6ft.

PLANET "EWS PICTURE No. LN 348083 OF 2ND FEBRUARY, 1958,
HEADED "MASS MEETING OF UNEMPLOYED IN CAERNARVON" -
THE MAN ADDRESSING THE MASS MEETING IN THE PAVILION AT
CAERNARVON HAS NOW BEEN IDENTIFIED AS MR. HUGH JONES, THE
CHAIRMAN OF THE NANTLLE VALLEY UNEMPLOYMENT PEOPLES
COMMITTEE, AND HE IS HOLDING IS FOUR-YEAR-OLD-DAUGHTER
NERYS IN HIS ARMS. AN AMMENDED COPY OF THE CAPTION IS
BELOW FOR YOUR FILES.

LN 348083                             MGN                               LONDON BUREAU

MASS MEETING OF UNEMPLOYED IN CAERNARVON.

CAERNARVON, WALES : A GENERAL VIEW OF THE MASS MEETING
IN THE PAVILION AT CAERNARVON, BEING ADDRESSED BY MR. HUGH
JONES, CHAIRMAN OF THE NANTLLE VALLEY UNEMPLOYMENT PEOPLES
COMMITTEE, WHILST HE IS HOLDING HIS DAUGHTER, 4-YEAR-OLD
NERYS IN HIS ARMS. HUNDREDS OF UNEMPLOYED FORMED A PROTEST
MARCH FROM THE VILLAGE OF PEN-Y-GROES, IN THE NANTLLE VALLEY,
TO ATTEND THE MEETING TO PRESS FOR THE EARLY ESTABLISHMENT OF
INDUSTRIES IN SOUTH-WEST WALES WHICH HAVE BEEN PROMISED TO
THE AREA. SEVERE UNEMPLOYMENT CONDITIONS PREVAIL IN THE
SOUTH-WEST WALES AREA, AND THE UNEMPLOYMENT FIGURES HAVE
RISEN FROM 3,500 IN OCTOBER TO 6,000 IN NOVEMBER AND IS
NOW AT 8,000. IT IS ESTIMATED THAT WHEN ALL THE OLD WORKS
HAVE BEEN CLOSED, ABOUT FIFTEEN THOUSAND PEOPLE WOULD BE OUT
OF WORK, REPRESENTING MORE THAN TEN PER CENT OF THE INSURED
POPULATION. ON MONDAY (FEB 3RD), THE MINISTER OF POWER, LORD
MILLS, IS TO RECEIVE A DEPUTATION OF WELSH M.P.S WHO WILL
PUT TO HIM THE URGENCY OF THE CASE FOR FINDING MORE WORK FOR
SOUTH-WEST WALES. THE DECISION OF RICHARD THOMAS AND BALDWINS
TO CLOSE THE STEEL WORKS AT LLANELLY IN A MONTH'S TIME, HAS
BROUGHT THE MATTER TO A HEAD IN THAT AREA.

CHILDREN with flaming torches led a march
of 2,000 homeless last night—a march
which ended with a bishop describing their
plight as “a disgrace to the nation.”
Among the women in the quarter-mile long proces-
sion which wound slowly from St. Paul's Cathedral to
Southwark were mothers with babies in their arms or
with toddlers in push-
chairs.

At the end of the "croco-
dile," men bore a huge
banner which said simply:
"No room at the inn . . ."
The two bishops who organ-
ised the march—Dr. Robert
Stopford, Bishop of London, and
Dr. Mervyn Stockwood, Bishop
of Southwark—took part in it
and from his pulpit at South-
wark Cathedral, hard-hitting
Dr. Stockwood spoke passion-
ately about the problem of Lon-
don's homeless—an emergency,
he said, as great as the war.
The cathedral, which holds
about 1,200 people, was
packed and Dr. Stockwood's
words were relayed by loud-
speakers to hundreds who
stood outside in the gather-
ing darkness.
The bishop said there were
80,000 families in London wait-
ing for homes—families living
in overcrowded rooms, with
inadequate facilities and shock-
ing sleeping accommodation.

REMEDIES
And he suggested these reme-
dies:
A national housing authority
with powers to borrow and lend
money at interest rates decided
by the Government.
Priorities based on need.
"If it is good for offices and
and if it is good for luxury
luxury buildings," he said,
control of land. "Is it right
to leave speculators to deter-
mine its value?" he asked.
"In times of war the Govern-
ment assumes control. Isn't the
present housing emergency as grave?"
Among his other suggestions
were mobile homes in London
parks and open spaces, and the
requisitioning of empty houses.

DESPERATE
As the bishop finished his ser-
mon, 28-year-old Mrs. Gwyneth
Cleaver, mother of ten children
who is living in an L.C.C. hostel
apart from her husband, said:
"This is our last desper-
ate hope—that this march
will move someone's con-
science. Christmas isn't
going to be much fun for us."
Later, Dr. Stockwood, said: "I
defy a man to make this an anti-
landlord thing. It's a question of
human cupidity. We're all guilty
of that—all ready to make a bit
of money where we can.
"What really sticks in my gul-
let is the fact that a single room
in, say, Hampstead, without
feeling, wallpaper or anything—
can be offered for £5 a week to
desperate people.
And they are forced to take
these rooms. They live in war-
rens—six rooms, and maybe 30
people in them. It's scandalous."

Stained Windows
MJH/HT.

94-YEARS-OLD CRAFTSMAN.

Still working on a craft which has been in his family
since 1820 is 94-years-old Mr. Samuel Caldwell
of Canterbury (Kent), who is in charge of the stained
glass of the Cathedral, comprising thousands of square
feet of priceless glass, dating back to the 13th.
century. Twice in his lifetime, Mr. Caldwell
has removed the Cathedral's glass -once during the
1914-1918 war and again when the last war started.
Under Mr. Caldwell's supervision, the replacement of the
glass - a long and skilful process requiring endless
patience - has just been completed and he is now
at work designing and making stained glass to
replace the modern glass which was not removed and
was destroyed by bomb-blast. An authority on his
craft, with 77 years experience behind him, Mr.
Caldwell started work in Canterbury Cathedral when he
was 17.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: MR. SAMUEL CALDWELL, the 94-years
old craftsman, seen at work in his Canterbury (Kent)
workshop, restoring a 13th. century medallion
representing "The last Supper". His health, sight
and hearing are all still exceptionally good.

                                 DAWLIES. 24TH JANUARY, 1966

             BIGGEST SHIP TO BE BUILT ON THE TYNE WILL
                           BE LAUNCHED NEXT MONTH
             NCPS                                 24.1.66.
             NOPE.
             THERE'S A CERTAIN MAGIC ABOUT HITTING THE TON.
             MOTOR CYCLISTS LIVE AND DIE FOR IT. OLD MEN OF
             99 PRAY THAT THEY WILL HANG ON FOR THE PRISE OF
             BEING 100 NOT OUT. CRICKETERS' CAREERS RISE AND
             FALL BY IT.
                  BUT NOWHERE IS THE ACHIEVEMENT SO PROUDLY AND
             COMPETITIVELY MEASURED TODAY THAN IN SHIPBUILDING.
             BUILD A SHIP OF 100,000 GROSS TONS OR MORE AND YOU
             CAN SAY YOU ARE IN THE 'BIG LEAGUE'. EVEN BY
             JAPAN'S GIGANTIC STANDARD. NOW, THE TOUGH,
             TRADITIONAL SHIPBUILDERS OF THE RIVER TYNE ARE
             PUTTING THE FINISHING TOUCHES TO THEIR FANFARE
             ENTRY INTO THE 'BIG LEAGUE.'
                  A THOUSAND MEN AT THE WORLD-FAMOUS YARD OF
             SWAN, HUNTER AND WIGHAM RICHARDSON, WALLSEND-ON-
             TYNE, ARE SCOURRING OVER AND BELOW THE GIGANTIC
             DECKS OF THE 100,000 TON "BRITISH ARGOSY"
             GETTING HER READY FOR LAUNCHING ON FEBRUARY 7TH.
             THE VESSEL IS BEING BUILT FOR THE BP TANKER
             COMPANY. SHE WILL BE THE FIRST BRITISH-BUILT
             SHIP TO ENTER THE "BIG LEAGUE" THIS YEAR AND IS
             THE BIGGEST SHIP EVER BUILT ON A RIVER RENOWNED
             FOR PUSHING THE BOAT OUT IN A BIG WAY.
                  FIFTEEN YEARS AGO, PRINCESS MARGARET WENT TO
             SWAN HUNTERS TO LAUNCH THE THEN BIGGEST SUPER
             TANKER OF THE DAY, THE 28,000-TON "VELLUTINA".
             THE BRITISH ARGOSY MAKES THAT LOOK LIKE A ROWING
             BOAT. SHE STANDS LIKE AN ENDLESS STRETCH OF
             ELASTIC 917 FT. LONG, 120FT. WIDE AND 66FT DEEP,
             WITH ENOUGH ROOM ON HER DECKS TO SWALLOW UP NEARLY
             THREE FOOTBALL PITCHES.
                  EVERY SINGLE PIECE OF DRAG CHAIN ON THE WHOLE
             OF THE RIVER TYNE, 1,250 TONS OF IT, IS BEING
             BERGED AND BORROWED TO CONTROL HER GRAND SLAM
             ENTRY INTO THE RIVER WHEN LAUNCHED BY LADY
             BRIDGEMAN (WIFE OF SIR MAURICE BRIDGEMAN, CHAIRMAN
             OF BP). EVEN THEN SHE WILL HAVE ONLY 25 YARDS -
             LITTLE MORE THAN A CRICKET PITCH LENGTH - IN WHICH
             TO AVOID HITTING THE RIVER'S OPPOSITE BANK.
                  THE "BRITISH ARGOSY" WILL BE ONLY THE SECOND
             BRITISH SHIP OF 100,000 TONS TO BE LAUNCHED, TO
             DATE. HER SISTER SHIP, BRITISH ADMIRAL, WAS
             LAUNCHED FROM VICKERS ARMSTRONG'S BARROW YARD
             LAST YEAR BY THE QUEEN.
             PHOTO SHOWS:
                  THE GIGANTIC "BRITISH ARGOSY"
                  (100,000 TONS D.W.) DOMINATES HOUSES
                  NEAR THE SHIP YARD.

THIS SPELLE
BECAUSE a handful of farmers
have been working a dis-
honest fiddle, thousands of
nimals must suffer agonies of
pain.
So forget the tigers and crocodiles of India for
moment and come along with me to the cattle
markets of Britain.
There you will see men armed with what look like
ver-size railway ticket
bunches. But these instru-
nents punch holes HALF AN
NCH wide in the ears of
igs and sheep.
The hole is punched im-
nediately an animal is sold. It
proves that a Government sub-
idy has been paid.
If there were no such mark,
inscrupulous farmers or
cattle-dealers could put animals
through the market again—
and collect more subsidies—
about 15s. for each pig or sheep.

Healed up
Up to a short time ago, the
punch used for piercing the
animals' ears was very much
smaller and less painful.
But a Ministry of Agri-
culture official noticed
that the wound quickly
healed and some ani-
mals were being sold over
and over again. So the
new, bigger torture-punch
was introduced.
Its use is backed by the
Government, accepted by the

Is this ghastly "ticket punch" the ONLY way of branding animals at market?
Must they be mutilated like this pig's ear (left)?

As the clock in the
square chimed out 10.30
a.m. the auctioneer climbed a
plank above a pen of pigs
and quietly called for bids.
They were quickly sold
and were moved to the next pen,
raising his voice now. I soon found
out why.
cattle dealers, and tolerated
uneasily by the R.S.P.C.A.—be-
cause no one can think of any
better way of marking the
animals.
But, every day, onlookers at
the markets recoil in horror at
the tortured squeals and spilled
blood of the "branded" live-
stock.
Last week I visited the cattle
market at the picturesque
Devonshire town of Newton
Abbot.

Screams, blood...
Into the first pen had gone
the ear-punching machine; sud-
denly, there were screams of
pain. The pigs scurried about
in fear. The blood flowed. A
man moved on to the next
batch.
He was 39-year-old Ivor Dore.
"Of course, it hurts the
animals" he told me. "And I
don't mind telling you it's not
a pleasant job. At holiday
times, in particular, tourists
think I'm cruel and call me
names.
"I try not to tear the
animals' ears but often they
struggle. I keep the machine
well oiled so I can make the
hole as quickly as possible."
I spoke to some farmers. "It
looks worse than it really is,"
said one of them, "It's only
like having a tooth out." With-
out anaesthetic.
The market manager, Mr.
C. H. Wilkinson, told me: "We
have two inspectors on duty to
see there is no undue ill-treat-
ment of animals. As for the
marking of animals, well, that's
not our choice. Until the
Ministry changes the method
there's little we can do."
Well, what does the Ministry
of Agriculture say?
"We agree that there may
be pain at the time of
punching, but veterina-
geons assure us it is tem-
porary.
"It is the Ministry
had to increase the
hole, but it was done
to prevent fraud from
Government."
Now the Ministry
seeking an alternative
method of marking, and will
recommend to the
Ministry.
"But it is clear this
method that causes pain
and foolproof, the farmers
told me.

This is
"We are by no means happy
about this ear-punching
because of so much dis-
honest practice, the farmers
must be something to be."
So that's the position. Farmers
can't be trusted. And animals
must suffer.
If the animal's ear is to be
marked, then surely the
Ministry, the farmers and the
veterinary surgeons can, as a
matter of urgency find a new,
new and painless way of
doing it.

BRITAIN                          our wheat harvest for 1943 which is

                                     If all goes well with the weather, it
                                   will be the biggest harvest ever garnered
                                   in Great Britain. The fact that this sum-
                                   mer has alternated between rain and sun-

                                   sufficiently here and there simultaneously
                                   to give the overworked harvesters a
                                   chance to gather it in good time.
                                     Today, Great Britain is growing two-
                                   thirds of her own food. Since the outbreak
A BUMPER                         of war we have ploughed up six million
                                   extra acres, and the Minister of Agricul-
                                   ture asks for yet another 500,000 acres in
                                   1943.
                                     Such is the magnitude of our harvest
                                   that the increased food production for
                                   1942 will save at least five million tons of
HARVEST                          shipping for other vital purposes.
                                     If the promise of Britain's 1943 harvest

                                   of between five and six million tons per

Milk production has been maintained
despite the many wartime difficulties of
food, labour and transport.
All this has been accomplished by the
help of a volunteer labour force gathered
from every strata of society. The call
for landworkers to bring in this bumper
harvest has reached drawing-rooms,
offices, factories and schools everywhere.
The next four weeks will see a race
against time to gather the harvest in its
best condition, and to protect it from
enemy air raids.
There are the Volunteer Land Clubs,
the Women's Emergency Volunteer Land
Corps, soldiers, sailors, airmen, police-
men, firemen, even prisoners of war—all
helping to bring home the harvest. The
countryside is filled with volunteers on
the land. Every inn and farmhouse occu-
pied to the full.

comes news of other bumper harvests
to sustain the United Nations in war. In
the ten Great Plains States of the United
States of America the production of small
grains alone is expected to total about
twenty-nine million tons as compared
with nine million tons in 1934.
Canada's harvest is reported to be a
new record of increased production. In
Russia, however, what was planned to be
a mighty harvest had been sadly depleted

           I have come to this conclusion after a
heart to heart talk with technicians who have
brought shaving to a fine art—with men who have
spent a lifetime in studying beards and their growth.
Hundreds of thousands of pounds have been spent

pluck out the average human whisker," the chief

a

   "In peace time the average user obtained six to

SHELLS IN THE BATTLE AGAINST FEVER
April 28th 1959 PAR 77114-3 (PNR-R)

SHELLS IN THE BATTLE AGAINST FEVER

Amid glittering metal and glass, breathing
'sterile' air and in clothing of surgical
cleanliness, men and women laboratory
workers are producing vaccines to combat
polio and other scourges of mankind and
of animals in new buildings at the
Wellcome Research Laboratories, Beckenham,
Kent, where on May 1 the first two stages
of the three-stage five-year development
plan for the Laboratories will be
officially opened by Sir Henry Dale,
OM, FRS, Chairman of the Wellcome Trust.
Work is already in full swing in the new
buildings, and the Polio building -
Phase I of the scheme - is helping
doctors to cope with the present rush of
young people for inoculation by exceeding
its production target of four million
doses a year.
The development plan for the Laboratories
was begun in 1955 to provide up-to-date
facilities for research and the production
of biological products. When completed,
it will have cost over £2,000,000.
PICTURE SHOWS:- Masked women in sterile
clothing harvesting virus infected chick
embryo for yellow fever vaccine
at Beckenham.

                                    Mount Pleasant, South Ruislip, Middlesex,
                                    is occupied only by 72-year-old Mr. Jacob
                                    James Harris, at a controlled rent of
                                    £2 0s 3d a week.
                                    His landlords are H. W. Cutler Property
                                    and Development Co. Ltd., of which 54-
                                    year-old Mr. Horace W. Cutler is a
                                    director. He is also chairman of the
                                    Conservative-controlled Greater London
                                    Council's Housing Committee, Britain's
                                    biggest landlord.

                                    No. 21, Mount Pleasant, is damp, shabby
                                    and neglected. Roof tiles are missing, gut-
                                    ters are rotting, paint is peeling. Hilling-
                                    don Council ordered the landlords to make
                                    it fit for human habitation by November
                                    23, 1967.
                                    "I could, of course, afford to carry out
                                    the work," bearded Mr. Cutler told me last
                                    week at his office in High Street, Pinner,
                                    Middlesex. "And I may yet do so.
                                    "But all over the country thousands of
                                                                        houses are falling into
                                                                        decay because of the
                                                                        stupidity of the Rent Acts,
                                                                        and that is my point."
                                                                        Mr. Cutler's refusal to
                                                                        carry out repairs is being
                                                                        made in protest against the
                                                                        Rent Acts which, he says,
                                                                        force landlords to spend
                                                                        large sums on repairs with-
                                                                        out any hope of return
                                                                        where rents are controlled
                                                                        and tenants are protected
                                                                        from eviction.

                                                                        'Too large'

                                                                        "Another tragic result of our
                                                                        present laws is underoccupation.
                                                                        It is ridiculous for a house of
                                                                        this size to be occupied by only
                                                                        one man.
                                                                        "Mr. Harris uses only the
                                                                        kitchen and one bedroom. The
                                                                        house is now far too large for
                                                                        Mr. Harris. He should be re-
                                                                        housed by the council."
                                                                        Mr. Cutler, a former mayor
                                                                        of Harrow, said he sympathised
                                                                        with Mr. Harris, who suffers
                                                                        from pneumoconiosis and whose
                                                                        only income is a £4 10s. a week
                                                                        pension.
                                                                        "With this chest trouble I
                                                                        cannot stand the cold," Mr.
                                                                        Harris said. "The house is
                                                                         chilly and damp. I keep wait-
                                                                        ing for the house to be put
                                                                        right."
                                                                        Mr. Harris moved into the
                                                                        house in 1940. Since his wife
                                                                        died several years ago he has
                                                                        lived there alone.
                                                                        Last year Mr. Harris was
                                                                        offered a place in an old
                                                                        people's home run by the
                                                                        council. "He refused it,"
                                                                        said Alderman A. J. Beasley, of
                                                                        Hillingdon Council, "as he is
                                                                        perfectly entitled to do."

The evidence: Betsy's seven-yolk egg

UNTIL yesterday no
one had very much
respect for the
chicken as a person-
ality.
It was, if it was
worth considering, the
symbol of the coward.
Although even that
symbolism was gradu-
ally being taken away
from it, cowards hav-
ing gained prestige
since they were up-
graded to anti-heroes.
What happened yes-
terday was, quite sim-
ply, the news about
Betsy. She (you cannot
call a chicken like
Betsy an it, and this is
a measure of what
Betsy has accomplished
for chickens every-
where) laid an egg
containing seven yolks.
It had never, as far
as was known, been
done before. Septuplets
are as rare among
chickens as they are
among humans.
But it wasn't the
purely biological aspect
of Betsy's achievement
that so impressed the
world. It was the tim-
ing of this exceptional
feat of productivity.
We British regard
ourselves as sophisti-
cated, but we are as
simple as a tribe when it
comes to seizing on an
event which sums up our
national predicament.
Here we were wallowing
in a great mass of words
from our leaders about
the economic situation,
when Betsy came along
to express the solution in
a simple, forceful gesture.
Where there was one,
Betsy seemed to be
saying, let there be seven.
How was she to be
rewarded?
The solution she had
provided to one problem
seemed to pose another.
For there could be no
material favours granted
in the period of the
freeze, not even where it
was related to produc-
tivity.
Betsy, it seemed, would
have to continue to
manage with chicken-
feed.
Perhaps one of the new
honours that are soon to
be announced will take
care of the matter.
What of Betsy's posi-
tion in regard to organ-
ised labour?
For this is the remark-
able truth: she is a free
enterprise chicken, out-
side the well regulated
authority of the Egg
Board. She carries no
card.
It will be interesting to
see what Mr. Macleod
makes of that.
Of course, there will be
knockers ready to dis-
parage Betsy's achieve-
ment.
What meaning, they
will say, has one isolated
example of productivity
to a nation which needs
a consistent pattern of
growth?
Answer these cynics,
Betsy, as only you can.
You must do it again.

A THOUSAND policemen last night fought a vicious
pitched battle with a screaming 2,000 - strong mob
trying to storm St. Pancras Town Hall. It was violence
such as London has not seen since the hunger marches
of the 'thirties.

Time and again, lines of 50 constables, waving truncheons, charged
the solid mass of people. Women and children fell to the ground whimper-
ing hysterically. The roads around the town hall were like a battlefield.
And above the screams and shouts was heard the clang of ambulance bells.

Some people said that, after day-long taunts,
abuse and violence against the police, some of the
constables suddenly cracked.

Early today the hospitals were totting up the
casualty list. At least 14 people were injured, in-
cluding six policemen. Sixteen men and a youth
were arrested.

The fantastic, frightening scene flared after demon-
strators outside the two rebel blocks of council flats-
Silverdale House and Kennistoun House-joined forces
and marched on the town hall in a massive, anti-rent
increase protest.

A council committee meeting was hurriedly aban-
doned and hundreds of police reinforcements were
rushed in.

There were roars of anger
when the procession found
themselves facing a
three-deep line of police in
front of the town hall.

Down a half-dozen side-streets
squads of 50 to 100 policemen
were waiting in reserve.

The marchers fell back for a
few seconds, surprised at the
sight of so many police.

Then from the rows behind
the leaders came cries of "For-
ward, forward!"

Thus started a headlong on-
slaught by about 200 of the
young men among the marchers
against the centre of the long
line of police.

An inspector standing on a
bus yelled to the men:
"Stand fast lads, stand
fast."

The last of a group of
demonstrators perched
on a window-sill over-
looking the battle of St.
Pancras is dislodged,
protesting loudly. It is a
woman in slacks. Police
reach out as she drops,
then turn to continue the
struggle.

Chin in hand, Mr. Bressington (centre) taking it easy yesterday
AGAINST his nature
Trevor Bressington be-came one of Lord Robens' absentees yesterday.

Instead of going down the 880 yards into Cwm Colliery, near Pontypridd, South Wales, he was asleep in bed.

After 42 years in the pits he has dust on his chest, and a pain across his back which he thinks may be a slipped disc or a chill on his kidneys.

By staying at home in Beddau he joined the 40 per cent. of the coalface workers who failed to arrive for work at Cwm Colliery.

Everyone, except the Coal Board takes the absentee situa-tion philosophically.

SCRAPHEAP

Mr. Bressington, at 56, is still a good worker. He is a member of the pit consultative com-mittee, an apprentice training officer, and he does not like to miss a day's work.

But he—and many others of his age—are finding one thing.
BY JOHN DODD

£10 10s. a week. It is too big a drop from the £19 I get for five shifts at the coal-face.”

In his 42 years down the mines he has lost three close friends in accidents, and nearly died in one himself.

Yesterday, when he should have been working, he sat in a club with other miners, drinking pints and telling stories. Why
weren't the others working? One woke up late, two were on holiday, and two more were suffering from “bumps” and were off sick.

Today Mr. Bressington will be back at work. “Back with the 'donkeys' and the machines.”

Last week Lord Robens, the Coal Board chairman, con-demned absenteeism in the pits as a “national malaise.” He said that voluntary absen-teeism cost the Board the equivalent of 27,000 men's work last year.
They cannot keep up the pace. His union secretary, Mr. Bryn Williams, says: “In the old days a man was on the scrap heap at 45 but he could do his work at his own pace. Now he is expected to keep up with a machine until he is 65.

“They took the horses out of the pits and left the donkeys.” The “donkeys” at Cwm are men—numbering 1,400. Accord-ing to Mr. Williams more than 100 wear belts to support slipped discs in their backs, and 400 are suffering from dust, ranging from 10 to 60 per cent. dis-ability.

EXCUSE

He would rather smother his grandchildren than let them go down the pit.

Mr. Bressington says there are several reasons why men don't go to work on Mondays.

Some have to get up at 4.30 am. to travel 10 miles to the pit; some are fed up with chang-ing jobs down the pit. Others, like him, are feeling the pace of trying to keep up with machines.

And there are those who, if they miss a shift, earn as much from the sickness and compen-sation benefits. He says the best excuse is an accident down the pit.

WORST

Cwm Colliery's absentee figures are among the worst in South Wales. Yesterday 27.8 per cent. of the overall staff failed to turn up, something like 400 out of 1,400.

Production at the colliery averages 26 cwt. per man-shift, compared with a national aver-age of 34. The geographical conditions are partly to blame.

MR. CHARLES PIKE - who
fitted the nut that caused
rt, the disaster - said last
as' night: "I feared every
oal knock at the door.
"Although I knew I was free
of blame, something kept
pricking me which said I had
caused it all."
He added: "I have not been
able to settle down to anything
since, not even a job. My wife
is on the verge of a nervous
breakdown."
Mr. Pike, a 49-year-old
labourer and experienced pipe
fitter, was cleared of any blame
by the inquiry.
The brass nut he had fitted in
the flat which blew up and sent
the others crashing was a faulty
one.
It was sold to him by the Gas
Board so that he could connect
the gas supply to a new cooker
bought by Miss Hodge, one of his
friends.
The nut, 1¼ inches in diameter
and worth less than a penny,
was faulty in three ways-the
depth of chamfer, the thickness
of flange, and the diameter of
the bore recess.
Yesterday a massive hunt was

The nut that caused the blast

under way to find thousands
of similar nuts which may have
been fitted in up to 200,000
homes in the North Thames Gas
Board area - the only area
involved.
Nine other nuts on cookers in
the London area have been
found to be defective in pattern,
though not cracked, like the
one at Ronan Point, it was
learned yesterday.
The board put an immediate
ban on the issue of nuts of the
faulty type the moment the
fault was discovered. Instruc-
tions have been given to the
board's fitters - who make an
average of 6,000 visits a day -
to check the connection if there
is a gas cooker on the premises,
no matter what the main pur-
pose of their call.
If the connector has a
"danger" nut it will be
changed.
Later, Mr. Pike-he lives 100
yards from the wrecked block
of flats-said: "A good deed has
wrecked my life. I'll never fit
another gas cooker as long as
I live."

-the collapse of one flat on top of another. If they are, the
building must be strengthened, and the gas supply cut off

FARM-WORKER Leonard
Algar claims a housing
record of his own.
In the little village of Carl-
ton Colville, near Lowestoft,
stands a well-built house, with
three bedrooms, three rooms
downstairs, bathroom, elec-
tricity, hot and cold water, and
three-quarters of an acre of
garden.

Built more than fourteen
months ago, this house is be-
lieved to be the first to be
erected under the Govern-
ment's scheme which helps
farm workers to have houses
built for themselves on their
own land.

Over their own front gate the
Algars chat with Farmer
Newson.

DAILY
18 FEB 1950
HERALD

His employer, Farmer Stan-
ley Newson, of Grove Farm,
told me about it. "Leonard
bought the land, had the house
built, and got married," he
said. "I think a lot of farm
workers would do the same if
they knew that the facilities
were available."
"What are these facilities?"

Up to 85 per cent. of the total
cost of building a house can be
borrowed at the rate of 3½ per
cent. interest, repayable within
30 years.
For example, if the house

cost £1,100 (the price Leonard
paid for his) as much as £935
could be borrowed, if necessary.
The cost of interest and re-
payment over this period would
then average less than £1 per
week, and less still, of course,
if the sum borrowed were
smaller.

SE 15/8x 2/2 PZ (DH)

The scheme also provides an
annual grant, increased by the
Labour Government to £15 for
40 years, a total of £600, for all
such houses occupied by farm
workers.
And no development charges
are made where these houses
are concerned.
The first step for a farm
worker to take is to apply to
the clerk of his rural district
council. Those councils that
administer the Small Dwellings
Acquisition Act, which deals
with this matter, should pro-
perly give priority in the grant-
ing of building licences to men
working on the land.
The farm worker who is a
member will find that his
union is always ready to help

PRESS INFORMATION

SUN EDITORIAL DEPT.
FROM BTR INDUSTRIES LIMITED

BTR REINFORCED PLASTICS LIMITED DEVELOP 3,000 GALLON
UNDERGROUND PETROL STORAGE TANK FOR ESSO

        In recent years the larger oil companies have been seeking ways
of increasing safety and cutting storage costs for petroleum spirit.
One of the major elements in the storage costs is the tank itself, and
also its concrete encasement.
Industries.. Plastics.
        Working to a specification from Esso Petroleum Company Limited,
BTR Reinforced Plastics Limited have developed a 3,000 gallon, glass
reinforced plastic, underground storage tank measuring 7ft. in diameter,
by 13ft. long, constructed entirely of Deeglas glass fibre and Artrite
polyester resins. The glass reinforced plastic construction of this
tank shows considerable advantages over other forms of storage tanks.
It resists bacterial and acid attack and will neither corrode nor leak.
It has a low installation cost, and because of its comparative light
weight, savings are made both in transportation and handling charges.

        Tests have been carried out by Esso Petroleum and the Battersea
College of Technology with the tank above-ground in a testing frame, and
buried in the ground to simulate all loadings to which the tank would be
subjected in service. The results show that the tank would be satisfactory
when installed in a simple excavation, and back-filled. In normal practice
where a tank is installed under the forecourt of a service station it is
protected by a 9-inch re-inforced concrete slab. To test the effect of
normal vehicle loadings the road slab was deliberately made weaker, and
the tank successfully withstood the abnormal stresses.

        These tanks can be made in sizes from 2,000 to 5,000 gallons
capacity, and in single and multiple compartment versions.

CAPTION: Technicians at the BTR Reinforced Plastics Limited, Camberley,
Surrey, factory assembling a 3,000 gallon glass reinforced plastic petrol
storage tank. This has recently undergone extensive testing by the Esso
Petroleum Company Limited, and the Battersea College of Technology.

23rd August, 1965

INDIA'S GREATEST RAILWAY TERMINI TRANSFORMED INTO
CAMPING GROUND FOR 6,000 MUSLIMS
18.10.47

India's greatest railway termini, Victoria Terminus
and Bombay Central in Bombay, have been transformed
overnight into camping grounds for 6,000 Muslims as
the sweeping tides of displaced minority peoples glow
in terror between India and Pakistan.
Eight men have died, children have been born and life's
entire meaning is compressed into an existence on bare
platforms and in open station enclosures between train
arrivals and departures.
They are all India Government, rail, postal, telegraphic,
income tax and customs workers, who on being given the
choice, expressed preference to work in Pakistan and are
being moved from inland Indian points to that capital
through this port.
The shift is being made by sea, but so heavy is the
rush that thousands have been inokloosed at the point of
embarkation, and have made their detraining stop their
temporary homes. Their descent on the two termini and the
natural demands have entirely dislocated sanitation and
hygiene in hitherto model and gigantic depots.

I.N.P. PHOTO SHOWS:- Some of the 6,000 Muslims who have
made India's greatest railway termini,
Victoria Terminus and Bombay Central their
temporary homes while enroute to their new
homes in Pakistan. Their descent on the two termini
and their natural demands have entirely dislocated
sanitation and hygiene in hitherto model and
gigantic depots. Eight men have died and children
have been born while thousands of people have been
crowded into primitive quarters like these. Screens
of clothing can be seen strung up to shelter the
usually screened and secluded Muslim women from a
traveller's wondering gaze.

HERALD REPORTER
VILLAGERS blinked in surprise when a 3,000-
gallon milk tanker drew up by their disused
coal mine. They wondered why. But they were
not left wondering long—for the milk was poured
to the bottom of the pit.
The tanker came again and again and the people of
Tunley, near Bath, found that their pit had been
turned into a 60,000-gallon “milk bottle.”
The tanks had been sent by the Wilts, United Dairy. Last
night a spokesman at the Trowbridge office explained:
“The pit milk was skimmed—it had been left over from
butter-making.
1 Increased production had left the company with an
abnormally large amount of skimmed milk on its hands.
2 There was a lack of demand for tinned condensed
skimmed milk.
3 Transport and other difficulties make it impossible to get
rid of all the skimmed milk to farmers and others who
could use it for animal fattening.
1954-709-1
“We are not allowed by law
to sell it as a liquid for human
consumption,” added the spokes-
man.
‘IN DEMAND’
A Ministry of Agriculture
official commented: “Skimmed
milk is a most important contri-
bution to the feeding of calves
and is much in demand. This
is the first we have heard of this
case and inquiries will surely be
made.”
And a local farmer thought
that many pig-keepers would be
glad to have the skimmed milk
delivered to their farms.
He pointed out that the
tankers were travelling more
than 20 miles—from Trowbridge
— “They might just as well be
using the petrol and labour to
bring it to the farmers.”
In Tunley, the villagers shake
their heads.
FUMES?
Mrs. Eileen Palmer, a miner’s
wife, said: “Surely something
better could be done with it?
One of my children brought
some home and it made a very
nice rice pudding.”
Mrs. Ethel Benwell, a village
shopkeeper, asked: “What about
the fumes when all that milk
goes sour?”
The point was put to a Coal
Board official. If there was any
unpleasant smell, he said, “no
doubt the villagers of Tunley
will get in touch with us.”

THE WORLD'S OUR MARKET FOR CARPETS.
18.3.46.
The famous Royal Wilton Carpet Factory was founded in the
17th century near Salisbury in a district noted for its
weaving since Elizabethan days. The factory received its
Royal Charter from William of Orange in 1701 and shortly
after, two Frenchmen, Anthony Dufessy and Peter Jemavie,
were said to have been smuggled over from France in
barrels to take charge of the factory. These Continental
weavers were masters of their trade, and the smuggling of
them was necessary owing to the strict laws of France
against craftsmen taking away the secrets of their trades
to foreign countries.
Hand-made carpets have been made at Wilton for many
important buildings in this country and throughout the
world, and now that the factory is released from war work,
it is busy on order from the United States, Canada and
South America etc. This picture taken recently at the
factory shows
Girls putting the finishing touches to handmade carpets

        TWENTY MINUTES after a gas fitter left a semi-detached house
        yesterday it blew up, killing the 74-year-old owner and injuring
        his wife.
        Retired gardener Tom Kearly was buried beneath the debris for
        an hour before being pulled free by firemen, police and workmen.

        He died on the way to
        Ashford Hospital, in Mid-
        dlesex.
        Mr. Kearly's 73-year-old
        wife Mabel was trapped be-
        neath a pile of bricks after
        the blast at their home in
        Spelthorne Lane, Ashford.
        She kept crying: 'Get me out,
        get me out,' as rescuers fought
        to lift the debris.
        Finally, a mobile crane being
        used by 40 workmen behind the
        house pulled Mrs. Kearly clear.

        BATHROOM

        She was treated on the spot
        for severe burns and cuts by a
        doctor and nurses from Ashford
        Hospital.
        Mrs. Kearly was taken to West
        Middlesex Hospital. Last night
        a spokesman there said she was
        on the "danger list."
        The blast hurled dozens of
        bricks into the kitchen of the
        Kearlys' next door neighbour,
        Mrs. Pamela Dear, who had
        been washing up with her five-
        year-old son Christopher only
        minutes before.
        Said Mrs. Dear: 'I had sent
        Chris into the front room to
        play and I was in the bath-
        room. It's just as well I did.'
        Mr. Fred English, a 58-year-
        old electrical contractor, whose
        house adjoins the Kearey home,
        said: 'It was just like a bomb
        going off. I was almost knocked
        down the stairs.'

        GAS COOKER

        A spokesman for the North
        Thames Gas Board said a full
        investigation was being made
        into the cause of the explosion.
        It is understood that the gas
        fitter had been to the house to
        repair a wash boiler and to
        move a gas cooker.

        An elderly couple were found
        dead in a gas-filled room at
        their home in Bridge Road,
        Uxbridge, Middlesex, 34 years
        after the gas supply was dis-
        connected.
        The gas that killed 76-year-old
        Harold Wilson and his 81-year-
        old wife Annie came from a leak
        in a gas pipe that had rusted,
        the Uxbridge inquest was told.
        Verdict: Accident.

Betsy yesterday, proud symbol of free-enterprise productivity.
Picture by Ron Burton

1966 - 2820

UNTIL yesterday no
one had very much
respect for the
chicken as a person-
ality.

It was, if it was
worth considering, the
symbol of the coward.
Although even that
symbolism was gradu-
ally being taken away
from it, cowards hav-
ing gained prestige
since they were up-
graded to anti-heroes.

What happened yes-
terday was, quite sim-
ply, the news about
Betsy. She (you cannot
call a chicken like
Betsy an it, and this is
a measure of what
Betsy has accomplished
for chickens every-
where) laid an egg
containing seven yolks.

It had never, as far
as was known, been
done before. Septuplets
are as rare among

chickens as they are
among humans.
But it wasn't the
purely biological aspect
of Betsy's achievement
that so impressed the
world. It was the tim-
ing of this exceptional
feat of productivity.
We British regard
ourselves as sophisti-
cated, but we are as
simple as a tribe when it
comes to seizing on an
event which sums up our
national predicament.
Here we were wallowing
in a great mass of words
from our leaders about
the economic situation,
when Betsy came along
to express the solution in
a simple, forceful gesture.
Where there was one,
Betsy seemed to be
saying, let there be seven.
How was she to be
rewarded?
The solution she had
provided to one problem
seemed to pose another.
For there could be no
material favours granted
in the period of the
freeze, not even where it

was related to produc-
tivity.
Betsy, it seemed, would
have to continue to
manage with chicken-
feed.

Perhaps one of the new
honours that will soon
be announced will take
care of the matter.
What of Betsy's posi-
tion in regard to organ-
ised labour?
For this is the remark-
able truth: she is a free
enterprise chicken, out-
side the well regulated
authority of the Egg
Board. She carries no
card.
It will be interesting to
see what Mr. Macleod
makes of that.
Of course, there will be
knockers ready to dis-
parage Betsy's achieve-
ment.
What meaning, they
will say, has one isolated
example of productivity
to a nation which needs
a consistent pattern of
growth?
Answer these cynics
Betsy, as only you can.
You must do it again.

WEEP
FOR YOUR
OLD
WILLOW
PLATE
By Robert Bickford
A DINNER PLATE which
tells a fairy tale of young
love and parental wrath—
the world-famous Willow
Pattern—is threatened with
extinction.
The old plates will gradu-
ally disappear until they are
collectors' pieces. But the
story, told to generations of
children, will live on.
That "ancient Chinese legend"
began in the English potteries
during an 18th-century craze
for Oriental knick-knacks.
This delicate Oriental-style
crockery will no longer be pro-
duced by Coalport China Ltd.,
the Stoke-on-Trent firm which
introduced it to the world in
1772.
An enterprising potter imitated
a well-known Cantonese design.

ELOPEMENT
It showed a mandarin's country
house. On a bridge near a
weeping willow were the ill-
starred lovers and the girl's
father.
An English magazine writer who
had been no further east than
Essex invented a story to go
with it.
It told how Li-Chi, the man-
darin's daughter, eloped with
Chang, her father's humble
secretary, and how the couple
hid from the angry old man be-
fore finding sanctuary.
Like the chinaware, the story has
been a success ever since.
Now Coalport and another firm,
The Cauldron Pottery, have
announced that they are ceas-
ing production but not going
into liquidation.
About 300 workers have been
dismissed. But Mr. Stanley
Harrison, boss of the two com-
panies, said yesterday he hoped
that another factory "with
more economic conditions"
would take over.
So someone may yet step in to
save the Willow Pattern.

THE SAD SADLER
One would think that 30-year-old Keneth Howard,
a sadler and harness maker of Framlingham,
Suffolk, would be pleased with life. He has just
commenced three months' leave from the Army, but
to Keneth this three months leave means work! From
7 in the morning until 9 at night. This work is the
accumulation of 9 months' horses collars, harness
pads, bridles, binder canvasses, the property of
local farmers. They are all waiting for his expert
hands to repair them, ready for the busy times
ahead.
Nine months ago Keneth Howard ended another such
3 months leave as he did in 1941. Farming equipment
is even more important today than it was then.
The Suffolk War Agricultural Committee were responsible
for obtaining Keneth his leave, but the 3 months
granted is not sufficient time for Keneth to get
through the work owing to the fact that new harness
is almost non existent and the harness now in use
is in poor condition. By the time Keneth gets
through with them his 3 months is up, leaving no
time to cope with the binder canvasses that will be
needed to gather the coming harvest.
What worries Keneth is the fact that 3½ years ago
he enlisted as a sadler and up till now he has not
even seen an Army horse, let alone a set of harness!
The Howard's have been sadler and harness makers
since 1853 in and around Framlingham, so Keneth feels
he would be of more use if left to carry on. The
Howards at one time employed 2 harness makers. These
went when the war came. His mother carried on the
business when his father died ten years ago. He is
now the sole worker.
He has a brother in the R.A.F. and two of his sisters
are nursing. His job in the Army is repairing
equipment.
O.P.S.1. Keneth Howard re-padding with rye straw
one of the many collars. These he also covers with
wool blanket cloth; a repair usually lasts two
years.

HIGHEST INDUSTRIALISED FLATS IN THE MIDLANDS

The Bison Wall Frame industrialised building system of high
flat construction has been chosen for two 24-storey skyscraper blocks
to be erected for the City of Leicester Corporation. These will be
the highest 'factory-made' blocks of flats to be built in the Midlands.
They will contain 264 one-bedroom flats, with six flats on each floor.
The contract is valued at £861,751 for the complete development, including
a car park.

Concrete Limited, manufacturers of the Bison Wall Frame system,
will begin erection early in 1965. Production of the concrete components -
a Bison Wall Frame flat comprises 25 separate units - will be carried out
in the factory of Concrete (Midlands) Limited at Lichfield.

The Bison Wall Frame system has been used for multi-storey flats
in the Midlands at Birmingham, Kidderminster, Rugby, Bilston, Lichfield
and Willenhall, as well as on many other sites in England and Scotland.
Already 75 blocks on 30 sites have been either completed, started or
ordered amounting to nearly 5,000 flats. The total cost is almost £14
millions. Current production of Bison Wall Frame flats is now running
at a rate of 4,000 flats per annum.

Concrete Limited have factories at Hounslow, Tilbury, Iver,
Lichfield, Leeds, Falkirk, and another under construction at Winsford,
Cheshire.

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION MONDAY'S EVENINGS JULY 18th 1949.
BRITAIN LEADS WORLD IN MOTOR RUSTPROOFING TECHNIQUE
JS 18.7.49.
Morris cars coming off the assembly lines at Cowley, Oxfordshire,
are now receiving a 100% anti-rust treatment from a special plant
known as the "Rotodip" which, as rated in conjunction with one of
the most up-to-date paint plants, forms an engineering project in
which Britain leads the whole world. Until the advent of this new
technique the procedure for finishing car bodies was to first
to thoroughly clean down the body to remove all grease, and to
finally rinse by hand or automatic spray, followed by a drying
process, after which the primer and finish coats or paints were
added by spray gun. This method, however, did not give complete-
protection because many important parts of the body were never
reached.

Now the bodies go through the plant which consists of a tunnel
some 20 feet square and 300 feet long, which they enter in the
plain steel, greasy state, and emerge some 1½ hours later having
been cleaned, rustproofed, and primer-painted inside and out,
entirely automatically. For their journey through the plant, the
bodies are mounted on a revolving spit with the bonnet, wings and
boot in position but spaced-inch from the body to allow free
circulation, and is then carried broadside through the length of
the plant on conveyor chains in such a way that the body revolves
on its own axis while passing through the machine. The process
is in two stages - first rustproofing by cleaning, rinsing and
proofing for which the bodies pass through six large tanks, and
secondly, primer-painting during which the body is dried in an
oven, cooled down, and painted.
This series of pictures illustrates the remarkable process which
the Morris engineers are confident will protect the bodies
against corrosion and paint flaking.

WHICH RESTRICTS THE MOVEMENT OF THE BUOY AT ALL STATES
OF THE TIDE.
THE HOSES FROM THE BUOY ARE BOLTED TO PIPES SECURED
TO THE ANCHOR BOX. BY EMPLOYING THIS ARRANGEMENT THE FLEXIB-
LE HOSES ARE KEPT AS SHORT AS POSSIBEL AND ARE AT ALL
TIMES CLEARR OF THE SEABED, THUS AVOIDING DETERIORAATION
AND WEAR. THE PENDANTS ARE LED THROUGH THE BUOY WELL WITHIN
ITS DIAMETER TO THE ANCHORBOX. CONSEQUENTLY IT IS NOT
POSSIBLE FOR A VESSEL'S HULL TO FOUL THEM SHOULD IT HUG
THE BUOY AT CHANGES OF TIDE.
IF THE EXPERIMENTS PROVE TO BE SUCCESSFUL THE
BUOY COULD BE USED IN AREAS WHERE IT IS NOT POSSIBLE TO
CONSTRUCT CONVENTIONAL BERTHS AND WHERE THERE IS
INSUFFICIENT DEPTH OF WATER AT EXISTING BERTHS A BUOY
MAY BE SITED IN DEEPER WATER TO ACCOMMODATE THE LARGER
VESSELS.

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION MONDAY'S EVENINGS JULY 18th 1949.
BRITAIN LEADS WORL IN MOTOR RUSTPROOFING TECHNIQUE
JS 18.7.49.

Morris cars coming off the assembly lines at Cowley, Oxfordshire,
are now receiving a 100% anti-rust treatment from a special plant
known as the "Rotodip" which, operated in conjunction with one of
the most up-to-date paint plants, forms an engineering project in
which Britain leads the whole world. Until the advent of this new
technique the procedure for finishing car bodies was to first
to thoroughly clean down the body to remove all grease, and to
finally rinse by hand or automatic spray, followed by a drying
process, after which the primer and finish coats of paints were
added by spray gun. This method, however, did never give complete
protection because many important parts of the body were never
reached.

Now the bodies go through the plant which consists of a tunnel
some 20 feet square and 300 feet long, which they enter in the
plain steal, greasy state, and emerge some 1½ hours later having
been cleaned, rustproofed, and primer-painted inside and out,
entirely automatically. For their journey through the plant, the
bodies are mounted on a revolving spit with the bonnet, wings and
boot in position but spaced-inch from the body to allow free
circulation, and is then carried broadside through the length of
the plant on conveyor chains in such a way that the body revolves
on its own axis while passing through the machine. The process
is in two stages - first rustproofing by cleaning, rinsing and
proofing for which the bodies pass through six large tanks, and
secondly, primer-painting during which the body is dried in an
oven, cooled down, and painted.
This series of pictures illustrates the remarkable process which
the Morris engineers are confident will protect the bodies
against corrosion and paint flaking.

Police chief
hurt in riot

TWO HUNDRED police battled with demonstrators
outside a factory last night. Nine demonstrators
were arrested and three policemen were injured.
One of the injured police-
men was 52-year-old Mr.
Tom Walker, deputy chief
constable of Stockport,
Cheshire.
He was taken to hospital
with a broken arm and a
chest injury.
The battle between police
and demonstrators started
outside the Roberts-Arundel
factory at Stockport during
a union protest meeting
against "American
methods."
Tempers flared among the
1,000 at the meeting after
union officials claimed that
automated production
methods introduced at the
American-owned factory
were "a threat to British
trade unionism."
Later, as the crowd surged
towards the factory gates
which were guarded by
police, union officials ap-
pealed for order.

PICKETS
Mr. Walter Burke, the
shop stewards' convenor at
the factory, said : “The
trouble started because the
police shoved our lads
against the wall when they
were trying to picket em-
ployees coming out of the
factory.
“If we had been allowed
to talk to the people at the
factory there would have
been no fuss. But police
came here determined not to
let us near them.”
Mr. Burke added: “Six
policemen got hold of one
lad, pulled him by the
hair and banged his head
on the police van door. Then
they flung him into the van.”
Disputes began at the fac-
tory 18 months ago when it
was taken over by an Ameri-
can textile firm.
In November 140 men
went on strike and were
dismissed by the firm.
Then the A.E.U. declared
the firm “black.” Union
pickets have been on duty
outside the factory gates for
12 weeks.

CHELSEA, once a name to be mentioned with the Paris
Left Bank and New York's Greenwich Village, has
become too fashionable and too expensive for artists.

tery wheels and a vast assort-

make way for a block of luxury
flats.

SEVEN firemen were in
seriously, and 11 oth-

in Collier's Wood, S.W., las
Neighbouring works were
shattered. Roofs were
stripped, walls blasted and
ceilings blown down in 22
cottages.
Windows and doors caved in a
quarter of a mile away.
The firemen were fighting an
outbreak at the British Gener-
ators, Ltd., in the High-street,
when the flames spread to an
acetylene cylinder.
Sub-officer Jenkins carried the
cylinder up from the basement
into the factory yard. Thirty
seconds later it exploded.

Like a bomb
Mr. R. Robins, proprietor of the
Royal Standard Hotel, said: "The
explosion was terrific, like a
bomb."
Mr. F. H. Clements, proprietor
of the Red Lion, said: "The doors
of my Lotei 200 yards away were
blown open. The damage might
have been caused by a V2."
Hundreds of people rushed to
the works and watched as
stretcher-bearers brought out the
injured.
Frames were held up in a quarter-
mile line. One of them, which
had been emptied of its passengers
just before reaching the works,
was shattered by the explosion.
Late last night the 22 families in
damaged Waterfall Cottages were
patching their homes with wood
from the wreckage and shovelling
debris into the road.

Home gone
White-haired Mrs. L. Few
opened up her grocery shop to
supply them with new gas mantles
Caretakers of British Genera-
tors, Mr. Ron. Butler, aged 51, and
his wife, Jean, 41, who live in a
flat above the factory, lost their
home.
Next door, Mr. and Mrs. Robert
Courteen, of the Waterfall Laun-
dry, returned two hours after the
explosion to find their home and
furniture wrecked.
Leading fireman James Gibb,
who went through all the London
blitzes, found that his home in
Waterfall-road had "received as
good a blitzing as I have ever
seen."
Mrs. Louise Senior, aged 72, who
was ill in bed next door to the
factory, was buried beneath debris
but dug out uninjured.
