186475-78 HUM
THE 'CROWNING GLORY' - AS SUPPLIED BY BRITAIN'S
HEALTH SCHEME.

London: A woman's crowning glory is her hair, so the
mere male is led to believe - but like other feminine
charms these days, it may be false, in part or in whole.
Britain's comprehensive Health Service aids and abets
the deception regarding hair, and teeth, but few would
deny the benefits it confers on both male and female.
Over eight thousand people have taken advantage of free
wigs obtained under the health scheme, and although the
number of women applying is not known, a considerable
number of the applicants are believed to be women who
have lost all or part of their 'crowning glory'.
Of the applicants some 2,600 have so far been supplied
with wigs. One well-known London firm of wig-makers,
who export a considerable number of wigs to the United
States each month, have had 1,500 National Health
Service customers up to date, against their monthly
average of 50 private customers.
The making of wigs is a complicated and skilled art,
needing clever fingers and a sharp eye, for when man
competes with nature, nature usually wins, and to make
a wig which will deceive at close quarters is more than
difficult.
Most of the hair used for wig-making is obtained from
Western Europe; Italy, France and Germany contributing
a great part. Prices of the hair varies according to
the quality and colour, and this price affects the
cost of the finished wig. The most expensive wig to
buy, owing to the difficulty of obtaining the hair, is
a white one, the price of which lies between 25 and 100
pounds.
PHOTO SHOWS: With skillful hands June Jackson and Iren
Kadd knot hair into wigs. Apart from wigs supplied by
the Health Scheme and wigs for private customers, wig-
makers do a lot of work for stage and films.

Plants.. Trees.. Fruit Apples

O NE of the most pleas-
ing jobs in the garden
is picking your own
fruit. Even a small garden
should have a few apple
and pear trees.

Many gardeners, however,
make the mistake of ordering
standard or half-standard
trees, which are best suited
for an orchard.

These take up far too much
room, produce an unusable
glut of fruit and are difficult
to prune and spray.

Apple and pear trees can
now be bought to fit the space
available, thanks to modern
methods of grafting on dwarf-
ing root stocks.

Dwarf bush
Take for example apple and
pear cordon trees. These are
grown in the form of a single,
slim, main stem with short,
fruiting branches. These trees
can be planted only 3½ft.
apart, either in a row to form
a division between the flower
and vegetable garden or run-
ning alongside a path.

The next size is the dwarf
pyramid which calls for 4ft.
between trees, followed by a
dwarf bush (apples) at 12ft. to
15ft. apart or semi-dwarf bush
(apples) at 15ft. to 18ft. apart.
Having decided how many
trees you can find room for,
the next question is which
varieties to order. You can
have early, mid-season and
late-ripening.

Perhaps the most important
point to bear in mind is that
many fruit trees, certainly
apples, must have a suitable
" mate" growing nearby so
that cross-pollination of the
blossom takes place. Other-
wise little or no fruit.

126-TON 'BRABAZON' NEARS COMPLETION, WILL FLY THIS SUMMER.

Under the hands of 700 workers, the world's biggest landplane
is nearing completion at the plant of the Bristol Aeroplane
Company at Filton, Bristol.
Designed to be the aerial counterpart of the 'Queen Elizabeth' -
world's greatest ocean liner - the plane is the 'Brabazon I'
the gigantic sections of which are almost ready for final assembly.
It is expected that the 126-ton monster will take the air
for the first time in May or June and that three other
Brabazons on order will be flying on the London-New York service
of British Overseas Airways by 1950.
The Brabazon is a high-altitude, long-range low-wing cantilever
monoplane which will accommodate 70 to 100 sleeping passengers
or 120 sitting passengers in the utmost comfort. The
143-feet cabin will be pressurised to maintain an equivalent
cabin altitude of 8,000 feet while flying at 25,000 foot.
Crew will number 13, including five stewards.
Wingspan of the aircraft is 230 feet - almost twice that
of Britain's largest bomber, the Avro Lincoln - and the hoight
over the rudder is 50 foot.
Eight Bristol 'Centaurus' 18-cylinder, sleeve-valve, air-cooled
radial engines, each rated at 2,500 brake horsepower for
take-off, will give a maximum level speed of more than 300
miles an hour at 25,000 foot, an economical cruising speed
of 200 miles an hour at the same altitude, and a still-air range
of 5,000 miles. Initial service ceiling will be 25,000 foot,
increasing as fuel is consumed.
PHOTO SHOWS.- A general view in the Brabazon's workshop at
Filton. Contro foreground is one of the hugo outer wing soctions
and on right is the loading edge of the wing. Loft background
is the mighty fusolago.

34 SIPS OF
CIDER
FAIL HIM
Herald Reporter
BRISTOL, Thursday.
HARRY PHILLIPS, 58-
year-old bespectacled
boiler-maker, of Ebbw Vale,
and Monmouth County
Councillor, is a man with a
mission.
Since he took a gulp of strong
rough cider while haymaking on a
Welsh hill farm as a boy, he has
been searching for a smooth, sweet
cider.
"If only the right blend of
sweetness could be found it might
take the place of beer in all the
pubs in Monmouth," he says.

Shade too sharp
So today the Ebbw Vale boiler-
maker went to Bristol for the
annual cider-tasting day at the
Long Ashton Agricultural Re-
search station. With growers and
cider experts from all parts of the
country, he sniffed and sipped 34
glasses of sharp bitter-sweet and
sweet varieties.
Clearing his palate witt a piece
of dry biscuit after each taste, Mr.
Phillips tried hard to find his
ideal, but his taste was too dis-
cerning.
Even those with fine sounding
names such as Foxwhelp, Chisel
Jersey, Dymock Red, and Pixley
Hangdown, brought the same com-
ment. "No, it's just a shade too
sharp.fl Its the tang I don't like."

Lot to tell
Shaking his head as he left, he
said, "I've a lot to tell our educa-
tion committee, but I don't think
I found the cider I have been look-
ing for."
Prof. Bertie T. P. Barker, past
director of the Institute, told the
experts of experiments to cure
"cider sickness," which ruins the
taste and aroma of sweet cider. It
is caused by a family of microbes
which experts have been trying to
isolate since 1907.
His tip to cider makers was:
"Blend as soon as possible with
a sharp cider with a high acid
content."

8410 AND LONDON BUREAU
NEW LOOK FOR LANDMARK.
LONDON: Battersea Power Station, first modern
power station built in London and massive landmark
familiar to Continental travellers arriving at
Victoria Station, is getting a new look.......
another chimney. Towering above railway lines and
river, the chimney is rapidly stretching up to the
337 feet of its three fellows. The power station
consists of two parts. Construction of the second
part was held up by the war and post-war shortages.
The new chimney will complete this second section.
Combined capacity of the two sections will be
503,000 kilowatts.
Power Stations are often blamed for the killing smog
which grips London during the fog season. (the
City of London has decided to obtain statutory
powers to reduce smoke in the City) but Battersea
and other modern power stations can plead 'not guilty'.
The towering chimneys emit no smoke, only steam
and vapour, for they are fitted with gas washing
and grit arresting plant.
PHOTO SHOWS: The view of Battersea Power Station,
with the new chimney on the right, seen from a
nearby gasholder - the tallest in London. Landmarks
cutting the skyline (in background) are the tower of
Westminster Cathedral (left); Westminster and Big Ben
(above new chimney) and St. Paul's Cathedral (right).

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION THURSDAY'S EVENINGS, July 24th.,

SILK WORMS THAT HELP BRITAIN'S EXPORTS
24.7.47.
A small but very important aid to British export trade is
being given by about six million silk worms which are being
reared at Lullingstone Castle Silk Farm, run by ZOE, LADY
HART DYKE, near Eynsford, Kent. The aim and object of the
farm, which is now getting going again after the war, is to
develop and assist production of raw silk in this country, the
Dominions, and the Colonies, and what started off as a girl's
hobby, developed on a business footing in 1932, is now a
flourishing industry housed in one of Britain's ancient homes.
The Lullingstone silkworms are known all over the world for
millions of them have been exported, and it was from their silk
that the Coronation Robes for the Queen and the Princesses
were made. One of the difficulties at present being ex-
perienced is the lack of mulberry leaves on which to feed
the worms, for the eighteen acre plantation at Lullingstone
is only producing about half the number of leaves required
to feed six million tiny mouths.
It is interesting to note that the method of using the silk
cocoon for spinning and weaving was first known in China at
least 5,000 years B.C. It was James I who endeavoured to
encourage silk worm rearing in this country by ordering the
importation and planting of thousands of mulberry trees, but
the Royal scheme was a failure. George I then took a keen
interest in the silk industry and in 1718 he granted a
patent to a certain John Appleton for silkworm rearing.
Shaking down a batch of cocoons to find the leading
threads for the reeling machine after boiling.

SHALE FOR SITE OF NEW HOVERPORT.
Lorries unloading shale from Chislet Colliery, Kent, at Pegwell Bay
where it will be used in the construction of the new international
hoverport. Half of Chislet's north west tip (about 150,000 cubic yards)
is being removed to form the base for the 12-acre landing and
launching pad.
Both black and red shales, which conform to Ministry of Transport
specifications for general fill, are obtainable from colliery sites.
The red shale - which has been used extensively for road making - is
becoming scarce but the black shales of the type used at Pegwell Bay
are in plentiful supply.
The National Coal Board sell shale from site and contractors are
responsible for collection. Contractors operating on colliery sites
have to conform with the Board's regulations regarding work on tips, but
the Board will advise on methods of working.
More than 6 million tons of shale was sold from pithead sites last
year and the demand is increasing. A small section dealing with sales has
been set up under Mr. M. Little, Marketing Department, National Coal
Board, Hobart House, Grosvenor Place, London, S.W.1.

A "RUSH" OF BUSINESS.

MJH/S. 28.

An enterprise which is enjoying the success it
well deserves is that begun by Mrs. N.E. Franklyn
of Salisbury. Four years ago, Mrs. Franklyn had
an hour's lesson from an old man in London, who
taught her the rudiments of the art of rush weaving.
He was highly skilled, but in the time available could
only pass on a fraction of his knowledge to Mrs. Franklyn.
However, with the little she had learnt, Mrs. Franklyn
with great determination, carried on to teach herself
this ancient craft, which goes back to the time when
rushes were spread on the floor for carpeting. Then
without any capital she took a little shop in East Street
(Salisbury) where she produced such articles as waste
paper baskets, table mats, seats for chairs and stools,
baskets for `ogs, dogs, fruit etc. etc. all made from
plaited rushes. These proved so popular that her business
steadily grew until today she employs a staff of four
and is looking for larger premises. Mrs. Franklyn collects
the rushes herself, from the rivers of Dorset and elsewhere,
and she has had many ducklings when rowing or wading to
harvest them. After the rushes have been cut, they have
to be dried out before being stored for subsequent use
and must be very carefully handled to prevent damage.
As far as can be ascertained, it is believed that there are
only two other businesses like Mrs. Franklyn's in the
whole country.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: MRS. N.E. FRANKLYN seen practising
the ancient craft of rush weaving at her premises in
East Street, Salisbury, while her pet dog sits in a
basket made from rushes by his mistress. Mrs. Franklyn's wares are all in their lovely natural
colours of pastel gold green and yellow.

STRANDED EX-CONVICTS FIND A HOME IN A CHURCH
A NEW USE FOR EMPTY PEWS IN KENSINGTON

In the Royal Borough of Kensington there is a church where
every night stranded ex-prisoners and other unfortunate wrecks
of humanity find a place to sleep and call their temporary home.
In the gallery over the pews, and with a view of the altar and
the organ, they roll out their mattresses and get a peaceful
night's sleep, their washing strung out on a line from side to
side of this unusual place of worship. Theirstomachs are well
filled with sausage and mash cooked by one of their number in
the church kitchen. No charge is ever made for all this, and
many of them are enabled by thus having an "address" to get
public assistance and then employment - so difficult for a
man with nowhere to go when he leaves his prison after paying
society's price, or for those other men who have fallen on
hard times and for whom the Welfare State doesn't cater.
The Rev. Bertram Peake - known in the war as "The Tin Hat
Pastor"-who refused all honours for his work among the blitzed
Londoners,- has found this new use for his old church a
satisfactory continuation of his good, although to some minds,
unorthodox, work of caring for men's bodies as well as souls.
No man is refused at Golborne Church. No charge is made.
Men stay there on average six six weeks. For many hope and faith
are renewed, and jobs found before they move on. But there are
always more who come to take their place in the gallery of
comfort in this Kensington Church.

By ANTHONY CARTHEW

YOU could call her the Esther Williams of the chicken
run—a couple of lengths of the swimming pool
before breakfast and she's happy for the day. Why the
chicken run? Well, Esther
is a 14-week-old pullet.
But no ordinary pullet.
Esther's a chicken who can
swim.
She learned the art at the
tender age of nine weeks
when most pullets are fully
occupied with the business of
pecking an existence.
And her teachers? A couple
of brown, rather aloof ducks,
her best friends.
The swimming chicken's
story is a success story. When
she arrived at Four Winds
Farm in the little village of
Chedburgh, near Bury St.
Edmunds, Suffolk, she was a
week-old outcast. All the
other 99 pullets pecked her.

EFFORTLESS

Came Esther's turn to chirp
when Mr. John Plummer, the
30-year-old farmer and his
pretty 24-year-old wife Ann,
an ex-Land Army girl, put
Esther with the ducks for
safety.
"When with ducks, do as
ducks do," thought Esther
and in no time she had taken
to the pool and was swim-
ming as effortlessly as—a
duck.
Her feet move in the same
motion as the ducks' and
when she needs a rest from
swimming, up she goes on to
one of her friends' backs—a
down-covered raft.

When it's time to dry her
feathers out, the ducks get to
work with their beaks with a
system that must feel like the
chicken's idea of a Swedish
masseur.
So Esther's happy in her
pool. And she has the last
laugh on the 99 land-lubbing
pullets who used to peck her
back in the chicken run.
And she only cost a shilling
like the rest.

RADIO-CONTROLLED PLOUGH IS NEW IDEA FOR BRITISH FARMERS.
A radio-controlled farm tractor, developed by a British firm,
Tractors (London) Ltd., in co-operation with the Automatic
Control Section of the Royal Aeronautical Establishment is
undergoing trials at Barnet, Hertfordshire.
Radio-control apparatus used in the 'Queen Bee', the target
plane devised for anti-aircraft artillery practice, has been
adapted for use in the tractor, which can be employed for
ploughing and other farm operations.
Incoming radio signals operate sensitive electrical relays in the
receiver, so that by means of compressed air servomotors the
tractor can be made to run on a straight course, or to turn
left or right. The plough can be raised when the tractor turns
at the end of a furrow, the plough-raising system being cut out
when other implements are attached to the tractor.
The radio-controlled tractor is so much lighter than the
conventional type that fuel normally consumed in one hour is
sufficient for a whole day's work.
PHOTO SHOWS:- The radio-controlled tractor ploughing a field
at Barnet, Hertfordshire, as farm dogs bark their annoyance
at a strange contrivance which has no need of a ploughman.

                                       SIR HARRY PILKINGTON ANNOUNCES
                                        NEW £5,000,000 FLOAT TANK

In a simultaneous release in 56 countries Sir Harry Pilkington, Chairman
of Pilkington Brothers Ltd., the glass manufacturers, today (Monday,
June 25th) announced that a new £5,000,000 float glass tank - the largest
the firm have ever built - is now operating at St. Helens and marks
a turning point in the development of this new high quality glass.

"The introduction of float glass is the biggest change introduced into
the flat glass trade for generations," said Sir Harry. "The process has
spelt the doom of the traditional grinding and polishing method for all
major purposes."

The statement went on to point out that although the traditional grinding
and polishing method will still be necessary for many fringe products for
probably many years to come, as a method of producing the bulk requirements
of plate glass it was made out of date as soon as Pilkingtons were able to
prove - as they now have without a doubt - that the float process could
produce flat, undistorted glass just as good in appearance as the traditional
product and serving the same purpose as plate glass.

"The plate process," said Sir Harry "requires a very high capital outlay
and very high maintenance costs; the float bath is a much smaller piece of
equipment, much less costly and fundamentally a much simpler means of
achieving the same objective."

The new tank, costing £5,000,000, took two years to build, and into it has
gone all the float glass experience gained over the past years.

A LOOK AT THE CITY OF THE FUTURE

Sea Cities
Sea City - designed by a team of Britain's leading architects and engineers
as a logical 21st century successor to the present-day mainland city - was
unveiled today (February 28) at the London Hilton by the Minister of
Technology, Anthony Wedgwood Benn.

The imaginative concept, produced by the Pilkington Glass Age Development
Committee and designed by architect Hal Moggridge and engineers John Martin
and Ken Anthony, embraces a self-sufficient community of 30,000 living in
comfort and safety many miles out to sea.

The picture shows how Sea City would look from the air. Built on concrete
stilts and protected by a floating breakwater (seen in the foreground) and
by a curved 180 foot high city wall, it could be built in any of the shoal
waters that exist over 10 per cent of the surface of the ocean.

The majority of its inhabitants would live in attractively designed and
adequately terraced flats, as the picture shows. The floating islands
visible in the central lagoon, artificially heated by waste cooling water,
carry both public and private buildings providing the educational, social
and cultural facilities required by modern civilisation.

Outside the walls (right-foreground) special articulated container ships
berth in the "moat" of calm water to unload stores, while a hovercraft
heads for the harbour entrace to discharge its human cargo.

HOUSING - POST WAR - ACCIDENTS

HEAP of rubble, match-
wood furniture, tattered
rags of curtains—this is all
that remains of two homes.
And, until dark last night, gas
and fire chiefs probed among
the debris to find a reason for
the mystery explosion, which:
KILLED 19-year-old shorthand
typist, Mavis Kay as she lay
sleeping in an upstairs bedroom;
INJURED her 52-year-old
father, Bill Kay, her mother,
May, 47, and their next-door
neighbour, Mrs. Lillian Jobson, a
58-year-old cripple;
DEMOLISHED the two homes
in Liverpool-street, Salford,
Lancs, scene of five gas explo-
sions in recent years.
The blast, which happened

Only the
basement
left

early yesterday, rocked the
district. Mrs. Jobson, who has a
broken leg, was said to be
"comfortable but ill" last night.
A lucky escape came for her
husband Tom and her 60-year-
old sister Mrs. Jane Beswick.
Mr. Jobson is recuperating at
Hope Hospital, Salford, after an

operation. Mrs. Beswick had
been helping her sister prepare
for her husband's homecoming
until late on Saturday night.
Then she decided against the
spending the night in Liverpool-
street because she had promised
her family at Darwen, Lancs, to
return home.
Mr. John Wilson, Manchester
regional manager of the North
Western Gas Board, said last
night: "We do not yet know
whether gas was in any way
responsible for the explosion."
A fire officer said that when
the clearing up was over, only
the basements would be left.
The Kays had converted
their tiny terraced home into
the only all-electric one in the
street—they did not like gas.

BUILDING UP OUR TIMBER STOCKS.

MJH/HT

During the two World Wars, our woodlands were
seriously denuded of timber. Today, the Forestry
Commission and private woodland owners are pressing
ahead with the vital task of forming new forests and
re-stocking the old. The year 1956 has marked a milestone
in the history of the Forestry Commission, for it has
seen the planting by the Commission of the one
millionth acre of new woodland. Thus the area of woodland
planted to date by the Commission is more than 1,500
square miles - an area larger than Kent, nearly
twice the extent of Glamorgan and nearly two-thirds
of Perthshire. This million acres is made up of some
500 forests, which are well distributed over the length
and breadth of Britain. In recent years, well over
100-million trees - including more than 10 million hardwoods -
have been planted annually by the Commission and many of
the forests are now producing timber in substantial
quantities; in 1955, the total production amounted to
600,000 tons. Today there is hardly a county without
a national forest and scenes such as these, in the
Commission's Rendlesham Forest in East Anglia, are typical
of what is to be seen in many other parts of the country.

GET OUT!
AFTER 60
YEARS IN
HER HOME

By Ken James
AN 80-year-old widow came
back from a seaside holi-
day at her son's expense to
the terraced house that has
been her home for 60 years.

Lying on the mat was a regi-
stered envelope containing the
Rent Act Form S—telling her
she must quit the house she
went to as a bride.

Last night white-haired Mrs.
Alice Thomas told me: "All I
want is to stay here until my
days come to an end. Yet they
mean to make me go."

The rent of the eight-roomed
house in Hatchard-road, Upper
Holloway—£11 18s. a quarter—is
paid partly by Mrs. Thomas'
married daughter, who lives up-
stairs.

No comment
But Mrs. Thomas pays the
rest and the £17 14s. 8d. a year
rates out of her only income, £2
a week pension. Rateable value
is £42—£2 over the maximum
under which a tenant is pro-
tected.

"If they'd only let me stay I'd
be willing to find a few more
shillings for a higher rent," she
said.

"I love my children very much.
But I'll sleep under an arch
sooner than live with them. I've
given myself blood pressure with
worry."

Hooper and Jackson, Padding-
ton estate agents who handle the
property, refused to comment
last night, or reveal the land-
lord's name.

With eight other tenants in
the road—the others have dif-
ferent landlords—old Mrs.
Thomas will be among the first
of the homeless in October, 1968.

THE INDUSTRY. METALS GOLD
KR. 52

2389) THE LOST GOLD, MINE OF YARROW FOUND.

The Ancient workers closed down their Gold mine and
thoroughly camouflaged the workings until every
particle of Quartz was hidden.
Huge s tones were erected to mark the place and a
chart would probably be made. Centuries have
passed and now it has been re-discovered by Mr.
John Nicol of Glem Cafe, St. Marys Loch, Yarrow.
In 1933 an article by a German about mining appeared
in a Canadian paper remarking about the lost Gold
mine of Yarrow. Was this mine worked by foreigners in
long ages past and information handed down through
the generations.
The Gold is both Alluvial and native(io. in the Sand
of the streams as well as in Reefs)
Back tracking was first noticed in the HENDERLAND
BURN (Backtracking for alluvial mining) as well as the
COM SIKE but particularly in the MILEHOPEBURN where
extensive sluicing had been carried out at two
distinct period s. The Gold is not free in the Rock
area, it is combined with other Reef Ores including
Manganese Copper, Gold and Silver.
Preliminary samples drawn from decomposed back of
Reef Assays showed 2.4. Dwts of Gold per ton of 2240
lbs or 53 grains to the Ton as well as 0.36 ozs of
silver and also included Manganese and Copper.
St. Mary's Lock is a very well known and beautiful
loch and a great many visitors are to be found there
in peace time. The situation is between Selkirk and
Moffat. It is in Selkirkshire and 18 miles from
Selkirk.

Milehopeburn, Yarrow, Selkirkshire.

Q/TAN

One of the biggest contracts for large diameter steel
pipes ever placed in Britain has just been secured by
South Durham Steel and Iron Company, an old established
Teesside firm. The order, from the Basrah Petroleum Co.

order will mean a saving of some 2½ million dollars, as
hitherto most large diameter oil piping has been obtained

THE GREAT JIB: STAR OF THE MACHINE AGE
Oct 31st 1951 PAR 26718-1 (V-K)

THE GREAT JIB: STAR OF THE MACHINE AGE

Billed as "The Biggest Walking Drag-
line in the World, incorporating The
Great Jib", a machine that can certainly
qualify as one of the eight wonders of
the technical world made its debut at
Corby, Northants., today (Wednesday).
The machine, titled officially W.1400,
took Messrs. Ransomes & Rapier four
years to build on the site. It weighs
1,600 tons, has electric motors that
give over 3,000 motor horse power,
works for 20 hours a day, actually
walks -- with seven-foot steps -- and
is controlled by one man. Its purpose:
to remove strata covering the ironstone
bed down to a depth of one hundred feet.
Ironstone sells for a little over seven
shillings a ton; the W.1400 is designed
to uncover 400,000 tons of it each year.
For this reason, huge machine that it
is, it must "walk" over the area. After
settling in a spot, the machine swings
out with the great jib -- an arm 282
feet long, the tip of which is 175
feet above the ground. Then it drops a
22 ton scoop, lifts and drags away 27
tons of spoil. Within 60 seconds, the
scoop has emptied and is back, digging
in once more. PICTURE SHOWS: The biggest
walking drag-line (W.1400) in the world
seen here from the top of the great jib
at/its Corby (Northants.) site today.

HERALD
D. I.
24 OCT 1962

IT would not be everybody's choice of
a way to spend a honeymoon—
perched in a decorators' cradle 350ft.
above the Thames. But that is where
newly married steeplejack Harry
Walker has just spent his.

Honeymooner Harry, who is pictured
on his way up the towering, 350-foot
chimney stack at Battersea power
station, said yesterday: "It could have
been worse. At least the view is nice."

Harry and two colleagues were given
a three-week deadline to paint the
chimney stack.

ON SCHEDULE

He explained: "The job was due to
start the day after I got married—so
I had to postpone my honeymoon and
spend it up the chimney instead."
As he daubed the finishing touches

to the cream-coloured chimney, 49-
year-old Harry, of Dagenham, Essex,
added: "Bang on schedule. Now my
wife Doris and I can go to Somerset
for our real honeymoon."

The four huge chimneys at Batter-
sea are painted at five-yearly inter-
vals. It takes 110 gallons of paint—a
special rubberised mixture to with-
stand weather conditions—for each
one.

SECRET FEAR

But no ordinary painter would
attempt to work up there—even with

THEY'RE BAKING BOATS FOR MASS PRODUCTION
February 15th 1958 PAR 69070-1 (Wo-R)
___________
THEY'RE BAKING BOATS FOR MASS PRODUCTION
___________

As sailing fast gains popularity as a sport,
modern mass production methods derived from
those developed during the war for making
wooden aircraft are being applied to the
manufacture of boats at the Hamble, Hampshire,
factory of Fairey Marine Ltd., a subsidiary of
the Fairey Aviation Company.
The craft are 'hot-moulded' from planks of
wooden veneer, a method which eliminates the
old and laborious method of boat-building by
individual craftsmen.
The shell of each boat is composed of layers
of planks applied to a mould to form 'skins'
glued together. Each shell is baked by
steam heat up to 100 degrees Centigrade for
about half an hour. Then it is taken out of
the oven and removed from the mould.
The resulting boat, it is said, will last a
lifetime and is proof against all the normal
ills which affect boats built by other methods.
More than 1,000 boats were produced at Hamble
in 1957, ranging from 7ft.6in. dinghies to the
28ft. Atalanta sailing cruiser.
Over one-third of the output is exported.
PICTURE SHOWS:- Hulls of Firefly, Finn and
Albacore craft awaiting finishing in the
central assembly hangar at Hamble.
The men at the trestles are working on masts.

BATTLING FOR BRITAIN'S FORESTS.
168852(DAW). NEW GOVERNMENT RESEARCH STATION AIDS RECOVERY
OF COUNTRY'S WOODLANDS.

FARNHAM, ENGLAND: At the Forestry Commissioners now research
station at Alice Holt Lodge, near this Surrey town, where
once the country's greatest surgeons fought for the lives
of Allied war-wounded, another type of 'doctor'is battling
to save something more than Britain sacrificed in the war
offort. Denuded by urgent demands for timber during the
war, much of Britain's forest land has vanished, and what is
left is endangered by pest and disease, and more scientists
are battling to preserve Britain's woodlands.
Not only do they battle forestry posts - they actually
cultivate some for export - certain insects are beneficial,
they prey upon parasites that infect trees.
The research station at Alice Holt Lodge, an old mansion
standing in some 2,000 acres of former Crown woodlands, has
an extensive library, laboratories, photography, and pathology
sections.
PHOTO SHOWS:- The Entomologist uses a suction tube to
collect parasites from brooding cages, in which parasites
and their enemies have been cultivated.
Under normal conditions, harmful insects are kept in check
by natural onomies. This calls for the introduction of
parasites to control the new pests. Natural enemies of
harmful insects are insectivorous birds and mammals, and a
large variety of parasites and predatory insects which destroy
a large proportion of eggs, larvae and pupae.

THE BATTLE FOR NYLONS - BRITISH FACTORIES CAN TURN OUT
MILLIONS AS WOMEN YEARN.

The English city of Nottingham, famed for its lace, is now
one of the key points in the battle against one of the
most irritating post-War shortages endured by Britain's
women - the lack of nylon stockings.
These pictures were taken in a Nottingham group of
factories which before the War were turning out stockings
at the rate of nearly a million dozen each year.
Now, after long experiment, overhaul of machinery and
adjustment of plant to handle nylon yarn, they are
striving to cope with the apparently insatiable demand
by millions of women eager for filmy, glamorous nylon hose.
The factories are equipped to produce stockings at the
pre-War volume, but to angry women who stand vainly in line
at shops Lord Hollenden, a leader of the British hosiery
industry, imparts this sad information: 'The short
supply of nylon yarn prevents us producing ample supplies
of nylon stockings'.
Cause of the yarn shortage is inadequate capacity at the
'twisting' stage of manufacture.
For the future, Lord Hollenden sheds a ray of hope - he
predicts full supplies of yarn by the beginning of 1948.
PHOTO SHOWS:- An operative works the pre-boarding machine.
The machine subjects the nylon stockings to steam treatment
which 'sets' the loop formation so that it is maintained
throughout the life of the stockings; this is one of the secrets
of nylons' durability.

OLD CORNISH COPPER MINE YIELDS URANIUM ORE. MJH/P. 1.

Wheal Edward Mine, on the edge of the cliffs at St. Just,
three miles from Land's End, Cornwall, may have a new lease
of life as the result of the work now being carried out their
by new modern prospectors with geiger counters. For years
the mine was worked for copper in the hey-day of Cornish
mining, but the financial structure of the old mineral companies
made no provision for the time when underground exploration
was necessary or when thinner lodes were met and by 50 years
ago, most had closed, until today only two are working, both
for tin. Wheal Edward, however, attracted the attention of a
prospecting geologist, Mr. Richard Rumbold of Streatham (London)
who was surveying the whole of West Cornwall for radio-active
materials, combining this work with the field testing of modern
prospecting equipment. His geiger counter ticked encouragingly
when samples of ore were produced from the ancient mine and by
scrambling down the cliff edge, he found a fairly easy means
of access. Otherwise an elaborate winch gear would be needed to go
down the vertical main shaft, which disappear dramatically
into the dark ground. Now it is likely that a company will
be formed to re-open the old mine for uranium ore.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS; MR. E. C. MURRAY and MR. RICHARD RUMBOLD
seen testing the native rock 120feet down the old heal Edward
Mine at St. Just, Cornwall, for uranium, with a gieger counter.

BUILDING UP OUR TIMBER STOCKS.
MJH/HT
During the two World Wars, our woodlands were
seriously denuded of timber. Today, the Forestry
Commission and private woodland owners are pressing
ahead with the vital task of forming new forests and
re-stocking the old. The year 1956 has marked a milestone
in the history of the Forestry Commission, for it has
seen the planting by the Commission of the one
millionth acre of new woodland. Thus the area of woodland
planted to date by the Commission is more than 1,500
square miles - an area larger than Kent, nearly
twice the extent of Glamorgan and nearly two-thirds
of Perthshire. This million acres is made up of some
500 forests, which are well distributed over the length
and breadth of Britain. In recent years, well over
100-million trees - including more than 10 million hardwoods -
have been planted annually by the Commission and many of
the forests are now producing timber in substantial
quantities; in 1955, the total production amounted to
600,000 tons. Today there is hardly a county without
a national forest and scenes such as these, in the
Commission's Rendlesham Forest in East Anglia, are typical
of what is to be seen in many other parts of the country.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: MR. CHARLES H. WELLINGTON, Head
Forester, seen inspecting a 2-years-old tree in
the experimental section of a plantation of Hybrid
Poplars in the Rendlesham Forest (Suffolk).

No hope remains of saving
the 13 miners missing in

yesterday. News of the disaster
reached him in Greece and he
decided immediately to fly home.

BANKSIDE POWER STATION: PRODUCTION GETS UNDER WAY

London: An industrial project which has aroused much
controversy from the time of its conception has just gone
into operation. It is the Bankside Power Station, at
which the first 60,000-kilowatt turbo-alternator, of
about 80,000 horse-power, has started to supply electricity.
The project was allowed, on condition that oil and not
coal was to be burned. Other conditions which had to
be observed were that the building must be set back
far enough from the Thames so as not to interfere with
the projected road and promenade.
Opposition to the power station was so strong that in
January, 1947 a public inquiry was held, with the result
that the scheme has given Government sanction.
On completion the Bankside Power Station will comprise
four 60,000-kilowatt generating sets, the oil
consumption at full-load (10-hour day) being 67 tons
an hour, consuming in one winter's day about 850 tons.
PHOTO SHOWS:- The pump house at the river jetty which has
been built to accommodate tankers and barges. The oil will be
brought up the river mainly by self-propelled barges from
which it will be discharged by these pumps through a tunnel
to underground storage tanks at the rear of the power
station.

Wilkinson Sword Company, of Acton, London, have
kept up the ancient industry. At present they
have orders for 2,000 swords. They are busy making
officers' ceremonial swords or refurbishing old ones
that will be used in the Coronation.
Some of the orders received have come from overseas.
The firm has the market largely to itself
- evening American manufacturers appear to have
gone out of business.
Ceremonial swords have not been a standard item
of officers' equipment in the Army since before the
war. Many orders have been placed by the Ministry
of Supply and service-owned swords are issued to
officers as required from a pool formed by
regiments. Nevertheless, many officers still possess
pre-war swords and hundreds of these have been
sent for renovation, which mostly involves
replating. The average cost of this work is about
£5..
Many existing swords, including those belonging
to the Yeomen of the Guard, are being sent to the
firm to be "brought up to date" - to be embossed
with the Queen's cipher.

factory is Mrs. May Fry, storekeeper and finisher.

'DOORMAT' STRETCHER CAN AID MINE RESCUES
October 8th 1963 PAR 105646-1 (PNR/P-R)

'DOORMAT' STRETCHERS CAN AID MINE RESCUES

An old piece of colliery conveyor belt that
was once used as a doormat looks like
revolutionising mine rescue work in the
South Yorkshire coalfields, and may win a
National Coal Board Divisional award for
50-year-old JACK HUBY of Carcroft, near
Doncaster, fire and rescue officer at
Bullcroft Colliery, near Doncaster.
Jack started experimenting with the 3/8in.
thick belt four months ago and came up with
a new type of stretcher which he is seen here
(on right) demonstrating.
In a recent demonstration, miners saw Jack
dragged by an engine along a rough railway
track at 10 miles an hour. Then, still
strapped in the stretcher - which fits snugly
around the patient - he was pulled through
a 3ft.6in. water pipe.
Mr. Albert Wilds, the Bullcroft Colliery
manager, said: 'There's no doubt it is a
real step forward in mine rescue work.
This stretcher can be used extensively in
underground coal seams where rescue teams
find it impossible to take conventional
stretchers. It will get injured miners
up from the coal face quicker than any other
type.'
Cost of making the Huby Stretcher is
negligible.

FORD'S PRODUCE THEIR MILLIONTH TRACTOR

The millionth Fordson tractor to be manufactured since
production in Great Britain and Ireland began forty-three
years ago, left the production line at Ford's Dagenham
factory today.
The tractor, which was driven off the line by Mr. J.
O'MAHONY, Economic Counsellor at the Irish Embassy in
London, is earmarked for shipment this week to Henry
Ford & Son Ltd., Cork, Ireland. It was at Cork in 1919
that the late Henry Ford built his first factory for the
manufacture of Fordson tractors in the United Kingdom.
In 1928, the entire tractor manufacturing plant of Ford
America was shipped to Cork, then in 1933 production moved
to Dagenham.
39,049 tractors were built in the period of Cork pro-
duction; the remainder have been built at Dagenham.
It is appropriate, therefore, that the millionth Fordson
should be exported to Cork, birthplace of UK Fordson
production.

A Century in Tractors

Among those present, as seen in this picture, to watch
the tractor leave the line today were three Ford employees
who have worked on tractor production since the early days
at Cork and whose combined service with Ford totals 101
years. They are Mr. Jerry Keane, Superintendent Tractor
Assembly (39 years), Mr. Dave Finn, Assistant Superinten-
dent (33 years) and Mr. Jimmy Quinn, Foreman (29 years).

Ends.

London-March 21st. 1962.

DEMAND FOR GLASS CONTAINERS ON THE UP AND UP. AP/TRU

Reasons for the rapidly increasing demand for glass
containers were outlined today, Wednesday 21st May
1969, by Mr James B. Livingston, DSC, Deputy President
of the Glass Manufacturers Federation and Vice-Chairman
of Rockware Glass Ltd., in London, The four
main reasons for the growing success of glass containers
in the face of increasing competition from other materials
were 1. The nature of the material - good for display, and
clinically clean; 2. The low price per unit, due to low
cost basic raw materials; 3. Technology - lightweighting
and strengthening; and 4. The advent of one-trip bottles.
A new, colourful film entitled "Glass Coloured Spectacle",
which promotes the advantages of glass containers, was
also premiered today. In the five years since the
Glass Manufacturers Federation made their first glass
container film, sales of bottles and jars have leapt
from 4854 million units in 1964, to 5652 units last year.
Picture shows

Mr James B. Livingston points out how technology has
assisted the increased demand for glass containers, and
in particular, milk bottles, which, as will be seen
from the diagram, are being made lighter and lighter.
It may soon be possible to drop such bottles and they
will bounce, rather than shatter, thus helping to keep
costs yet again.

BY HENRY STANHOPE
Science Reporter
OUT of the silvery North Sea
yesterday shot a 40ft. fountain
of flame—high enough to kindle
the hopes of every money-minded
housewife in the land.

For behind that flame is gas.
Enough in a day to cook the dinners
and heat the sitting rooms of a
300,000 people.
And enough to allow British Petro-
leum, who have been drilling for gas
deep under the North Sea along with
7 other strike-hungry companies, to
announce cautiously: "We are
optimistic."

DIAMOND TIPPED

Yesterday was flare-test day on Sea
Gem, BP's 5,600-ton, 136ft.-high boring
rig, whose diamond-tipped drills first
struck a reserve of natural gas two
miles under the North Sea last
September.
Engineers who have been busily
constructing a well to draw up the
precious fuel, brought up their first
large "bucketful" to sample it for quality
and quantity.
Their announcement: excellent gas,
and enough of it to provide 10million
cubic feet a day, "a very encouraging
start."

SECOND DRILLING

This is enough to satisfy the needs
of a town the size of Nottingham. Or,
of course, 10 towns of 30,000 each.
I flew in a Heron plane, 200ft.
of the gaunt, black skeleton of Sea
Gem, 42 miles east of the Humber, and
the yellow spindle of flame burning off
the surplus gas as it emerged.
BP's North Sea project co-ordinator
Bob Holroyd said that a
second drilling would start
before the end of the year
in a spot two miles west of
Sea Gem.

If that one shows equal
promise, there will be a
third, and a fourth, and a
fifth. "Until, in fact, BP are
satisfied they can find the
500million cubic feet of gas a
day they regard as the
minimum to make their
North Sea scheme a going
concern.
Pipelines would follow, pump-

Britain, at the lowest price to
consumers yet. It will be
some of the purest gas discovered.
And if the Gas Council fer-
vently hope, one day may mean
us cheaper prices, lower bills
every quarter.
Last week Continental Oil
ended drilling because their
North Sea strike showed insuffi-
cient promise.

1983-5236 / 50945
INDUSTRY, FUEL AND POWER. ELECTRICITY. POWER STATIONS
FERRYBRIDGE . YORKSHIRE.
THREEX 350-ft. cooling towers
were blown down and a
huge oil rig was torn from its
moorings yesterday as gales of
up to 100 mph. swept Britain.

At least seven people were killed
and scores were injured.

In the cooling tower collapse at a
£70million power station, hundreds
of workers escaped—because they
were on a tea-break.

Last night another tower at the
power station in Ferrybridge, York-
shire, was in danger of collapsing.

FALLING CONCRETE

The station is due to come into
operation this year and is one of the
biggest in Europe. Only three men
were slightly hurt by falling concrete
as the towers crashed into rubble.
Damage is estimated at £2million.

But the luckiest men alive today
are the 30 workers aboard the
£21million oil rig Ocean Prince which
snapped a dozen steel hawsers at
Middlesbrough, Yorkshire, and
floated into the River Tees before
dawn yesterday.

Four times the men escaped death.

Escape No. 1 came when
the rig crashed into the side
of an oil tanker.

Escape No. 2 came a quarter
of a mile downstream when the
rig's crane sliced through two
power cables strung across the
river lighting up the sky with
huge flashes.

Escape No. 3 happened as the
rig bore down on a small dredger
in the river. Aboard the
dredger was 2,000lb. of gelignite
—but the dredger crew towed it
to safety and then took to their
boats to escape. Finally came:

Escape No. 4, when the oil rig
bit deep into a mudbank with-
in sight of the open sea and
almost capsized.

Last night, after the men had
been rescued by launches, the
River Tees was closed to ship-
ping with the oil rig blocking
the sea route. Tugs were stand-
ing by.

Today an attempt will be
made to tow the rig back up
river, where she is being fitted
out before joining the North
Sea oil and gas hunt.

In London, nine people were
injured when sheets of corru-
gated iron crashed from the
roof of a restaurant at Victoria
station on to a bus queue. Two
were detained in hospital.

TWO KILLED

THEY'RE BAKING BOATS FOR MASS PRODUCTION
February 15th 1958 PAR 69070-4 (Wo-R)
CHESTER
NO 8003 17 FEB 1958
DUPLICATE SENT
THEY'RE BAKING BOATS FOR MASS PRODUCTION

As sailing fast gains popularity as a sport,
modern mass production methods derived from
those developed during the war for making
wooden aircraft are being applied to the
manufacture of boats at Hamble, Hampshire,
factory of Fairey Marine Ltd., a subsidiary of
the Fairey Aviation Company.
The craft are 'hot-moulded' from planks of
wooden veneer, a method which eliminates the
old and laborious method of boat-building by
individual craftsmen.
The shell of each boat is composed of layers
of planks applied to a mould to form 'skins'
glued together. Each shell is baked by
steam heat up to 100 degrees Centigrade for
about half an hour. Then it is taken out of
the oven and removed from the mould.
The resulting boat, it is said, will last a
lifetime and is proof against all the normal
ills which affect boats built by other methods.
More than 1,000 boats were produced at Hamble
in 1957, ranging from 7ft.6in. dinghies to the
26ft. Atalanta sailing cruiser.
Over one-third of the output is exported.
PICTURE SHOWS:- Workers at Hamble laying on
a 'skin' for a 9ft.10in. 'Duckling' general
purpose dinghy. The wood is drawn from the
oven in background which keeps it at even
temperature.

OIL-DIPPING AIDS EGG STORAGE

A special process is now being used in the packing stations
of the Yorkshire Egg Producers Limited, Drighlington,
Yorkshire, to preserve eggs during storage. This process,
known as "egg dipping", has so far only been carried out on
a small scale in the U.K., although it is widely used in the
U.S.A., Canada, Denmark, Holland and Australia. In 1949, the
Food Ministry carried out large-scale trials of the process.

Deterioration of eggs is caused partly by bacterial
infection through the shell and partly by the escape of
moisture and carbon dioxide, causing the albumen to break
down. The odourless, colourless and tasteless mineral oil,
in which the eggs are dipped before being placed in cold
storage, fills the pores of the shell and prevents microbial
invasion and greatly reduces the loss of moisture and carbon
dioxide. The Shell grade recommended for this application is
Shell Ondina Oil 17.

The Yorkshire Egg Producers Ltd. handle approximately
1/19th of the total eggs packed in the U.K. (in 1953, this
represented nearly 200 million eggs). They possess 9 packing-
stations, at which eggs are sorted, "candled" to detect
interior flaws, graded by weight, stamped and repacked for
delivery to retailers.

PICTURE SHOWS:- Trays of eggs being lowered into the oil bath.
Operated by 3 assistants, the oil-dipping machine can dip up to
750 dozen eggs per hour.

THE PROGRESS OF A NEW TOWN

JS 16.8.50.
HARLOW is one of eight New Towns designed for the reception of
population and industry from the crowded areas of inner London,
and which are expected to take about 230,000 Londoners. Harlow's
contribution to this will be an increase in population of
55,000.
HARLOW recently reached a distinct stage in its development with
the commencement of work in building in the MARK HALL area -- a
step which marked the beginning of work on the New Town proper
and the end of preparation which has lasted since the approval of
the Master Plan. This Master Plan was the first to receive
official approval despite the fact that the Harlow Development
Corporation was by no means the first to be set up. Much work
has also been done in the Chippingfield area where terraced and
semi-detached houses have been erected, and some of which are
already in occupation by members of the Corporation's staff and
employees of the contractors.

17 POLICE INJURED IN A MOB ATTACK.
Seventeen policemen were injured on Sunday (9-8-70) when a Black
Power march in London erupted into a bitter street battle. Eight
coach-loads of police were called in to control the violence as
demonstrators hurled bricks, broken milk bottles and beer cans.
Nineteen people were arrested and will be appearing in court on
Monday. Fighting flared after 200 Black Panthers set off on an anti-
police protest march in London's Notting Hill. They carried the
heads of slaughtered pigs on poles and chanted: "Kill the pigs!"
outside two local police stations. The Panthers were on their way to
a third police station when escorting police tried to make them form
into an orderly column, in a street in Paddington. A scuffle broke
out. Then, as one policeman said later, "All Hell broke loose."
Police, coloured and white demonstrators punched, kicked and dragged
each other to the ground. Young coloured girls screamed and beat at
policemen struggling with Panthers in the gutters. As the police
reinforcements arrived to join the battle, demonstrators fled
down side streets and over garden walls as the police slowly gained
control.

SEARCH FOR OIL IN LANCASHIRE.
Somewhere beneath the sand-dunes of the Lancashire
est coast, seven miles from Southport, lies a huge
untapped supply of oil.
Sixteen engineers who have just sunk a bore hole hope
to find it before their instruments register 7,500 ft.
They cannot go any deeper than that with their present
equipment and if they have not found it at that depth
they will try somewhere else.
An official at the D'Arcy Exploration Co, who is doing
the work, said "for ten years we have been getting 400
tons of oil a year from eight 'surface wells' at
Formby, but those wells are only 100 ft deep and we are
confident that a large oilfield, much deeper is
supplying them".
They tried three times before at Scarisbrick and
Bickerstaffe, but although they went down to 7,600 ft
they could not find the source.
Pointing to a thick, pinky fluid oozing out of a large
pipe alongside the towering derrick on the new site,
John Gibson the drilling superintendant explained
"that is the circulating mud which we pour down the
centre of the drill pipe, it seeps through the drilling
bit and brings up the small pieces of rock formation".
After the formation has been sieved out, the mud goes
back down the drill pipe.

A NEW TUNNEL UNDER THE THAMES.
17.3.49.
A new tunnel, driven under the river Thames from Battersea
Power Station to Chelsea, will carry cables between the power
station and a new sub-station in north-west London. The
2,500 ft tunnel - one of the most remarkable engineering feats
in London - takes two 500-ft-radius bends to miss the piers
of the Victoria Railway Bridge, but in spite of this
it was only 3/8-inch out when it connected with the pit dug at
the Chelsea end. Continuous shifts working day and night
since 1st September have averaged 80 feet per week, and
pressurised air a hd to be used to keep the engineers going.
At one point the tunnel air pressure of 101b per square inch
had to be increased to 281b to stop the water from bursting
through. The internal diameter of the tunnel is eight feet
and it is being lined with 1,900 tons of cast-iron lining.
It is 76 feet below ground level on the south bank, and is
18 feet under the river bed at the highest point.
The picture shows:- the end of the tunnel at Chelsea
Bridge Road showing the access manhole.

NEW CREPE & RAYON INDUSTRY IN NORTHERN IRELAND.
A new industry which has sprung up in Northern
Ireland is the preparation and weaving of
rayon crepe and other rayon fabrics.
Crepe Weavers Ltd., of Newtownards, Co. Down,
which commenced in 1948 occupies part of Newtownards
Airport which was originally built for the production
of aircraft.
It employs 125 people at present but will employ 200
people by the end of the year when the mill is fully
equipped.
Owing to the male unemployment situation in the
district it is the intention of the firm to employ
60 per cent men and 40 per cent women.
The production target for the end of the year is 30,000
yards of Rayon fabrics per week, of which between 50
and 60% will be for export.
Most of the workers engaged are trainees formerly
agricultural labourers and laundry workers.
Care has been taken not to engage workers from linen
textile mills in the district which would have added
to the production of the new firm but would have
caused difficulties in the established firms.
OPS. One of the employees works on an improvised

the works for the looms.

LONDON: Driver Ken Coles, of Peterborough

designed at the Government Building Research

horizontally across the building site to the
spot where the craftsmen need them.

which is used to remove excavated earth, unload
material from lorries, lifting floor joists and
window and door frames, roofing timbers and tiles,

BY ARTHUR OSMAN
block of flats was ordered to be
closed yesterday after five people fell
when a balcony collapsed under them.
All five were taken to hospital with head and

The flats, part of a £235,000 development at
West Bromwich, Staffs., were handed over to the
local council only this week.
Tenants were due to move in early next week.
After the accident,
technicians and de-

lapsed balcony and
others in the four-
storey block at Ten-
score Straight, West

The contractors, Sir

West Bromwich Council
ordered a full-scale in-
quiry and called in all keys
which had been handed to
tenants.
INJURIES
A spokesman said: “No
one will be allowed to enter
until inquiries are com-
pleted.”
The five people were
inspecting a new flat
when the second-floor bal-
cony collapsed.
Mr. Horace Hall, aged 59,
is in hospital with head
injuries, his wife Minnie,
55, with leg injuries, their
daughter, Mrs. Margaret
Greenhalgh, 33, with back
injuries, and her 10-year-
old daughter, Deborah,
with a fractured skull.
NO WARNING
Also hurt was Mr. and
Mrs. Hall's other daughter,
25-year-old Mrs. Barbara
Timmins, who went home
after treatment for leg
injuries.
She said last night:
“The balcony collapsed
without warning. We had
no time to get off.
“My sister and I were
going to clean the new flat

BESPOKE BOOTMAKERS CLOSES DOWN THROUGH LACK OF CRAFTSMEN.

Last week saw the closing down of the World-famous
bespoke bootmakers PEAL & Co.Ltd. of Wigmore Street.
Up to the end the business was still being run by
father and son directors MR.CECIL and MR.RODNEY PEAL,
fifth and sixth generation of the family who founded
the business 174 years ago. Among it's clients, are
EARL MOUNTBATTEN, the DUKE OF WINDSOR, the late SIR
WINSTON CHURCHILL, for whom they made boots and shoes
for 40 years up until his death, and host of Royal and
other prominent personages. Although they have been
getting about 1,000 new clients every year, they are
closing because they just cannot get the skilled
craftsmen essential to maintain their high standard.
Most of the clients had their owns lasts, from which the
shoes were made, measurements being exact to the
millimetre, and the lasts are now being sold to the
customers for 3 guineas each.

PHOTO SHOWS.
At PEAL's, 71-year-old MR.W.L.PIGGOTT,
of Bosham, Sussex, who has been with the firm for 57 years,
during which he has made 158 crossings of the Atlantic in
the course of his duties. He is seen sorting put lasts
for return to customers. The one he is holding is the
DUKE OF WINDSOR's.

MACE FOR BRITISH JEWELLERS' ASSOCIATION 26.1.55.

The British Jewellers' Association, which
represents nearly 2,000 manufacturing and
wholesale jewellers, has become a patron
of its own trade. The Central Council of the
Association recently decided that the ancient
art of silversmithing was in serious danger
of extinction without public support.It was
decided that the Association should commission

own collection of fin silver-ware and, at the same
time, setting an example to similar organisations

piece,amodern silver mace for use upon ceremonial
occasions, has now been completed, designed by the
well-known designer R.H.Hill, and made by a london
firm of silversmith's.

with an effective cockerel-

if I was disturbed before

SEARCH FOR OIL IN LANCASHIRE.
Somewhere beneath the sand-dunes of the Lancashire
XXXXXXX coast, seven miles from Southport, lies a huge
untapped supply of oil.
Sixteen engineers who have just sunk a bore hole hope
to find it before their instruments register 7,500 ft.
They cannot go any deeper than that with their present
equipment and if they have not found it at that depth
they will try somewhere else.
An official at the D'Arcy Exploration Co, who is doing
the work, said "for ten years we have been getting 400
tons of oil a year from eight 'surface wells' at
Formby, but those wells are only 100 ft deep and we are
confident that a large oilfield, much deeper is
supplying them".
They tried three times before at Scarisbrick and
Bickerstaffe, but although they went down to 7,600 ft
they could not find the source.
Pointing to a thick,pinky fluid oozing out of a large
pipe alongside the towering derrick on the new site,
John Gibson the drilling superintendant explained
"that is the circulating mud which we pour down the
centre of the drill pipe, It seeps through the drilling
bit and brings up the small pieces of rock formation".
After the formation has been sieved out, the mud goes
back down the drill pipe.

HERALD REPORTER
A 16TH-CENTURY house made 20th-century history
yesterday by being moved in one piece from the
place where the Tudor builders put it up. Crowds
watched it trundling up a slope towards its new site
300ft. away.
The move will cost Exeter Council £8,000. Originally
they took over the house—in Frog-street—with the idea
of pulling it down to make way for the city's new inner
by-pass. But there was a
storm of protest.
The Ministry of Works told
the council to move it to
another site. For more than
a month workmen "crated"
the 30-ton, three-storey
house in 10 tons of timber.
And yesterday looking as
stately as possible on its
special wheels, it was winched
up a one-in-ten gradient.
TOP-HEAVY
At first two winches were
used. But the house moved too
fast and the removal team
switched to one.
Spirit levels were used to
make sure the house was
kept on an even keel.
Mr. David Nye, the London
architect who has advised the
council on the move, watched
the operation.
Haul away! A piece of old
England gets going on wheels.

CALMED
Police blocked the
entrance, and the crowd
were calmed by an
announcement that a man
had been arrested.
A woman in the crowd
said: "I was horrified when
something sailed over our
heads and crashed on the
car. But the royal couple
seemed to remain very
calm."
The rear hood of the Rolls
had been removed for the
drive through the city, but
a transparent plastic shield
covered the rear of the car.
A few minutes before the
concrete slab incident, a
bottle of beer was thrown at
the Rolls. The bottle
smashed on the road under

A FARM WITH A DIFFERENCE.
MJH/HT.

A farm with a difference is that run by Mr. T. Donnellan
at Warsash, Southampton. For on his farm Mr. Donnellan
has no cows, horses, pigs or sheep - his "stock" consists
of crabs, lobsters, crawfish, prawns, oysters etc., for he
is a sea-food farmer. His "fields" are 4,000 sq. yards
of water where thousands of sea-animals caught by Hampshire
and Cornish fisherfolk are kept in salt-water storage ponds
for 30 days before being sent away to end up on a plate.
Mr. Donnellan's two daughters Catherine (9) and Mary (7)
love to help on this fascinating farm and are not the least
bit frightened of the crabs, lobsters etc. - on the contrary
they love them and can name all the 5,000 different species
and varieties of sea animals, worth £4,000 kept on the farm.
The little girls even wade in the ponds at low water in bare
feet and are X not the least afraid of getting their toes
nipped.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: Bare-footed CATHERINE (9) and MARY (7)
are seen helping their father MR. T. DONNELLAN, who is holding
a giant crawfish, to collect crabs, lobsters etc. for
despatch to various hotels, restaurants, etc. on their
farm at Warsash, Southampton. Mr. Donnellan also supplies
many ocean liners with fresh crabs, lobsters etc.

AIDING THE AIRCRAFT DESIGNER OF THE FUTURE AND
BRITISH FAME FOR THOROUGHNESS.
27.11.47.

A new altitude chamber has been built at Hatfield
works of the de Havilland Aircraft Co.Ltd., makers of
the famous jet aircraft, etc. The purpose of this
chamber is the research into the use of equipment at
high altitudes - altitudes that may be in common use
in the future as more and more knowledge is gained of
the stratosphere and jet engine performance. The main
chamber is 35 feet long and 14 feet in diameter, and in
it conditions of atmospheric pressure, temperature and
humidity can be reproduced of varying altitudes up to
80,000 feet. A team of technicians controls the tests ;
a number of the observers are stationed inside the
chamber, and a two-way system of communications with
those outside enables a complete check to be made of the
happenings to whatever material is being subjected to
the tests. Confirming these reports is a complicated
system of strain gauges and other indicators, supplemented
by a microphone which amplifies the sounds of structure
breaking up, and transmits them to the outside
observers. The following pictures show

a general view of the main chamber. The end cover is
attached by means of the hinged bolts seen around the
periphery of the cylindrical portion.

description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Industry ÃƒÆ’Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â» Agriculture ÃƒÆ’Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â» Poultry - Birds + Farms - Miscellaneous.
Transcribed_Text:
A BROWN - AND - WHITE
hen, nesting in half an
orange-box last night in a
backyard at Barr-road,
Gravesend, looked quite
ordinary.

But, said her owner, carpenter
Charles Woodbine, she has laid six
eggs in one day—three times.

Experts are astonished. Four
eggs in a day is the record, they
say, and the normal for a fast
layer is an egg every 25 hours.

Said Mr. Woodbine: “I'm used
to people not believing me. But
none of my neighbours keeps hens
and I am satisfied no one is put-
ting eggs in the nest for a joke.”

He said he discovered he had a
“wonder bird” in February when
she was put in a pen away from
his other birds because she was
pecking at them.

• Kept a log

One day he found six eggs in her
nest—and started keeping a log.
This is what it shows:

March 1 to 14, one egg a day;
March 15, four (between 8 a.m.
and 6 p.m.);
March 16 to 18, two, three and
three.

Then a few “nil” days, followed
by a routine one, two or three, and
another four. But on Monday it
happened again—six between
breakfast and bedtime.
Mr. Woodbine showed me a
bowl of six eggs, saying: “She
laid these today.” Each had a
small dent in the crown.
The hen is a crossbreed—Rhode
Island Red and Sussex. Mr. and
Mrs. Woodbine got their poultry
knowledge from books. The “won-
der bird” was one of a batch of
six-week-old chicks they bought in
January.

1983-5236/84039 14.7.39
AT 5.30 yesterday evening Thomas
Atkinson tidied up his desk in the
counting house of a London store and went
home to Landseer-street, Battersea Park,
S.W.
This morning he will walk into the
barracks of the Queen's West Surrey Regi-
ment at Guildford, and become for six
months Militiaman Thomas Atkinson.
He will be one of 30,000 men, the first batch of
conscripted militiamen, who to-day leave their jobs
and their families to begin their military training
in dozens of barracks and camps.
Since, whether he wants to or not, Thomas Atkin-
son is making history, you ought to watch him
closely.
Militiaman
Thomas Atkin-
son bids six
months' fare-
well to his
office desk be-
fore going into
training with
the first batch
of the 20-year-
olds to be
called up.
Every day next week, and after that
from time to time, I am going to describe
his training. But first I should like to
give you a clear picture of Thomas Atkin-
son.
He told me when I spoke to him yester-
day that his grandfather, who fought in
the Boer War, died a few days ago at the
age of 71. I am not going to pretend
that his grandfather was the original
Thomas Atkins, the legendary British
private soldier. Nor do I pretend that
Thomas Atkinson is the real name of the
Militiaman whose adventures you are

A YOUNG ex-Navy pilot
parked his newly-bought
sports car in Hertford-street,
Mayfair, last night while he
went for a drink. Half an
hour later he found the car
buried under a pile of bricks
and rubble 4ft. high.
A three-storey empty
bombed house had collapsed.
Bricks had crashed right
across the road, but no one
was hurt.
The owner of the car, 24-
year-old Peter Brodhurs, of
Leamington-avenue, Morden,
Surrey, said when he saw his
wreck: “I’m furious. I only
bought the car four days ago
with my gratuity. I was
invalidated out of the Navy a
week ago because of a
crash.”
Miss Harriet Johns, TV
actress, was driving along
Hertford-street to park as the
house fell. “I couldn’t see
anything for dust,” she said.
Police roped off the area as
firemen (pictured above)
cleared the debris.

PITHEAD SHALE FOR SITE OF A HOVERPORT.

Lorries unloading shale from Chislet Colliery, Kent, at Pegwell Bay
where it will be used in the construction of the new international
hoverport. Half of Chislet's north west tip (about 180,000 cubic yards)
is being removed to form the base for the 12-acre landing and
launching pad.

-------------

Both black and red shales, which conform to Ministry of Transport
specifications for general fill, are obtainable from colliery sites.
The red shale - which has been used extensively for road making - is
becoming scarce but the black shales of the type used at Pegwell Bay
are in plentiful supply.

The National Coal Board sell shale from site and contractors are
responsible for collection. Contractors operating on colliery sites
have to conform with the Board's regulations regarding work on tips, but
the Board will advise on methods of working.
More than 6 million tons of shale was sold from pithead sites last
year and the demand is increasing. A small section dealing with sales has
been set up under Mr. N. Little, Marketing Department, National Coal
Board, Hobart House, Grosvenor Place, London, S.W.1.

ROYAL PRESENT FOR KING OF THAILAND. 26.4.50.

For their wedding present to the King of Thailand,
their Majesties, have chosen a service of Worcester
Royal Porcelain. The pattern chosen is known as the
Royal Lily Pattern and is printed in underglaze blue
and enriched with gold. The design was originally adapt-
from the Chinese in the Worcester factory between 1757
and 1788, and was selected by King George. III and Queen
Charlotte when they. visited the works in 1788.
Throughout its 200 years history, the Worcester factory
has produced distinguished underglaze blues. The Worcester
factory was one of the first to be established in England
in the middle of the eighteenth century. European potters
were discovering how to produce porcelain similar to the
Chinese ware, and its early products rank with those of
Bow and Chelsea in the "Golden Age" of English porcelain.
The craftsmanship inherited from those days has helped
to produce this royal present.

which forms the wedding present
of their Majesties, to the King of

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION EVENING PAPERS MARCH, 12th, 1946.

THE REVIVAL OF THE BRITISH COTTON INDUSTRY.
The world hunger for cotton goods and textiles of all kinds,
together with the Government's realisation that maximum exports
are necessary if Britain is to recover the war years, have
given a new lease of life to the mills of Lancashire, which
represent Britain's greatest export industry. Cotton being
even more important in peace than in war, a constant and
sustained demand is anticipated, and it is good to know that
the bitterness of the years of depression is being eliminated
by regular work, and such in improvements of holidays with pay
and better working conditions, and up-to-date plant and machinery.
This old industry is once again attracting youth, because there
are now more opportunities for promotion than ever before, for the
boy willing to study, and for the bright girl who has always been
essential in the mills. These photographs illustrate how youth is
taking over from age in Lancashire, and how the chimneys are
smoking again after years of depression idleness. They include the
operations of spinning and weaving in two mills. The picture shows:-
Mrs E. Cocker, aged 50, with 35 years in the cotton industry,
9 instructs the young idea in the art of piecing up on the ring frame.
Her assistant is Miss Edith Croasdale, aged 15. They work at the
Talbot Spinning and Weaving Mills at Chorley, Lancs.

XH) KENT HOP STRINGING COMPETITION

Believed to be the only contest of its kind in the world,
the annual Hop Stringing Competition, organised by The
Weald of Kent Ploughing Match Association, took place
to-day at Spitzbrook, Collier Street, Kent. About 40
Kentish farmworkers, all experts in hop stringing, and
many of them coming from families which have worked in
the hop gardens for generations, took part. The
stringer's job is to prepare hop gardens for the next
crop by putting up a complicated pattern of strings which
the hops can climb. He works from with a pole 10 feet
long, guiding the string (drawn from a bag slung over
his shoulder) from hooks in the ground to others hanging
on wires overhead. He is followed by a "bander in"
(usually female) who binds together the groups of
vertical strings comprising a "hill". In the
competition, each stringer completes a "cant" of 200
hills. Some 40 miles of string are used in the process.
Competitors score points for speed, neatness and economy
in the use of string. The object of the competition is
to stimulate interest in the craft and to encourage
ability in a highly skilled branch of agricultural work.

Photo shows:- Mr. F. Bond stringing during the
competition.

BY ANNE BUILER
ARCHITECT Mr. Eric Lyons tried to design ultra-modern houses when he
planned a small estate of 51 houses. And he succeeded—say the experts.
So well, in fact, that he has just received one of the principal awards in this
year's Good Housing Design Competition.

The competition was organised jointly by the Ministry of Housing and the Royal
Institute of British Architects to “promote the highest standards of design in
housing schemes.” Both local authorities and private developers competed.

The 1961 design for living

But what do the people
living in Lyons-designed
houses think of them?

I went to Waldegrave-park,
Twickenham, Middx, yesterday
and the verdict from the people
who live in them was over-
whelming. They like them.

Mrs. Kathleen Kaye, 32-year-
old wife of a civil engineer,
listed her likes:

Safety—for my children. The
garages are behind the
houses. And the houses are built
round a green cut off from any
traffic.

Refuse collection: easy, with
dustbins hidden near back gates.

Every house is roomy. Small
by accepted standards, but they
seem spacious.

There is under-floor electric
heating. There are no open
fires. And we don't miss them.

I am impressed with the way
every inch of space is utilised.
Instead of walls between the
bedrooms, there are large roomy

Food 131
Meat & Sausages
INDUSTRY. FOOD. MEAT

SPICER
THE SKIN is lifted off
Britain's beloved
banger in an all-revealing
report issued today.
And the verdict after
a massive survey of
sausages is: They're
better than ever.
Which?, the Consumers'
Association magazine, did
the survey.
They say that sausages—
also known as hangers,
snarlers, dogs, wallies and
snorkers—are bursting with
popularity.

60 TYPES
Every man, woman and
child in Britain eats an
average of three-and-a-half
sausages a week—a total of
9,000million in a year.
But what exactly are they
eating?
Which? tested 60 varieties
of large, fresh pork sausages

MORE MEAT AND VALUE
THAN THERE USED TO BE
and found that their meat
content varied from 55 to 96
per cent.
All but three brands had
more than the 32-and-a-
half per cent. minimum of
lean meat laid down by the
Food Standards Committee
eight years ago.

RICE
Sausage fillers analysed
by the experts included
wheat, rice, potato, skim
milk powder and soya.
Which? say: "Sausages
are better now—as far as
the amount of meat is con-
cerned—than they were
eight years ago.
"Prices now bear more
relation to meat content.
With a few exceptions, the
more you pay the more
meat there is." The experts
say there is a strong case
for having a compulsory
standard of meat content or
for sausage makers to print
the content on labels.

'DEFEAT'
About a third of the saus-
ages were considered to
have a slight, or very slight,
taste of pork and 11 brands
had a strong pork taste.
But when it came to pick-
ing the best sausage on sale,
the experts had to admit
defeat.
They say: "We obviously
can't make up your minds
for you about which saus-
age you prefer.
"Pork sausages, thank
goodness, have no standard
taste."

(XM) L.C.C.'S NEW PAINT-TESTING LABORATORY

In order to enable a systematic check to be maintained
on the qualities of the 200,000 gallons of paint used
annually by the London County Council the chemical
laboratories at County Hall, London, S.E., have been
extended and re-equipped at a cost of about £2,000.
The Public Health Department's Chemist-in-Chief has for
some years been responsible for testing paints used by
the Council on its housing estates, schools and other
establishments. The large quantities of paint now
needed and the increasing complexity of materials used
in manufacture have made it necessary to improve testing
facilities and to instal modern equipment for measuring
such qualities as weathering, hardness and anti-corrosion.
The new paint laboratory has been equipped to supplement
the examination of decorative and protective coatings
which has been made hitherto. The L.C.C. spends
considerably more than £1,000,000 each year in
its painting programme.

Photo shows:- "Mr. K.F.W. Doughty, a chemist in the
L.C.C. Paint-testing Laboratory, putting a sample of
paint in the accelerated weathering machine. This is
designed to produce the effect of years of exposure
to weather in a relatively short time.

EMPLOYMENT EXCHANGE JUBILEE.

The 50th. Anniversary of the establishment of the Employment
Exchange takes place on Monday, 1st. February, 1960. On that
date in 1910, 62 exchanges in England, Wales and Scotland were
opened for business and many other were strated in the following
months. The Labour Exchanges (as they were then called) had
been set up as a result of legislation piloted through the House
of Commons by Sir Winston Churchill who was then President of the
Board of Trade. to-day there are nearly 1.000 Employment Exchanges
and the Ministry of Labour has been responsible for their
administration since 1916. An average of over 2,000,000 jobs a
year have been filled by the Exchanges since the were set up.

D. 101089.
An exterior view of the most recently opened Employment Exchange.
It is in the new town of Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire, and
was brought into use on the 10th. November, 1959. The building
is shared with other Government Departments.

9 - AUG 1946

MORE FURNITURE GOES INTO ARMY HUTS DESPITE QUIT NOTICES.

A policy of 'sit tight' and await developments has been adopted
by ex Servicemen who, with their wives and children, have moved
into unoccupied military huts in St. Paul's Road, Peterborough,
Northamptonshire, because they were unable to find other
accommodation as a result of the housing shortage. Notices to
quit have been served on some of the 'squatters', and German
prisoners have been brought in by the military authorities to
start pulling down huts on the site scheduled for demolition.
Among the families installed are Mr. and Mrs. Harry Joseph Vines
and their 3½-year-old daughter Patricia. Mr. Vines, now an
inspector in a Diesel factory, is a former Petty Officer in the
Navy who won the British Empire Medal for bringing a lifeboat
safely to land after it had been 39 days in the Atlantic following
the torpedoing of a troopship. Whilst recovering from his
ordeal in New York he met Caroline - now his wife - who comes
from Brooklyn.
PHOTO SHOWS:- Mr. Derek Mottram, former paratrooper, pushing a
truck laden with some of his belongings to one of the Nissen huts.
Assisting him are Mrs. Caroline Vines (right), holding Patricia's
hand, and Mrs. Helen Holmes (left). Both women are occupying huts.

THE PROGRESS OF A NEW TOWN

population and industry from the crowded area of Inner London,
and which are expected to take about 250,000 Londoners. Harlow's

PITHEAD SHALE FOR SITE OF NEW HOVERPORT.

Lorries loading shale at Chislet colliery, Kent, for the 10 mile
journey to Pegwell Bay, where it will be used in the construction of the
new international hoverport. Half of Chislet's north west tip (about 280,000
cubic yards) is being removed to form the base for the 12-acre landing and

RADIO-CONTROLLED PLOUGH IS NEW IDEA FOR BRITISH FARMERS.

A radio-controlled farm tractor, developed by a British firm,
Tractors (London) Ltd., in co-operation with the Automatic
Control Section of the Royal Aeronautical Establishment is
undergoing trials at Barnet, Hertfordshire.
Radio-control apparatus used in the 'Queen Bee', the target
plane devised for anti-aircraft artillery practice, has been
adapted for use in the tractor, which can be employed for
ploughing and other farm operations.
Incoming radio signals operate sensitive electrical relays in the
receiver, so that by means of compressed air servomotors
the tractor can be made to run on a straight course, or to turn
left or right. The plough can be raised when the tractor
turns at the end of a furrow, the plough-raising system being
cut out when other implements are attached to the tractor.
The radio-controlled tractor is so much lighter than the
conventional type that fuel normally consumed in one hour is
sufficient for a whole day's work.
PHOTO SHOWS:- The tractor with radio-control apparatus, and
the transmitter (on ground in foreground). The man on right
is holding the tiny master switch by means of which the
tractor is directed.
