27.11.47.
A new altitude chamber has been built at the
Hatfield works of the de Havilland Aircraft Co.Ltd.,
makers of the famous jet planes, etc. The purpose
of the chamber is the research into the use of
equipment at high altitudes - altitudes that may be
in common use in the future as more and more know-
ledge is gained of the stratosphere and jet engine
performance.
The main chamber is 35 feet long and 14 feet in
diameter, and in it conditions of atmospheric pressure,
temperature and humidity can be reproduced of vary-
ing altitudes up to 80,000 feet. A team of observers
control the tests; a number of them are stationed in
the chamber, and a two-way system of communications
with those outside enables a complete check to be made
of the happenings to whatever material is being put
to test. Confirming these reports is a complicated
system of strain gauges and other indicators, supple-
mented by a microphone which amplifies the sounds of
structure breaking up, and transmits them to those out-

DUCHESS' CORONATION GOWNS.
,000-YEAR-OLD ART MASTERED AT KENT CASTLE

The only English silkworm farm, established at
Lullingstone Castle, Kent, by Lady Hart Dyke,
is producing the silk which will be used to make
the purple velvet Coronation gowns for the
Duchesses of Gloucester and Kent.
The 5,000-year-old art of cocoon reeling has
been mastered at the farm and five years after
its foundation millions of silkworms are bred.
The brooding and feeding rooms occupy the entire
west wing of the Castle and to food the worms
27,000 mulberry bushes are grown.
The silkworms spin their cocoons on straw
structures producing one thin thread up to
half a mile in length in 48 hours.

ESTEN ILLUS. 10.6.42
LAND GIRL DISCOVERED AS WATER DIVINER.
It has taken the Women's Land Army to find out
that Miss Littler, a volunteer in the employment
of the Flintshire War Agricultural Executive
Committee possesses the gift of water divining.
Miss Littler joined the Women's Land Army March 1941
and is one of 9 girls employed on gang work.
Recently they were working on a piece of land which
was constantly being flooded by a hidden spring.
Mr.J.T.Richards, the Executive Officer of the
Flintshire War Agricultural Executive Committee,had
made extensive efforts to have the spring located.
Finally, he asked the 9 members of the Women's Land
Army, who were clearing the land, to try with a
hazel stick to see if they could divine this spring.
Miss Littler was found to be the only one who
possesses this unusual gift. 1983-5236/66652
Since Flintshire farmers have heard of this there
have been many requests for her services, to help
in reclaiming flooded land and so save hundreds
of pounds in drainage. Also farmers wish to use
her to help to discover water for sinking wells.
O.P.S.1. The first step to becoming a Diviner
is to cut a forked twig from a hazel tree.
Miss Littler who is 19 years of age is seen on
right.

The day the flats collapsed.

MISS IVY HODGE, grey haired and marked
by the memory of Ronan Point flats disaster, was helped
into a packed Newham Town Hall yesterday (Tuesday)
to re-live those moments of horror.
"I went to bed at 10.45 - and read a little,"
said the 55-year-old woman, released especially from
Poplar Hospital to give evidence at the inquiry.
"At 2.25 I was awake and I went into the
kitchen to fill the kettle for a cup of tea ... I
cant remember any more. There was a flash across
the ceiling and then the ceiling began to flake."
The inquiry was hushed as Miss Hodge
who lived in a 19th floor flat at Ronan Point - and
is still alive - chose her words. Asked if she
smelt gas she replied : "I didn't smell nay gas
and I have a good sence of smell."
She sobbed at the end of giving evidence
and was helped back to hospital by two friends.
She is under treatment for burns to her
face arms and legs.

LORD ROBENS SEES 'FANTASTIC' NEW
COAL-CUTTING MACHINE
March 12th 1962 PAR 95059-2 (Sh-R)

LORD ROBENS SEES 'FANTASTIC' NEW
COAL-CUTTING MACHINE

LORD ROBENS, Chairman of the National
Coal Board, is pictured (centre, right)
as he watched a revolutionary new mining
machine, the Collins Miner, being demonstrated
to-day (Monday) at the Swadlincote
(Derbyshire) Test Site of the Board's Central
Engineering Establishment.
Seen with Lord Robens is Mr. H.E. COLLINS,
National Coal Board Member for Production,
who pioneered the project.
Lord Robens, who described the machine as
'fantastic', said that manned by 20 men for
three shifts it could produce 1,000 tons of
coal a day, normal output of 300 miners.
The Collins Miner, a cutting and loading
machine which has already cost £100,000 to
develop, has been designed to extract coal
from thin seams where narrow, confined spaces
make conditions exhausting for men.
It consists of a train of special vehicles
run on rails into an underground roadway.
A boring machine remotely controlled by one
man, thrusts into the coal seam feeding the
cut coal back to an extending conveyor belt.

July 13th 1953 PAR 36404-1 (BKS-R)

MODERN GIRL IN THE WEB OF CENTURIES

For at least seven centuries, the manufacture
of nets, ropes, sailcloth and other hempen
products has been the staple industry of
the town of Bridport, Dorset.
Of Bridport's present-day population of about
6,000, over a thousand - many of them young
women - are engaged in the industry,
directly or indirectly.
At one time locally-grown flax and hemp were
used, but nearly all the raw material is
now imported.
It is recorded that all the ropes and sails
for King John's Navy (he reigned from
1199-1216) were made at Bridport. And the
expression 'stabbed by a Bridport dagger' for
a person who had been hanged was current
in 1530, when King Henry VIII reigned.
This picture was taken in the Bridport works
of Joseph Gundry and Co.Ltd., a firm founded
in 1665 and still controlled by lineal
descendants of the founder. There were
Gundrys engaged in the trade as early as 1580.
PICTURE SHOWS:- A modern girl of Bridport
plying a centuries-old trade. She is
MARJORIE KINDELL, soon mending nets.

MJH/FM.
Crossing the Atlantic by the ton are British-made
darts and dartboards which are proving a very
valuable export in the dollar market . For a dart-
craze is sweeping America and the British version of

manufacturer (Thomas Salter, Ltd. of Winchmore Hill) is
exporting "Anglo-American" dart boards, which have the
British board on one side and the American -style board
on the reverse side.

Winchmore Hill Games and Toy Factory (Thomas Salter, Ltd)
showing the dart boards which are proving such a valuable
dollar export. The board she is holding is turned to
show the "American-style" dartboard, while above it, is a
similar board turned to the reverse side, which has the
British version of the dartboard on it. The game of
darts as played in this country is becoming very popular
in the U.S.A.

Transcribed_Text:
IN SOME WAYS Beaconsfield
Buildings, just a short bus ride
from the glitter of Piccadilly
Circus, could be considered a
showplace.

For to film producers at least, the
grey-bricked, five-storey blocks of flats
seem to have an irresistible fascina-
tion.

There was Max Bygraves in Cry From
the Streets, and Spare the Rod and
Spoil the Child. There was Joe Brown
in What a Crazy World. And Jess
Conrad in The Boys.
Each finding in the rows of miserable
flats—known without affection as The
Crumbles—the perfect setting for a film
about slums.

For today Beaconsfield Buildings has
about as much in common with the
affluent gadget world of 1964 as it did
when Prime Minister Disraeli laid the
foundation stone in 1875.

The plumbing is still Victorian. There
are few separate kitchens, few bath-
rooms, and landing lavatories shared by
between five and eight families.

On Sunday 200 of the 440 tenants
marched five miles from the flats in
Randall's Road, near King's Cross, to the
Chelsea home of Housing Minister Sir
Keith Joseph. To ask him to pull The
Crumbles down.

Their case? Well, it can be found in
the story of just three families.
CASE ONE: Mrs. Bridget Welsh, aged 45,
wife of a labourer, lives in three rooms
and a partitioned kitchen at £1 14s. 2d.
a week. Her flat is spotless.
She said: "Six weeks ago my girl
Geraldine—she's 10—caught dysentry.
Not from our lavatory because I clean it
constantly, and not from her school be-
cause she was the only one.
"I'm afraid she caught it round the
Buildings—from open dustbins, bad, smelly
drains, or dirty walls."
CASE TWO: Mrs. Bridget Sullivan, aged
26, wife of a factory worker, with children
Michael, 3, Theresa, one, in two rooms, no
kitchen, at £1 6s. 10d. a week. Her flat
is spotless.

XD) AUSTRALIAN BINDER AT WORK ON FORMER
PARKLAND. REMINDER OF A FORMER INVASION
THREAT.

Delving back into history when Europe was dominated
by Napoleon and England stood on the waiting list,
the fine old park lands at Bushy Park, Hampton,
Middlesex, were turned over to the needs of agricul-
ture and food production. After that period they
became park lands again up till to-day. Now
invasion threatens again and once more food production
must be served. To-day, the McKay Massey Harris
Sunshine Binder - new importation to this country
from Australia - is at work on the park lands: gave
interesting demonstrations to officials and Dominion
representatives. Fine oats are being grown on the
fields which were first ploughed up last November and
cross-harrowed in March. Yield is now 60-80 bushels p
per acre. Wheat and barley are also being grown.
The new binder, which should prove very satisfactory
to the English market, has a six-foot cut; refinements
include grease-gun pressure lubrication; gun-metal
bearings for the packers; enclosed oil-bath for the
main bevel gear drive. The big wheel is all metal,
wood is replaced in the decks by galvanized steel.
The sheaf carrier is simplicity itself.

Photo shows:- The horse team cutting the oats.
MR. A.R.MANTHYLLOW (Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries)
can be seen at back examining the cut.

MACE IN THE MAKING

Craftsmen employed by a 74-years-old firm of London
silversmiths are now engaged on a task which is a
test of their skill - the production of the massive
mace to be presented by the House of Commons to the
new parliament for the Federation of Rhodesia and
Nyasaland. 100 ounces of silver are being used for
it and seven different categories of craftsmen are
putting their knowledge and skill into its
completion. 20 separate pieces are being soldered
together to make the finished piece. When completed
it will be 32 3/4 inches long. Nobody yet knows how
much the mace will weigh as it cannot be estimated
in advance how much gold will be required to guild
it. Only a single piece is being made to the design
and the craftsmen have no completed "article upon
which to base their calculations. The mace, which
is an exact replica in outline of the historic
House of Commons Mace, has been designed by Mr. R.H.
HILL, an instructor at the London County Council
Central School of Arts and Crafts.

RECORDED 17 JUL 1947

WAR ON THE COLORADO BEETLE.
Drastic measures are being taken to combat the threat of invasion
of the Colorado beetle, and war has been declared by the authorities
responsible for the protection of the crops in Great Britain.
The agricultural areas around the airports, where aircraft from
overseas land, where potatoes are grown, are being sprayed as a
precaution against this pest.
Members of the National Fire Service are rendering valuable
assistance by carrying the water used to make the spray.
A solution of lead arsenate, deadly to the beetle but not harmful
to the crops, is sprayed over the halms of the potatoes from multi
jets at the back of the tractors.
The beetles stow away in aircraft from the Continent, and, as they
live only on potatoes, make for the nearest field of them.
These photographs were taken near Staines and Harmondsworth, to
the North and South of the London Airport at Heathrow.
PHOTO SHOWS:- The sprayers in action against the Colorado beetle
in a thirty acres field of potatoes in the Harmondsworth area.
Behind is a National Fire Service water-carrying team,

Transcribed_Text:
1983-5236/44033
Housing--Accidents--Flats Disaster at Canning Town,London
May 1968.
F S.N.A
MISS IVY HODGE (56)
in hospital
6 severe sms?

A GAS explosion in a kitchen
where a woman was making
a cup of tea is believed to
have caused yesterday's
collapse of skyscraper flats in
East London.
Three people died, and 11
were injured, as a wing of the
22-storey block broke away from
the rest of the building and
crashed to the ground "like a
pack of cards."
One of the injured was the
woman making a cup of tea, 56-
year-old Miss Ivy Hodge. Last
night she was recovering from face
burns in hospital.

As inquiries into the
collapse went on last
night scores of families
evacuated from the
block's 110 flats said they
never wanted to live in a
skyscraper flat again.

Mr. James Callaghan, the
Home Secretary, went to the
flats a few hours after the
collapse and appointed a
team of experts to make a
preliminary report to him by
lunchtime today.

At least three other in-
quiries will be held—one of
them by the Taylor Wood-
row firm who built the block,
and others like it, in the
London borough of Newham.

The cause of the explosion
was confirmed by Com-
mander Arthur Milbury,
head of the eastern area of
the London Fire Brigade.

He said: “There appears
to have been a gas explosion
in one of the flats. Gas fit-
tings were completely blown
away."

MISS IVY HODGE, the
woman who was making a
cup of tea when the ex-
plosion came, lay in a
hospital bed last night
(above) and told of her
miracle escape.

She said: "I had just
filled the kettle when I
suddenly found myself on
the floor.
"I managed to stagger
to the door and people
helped me down to safety."
Miss Hodge, who lives in
Flat 90 on the 18th floor,
said she could not remem-
ber turning on the gas or
striking a match.

WORLD'S FIRST ROTODIP PLANT GUARDS BRITISH CARS AGAINST
RUST.
Coventry, Eng: The turnspit went out with the stage-
coach but the idea has been revived in the great
Fisher and Ludlow plant - subsidiary of Standard Motors -
near here to protect bodies of the latest 'Vanguards'
from rust.
'Spitted' on a revolving ro d 20 feet long by four
inches in diameter, the bodies pass through the
world's first Rotodip plant of six process tanks each
holding five to seven thousand gallons of cleaning
and phosphating liquids.
From this section the bodies pass into the hot-air
drying oven then into the primer paint compartment.
Throughout the journey the bodies are evenly rotated
until reaching the baking oven.
Full complement of the 300 feet by 20 feet plant is
33 bodies, processed at the rate of 18 an hour.
Treatment time is one hour fortyseven minutes.
PHOTO SHOWS: 'Spitted' Vanguard bodies pass into the
Rotodip at the Coventry plant. Rollers at the end
of the spit engage on the traction chain passing

"ROLL OUT THE BARREL"
A FULL-FLEDGED COOPER IS BORN
DG/Tan
Among the last of the craftsmen to retain
their ancient customs and ceremonies is the
ancient trade of Cooperage, and at the
Guinness Brewery, Park Royal, Apprentice
G. E. R. BARNS was literally "put through
the hoop" when he came out of his time
and became a full fledged cooper. First
he was dumped into a new barrel of his own
making, then shavings, coloured dyes, and
all the most obnoxious brewery material his
comrades could find, tipped over him. During
the pouring an "orchestra" of tubes, pipes
and pieces of metal kept up a continuous
clamour. Apprentice BARNS was then rolled the
full length of the brewery at Park Royal.
After the rolling, he was permitted to "come
up for air", given a drink, and then "tossed
up" by his workmates. Still smiling, he
cleans himself up and is "sacked" and re-
engaged by the Head Cooper in the status
of a fully qualified COOPER.
PHOTO SHOWS:- Covered in muck and slush,
Apprentice G.E. BARNS emerges from his cocoon (barrel)
with a broad smile. he is almost a full fledged
cooper.

STANMORE POTTERS HOID THEIR OWN EXHIBITION. EH/FM
Probably for the first time since it was made, about 5,000
years ago, a large Minoan vase is back in a pottery, for it
is the central exhibit in an exhibition in the Orchard Studio,
Stanmore-hill, Stanmore, now being staged by Mr and Mrs E.C.
Collyer. Mrs Collyer is better known as Pamela Nash. The vase,
which is 20 inches high, 50 inches in circumference, and would
hold about four gallons of water, is made of a sandy-coloured
clay, and is decorated with the traditional spirals, or "bull's eyes"
of the period, which depicts the worship of the bull in the Palace
of Minos, in Knossos, Crete.

Photograph shows :- Mr and Mrs E.C. Collyer seen studying the
5,000 year old MINOAN VASE. Mrs Collyer is known as PAMELA NASH
who is an art painter and potter. She is seen holding the vase
while her husband is seen examining the design, and checking the design
with a reference Book. It us on show at No.2 Stanmore Hill, Stanmore,
Middlesex.

RESTORATION WORK AT ETON COLLEGE.
MJH/30G.
Extensive restoration work is now in progress on the
Cloisters of Eton College, the cost of which is being
borne by the Eton Appeal Fund, to which the Dulverton
Trustees have contributed the sum of £20,000 to be
expended on this work. Restoration has been made
necessary due to the following defects a) general
deterioration of stonework; b) flaking of the stone
facing on the upper part of the Cloisters; c) dry
rot and death watch beetle in roof timbers : d) on
the upper part of the Cloisters, the bonding between the
outer stone facing and the brick wall behind it, was no
longer effective, resulting in bulging of the outer stone
wall which had become dangerous in places. The original
stone used on the Cloisters, believed to be some form of
Clunch, is being replaced by Clipsham stone from Rutland
which is much more hard-wearing.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS; Brothers ALBERT and JAMES WINCH
of Ascot seen working on the restoration of a stone
arch in the Cloisters of Eton College.

PEER TO VISIT PIT GIRLS. MJH/VIG

In reply to a challenge by Viscount Hall, arising out of
controversy over the second reading of the Mines and Quarries
Bill in the House of Lords, the Earl of Selkirk, Paymaster
General, is to spend part of his holidays touring collieries
to "see for himself" conditions under which the "pit brow
Lassies" work. Viscount Hall declared that there were
still about 1,000 women employed at the pit tops in conditions
almost as bad as those prevailing at the time when women were
taken out of the pits nearly 100 years ago.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: A general view of "pit brow lassies" at
work on the cleaning of coal at Bickershaw Colliery, Leigh
near Manchester. Some of the women have been doing this work
for more than 20 years and all say that although the job is very
dirty, it is quite congenial. They work 8-hour shifts, 7a.m.
to 3p.m. or another short finishing at 10.30 p.m. A modern
bath-house similar to the miners pithead bath is provided so that
the women can leave the colliery quite clean. Protective
clothing is also provided.

AUSTRALIAN PRIME MINISTER TO OPEN GAUR DAM
(pr. 17.6.53.
Mr ROBERT G. MENZIES, Prime Minister of Australia,
will open the Nth of Scotland Hydro-Electric Board's
new Dam and Power Station on the river Gaur, 3 miles
from Rannoch Station on the fringe of the dreaded moor
of Rannoch, in West Perthshire on June 20th.
The scheme is on the ancient lands of Glen Menzies, near
one of the few surviving parts of the old Caledonian Forest.
Loch Eigheach will be enlarged and raised 30' by a
crescent-shaped dam 40' high and 370' long. A 6,000 KW
power station on the River Gaur will produce 17 million
units of Electricity each year. The picture shows:-

No 1. The setting of the Gaur Dam showing Loch Eigheach
behind the rocky River Gaur in right foreground. The
ancient "Road to the Isles" now has a dam sitting on it
(see wall on right) and the road behind the dam will be
submerged. 1½ miles of new road has been built to take
its place.

FIRST PUBLICATION WEDNESDAY'S EVENINGS 18.12.46.

WINTER'S PROBLEM FOR WORLD'S BIGGEST GAS WORKS

Mr Shinwell's latest pronouncement on the coal situation
will have been received nowhere with greater interest than at the
Beckton plant of the Gas Light and Coke Company, of London, which
is the largest gasworks in the world. The works are capable of
producing daily 120 million cubic feet of gas equalling 600,000
therms, but actual production is, of course, dependent upon the
amount of coal available. Beckton is situated upon the North
bank of the Thames just East of the Royal Albert Dock, and has
a river frontage of 2500 ft for the handling of its coal, which
comes by water mainly from the coalfields of Durham. The works
cover 280 acres (540 acres including the adjoining chemical works)
and there are over 70 miles of full-guage railway tracks for
internal transport. The picture shows: Horizontal retort being
re-charged with coal by projector machine on other side of retort

WHEN you're only 23
months old, nobody's

Wee Jimmy Smith, wearing

flight—in a Comet II—from
Marham to Leuchars.
As the plane brought the
Queen to earth, men of the
famous 43 Squadron stood ready
for the presentation of their
blue and gold standard.
Another thrilling moment for
the Queen was when she took
over the microphone of the air
control tower at Leuchars.

THE MODERN GIRL PLIES A CENTURIES-OLD TRADE
July 13th 1953 PAR 36404-3 (BKS-R)
---------------------------------------
THE MODERN GIRL PLIES A CENTURIES-OLD TRADE

For at least seven centuries, the manufacture
of nets, ropes, sailcloth and other hempen
products has been the staple industry of
the town of Bridport, Dorset.
Of Bridport's present-day population of about
6,000, over a thousand - many of them young
women - are engaged in the industry,
directly or indirectly.
At one time locally-grown flax and hemp were
used, but nearly all the raw material is
now imported.
It is recorded that all the ropes and sails
for King John's Navy (he reigned from
1199-1216) were made at Bridport. And the
expression 'stabbed by a Bridport dagger' for
a person who had been hanged was current
in 1530, when King Henry VIII reigned.
This picture was taken in the Bridport works
of Joseph Gundry and Co. Ltd., a firm founded
in 1665 and still controlled by lineal
descendants of the founder. There were
Gundrys engaged in the trade as early as 1580.
PICTURE SHOWS:- Two of the girls in the
Bridport net trade - ARINA RUNDELL (left)
and SHIRLEY WARD - rigging seine fishing-net
25 yards long. It will fish to a depth
of eight feet.

ROYAL PRESENT FOR KING OF THAILAND.
26.4.50.

For their wedding present to the King of Thailand
their Majesties, have chosen a service of Worcester Royal
Porcelain. The pattern chosen is known as the Royal Lily
Pattern and is printed in underglaze blue and enriched with
gold. The design was originally adapted from the Chinese at
the Worcester factory between 1751 and 1788, and was selecte
by King George III and Queen Charlotte when they visited the
works in 1788. Throughout its 200 years history, the Worceste
factory has produced distinguished underglaze blues. The
Worcester factory was one of the first to be established in
England when, in the middle of the eighteenth century,
European potters were discovering how to produce porcelain
similar to the Chinese ware, and its early products rank wi
those of Bow and Chelsea in the "Golden age" of English
porcelain. The craftsmanship inherited from those days ha
helped to produce this royal present.

on a sauce tureen for the Royal
Present. In the foreground
are two of his tools, old moulding
pitchers handed down from one generatio
to the next. These tools are so valued
by the workman that they were once
accepted as currency in the factory.

"GRAVEYARD OF GIANTS"
WHERE BATTLESHIPS GO FOR SCRAP DG/PR

"Abandon Hope All Ye That Enter Here" is the ironic
warning over the entrance to the jetty of Messrs.
Thomas Ward, shipbreakers, of Inverkeithing,
Scotland, and so far as warships are concerned, the
phrase applies down to the last rivet.
Wards are the biggest shipbreakers in Britain, and
one of the largest in the world. Not only are they
the biggest shipbreakers, but they break up the
biggest ships. To their yards--and to others
such as Metal Industrials, or Arnott and Young's--
come such floating giants as "Rodney", "Revenge",
"Renown", the "New York", once Hitler's "strength
through joy" liner, and many others. Mighty fighting
ships which sailed triumphantly through two world
wars, find their last resting place under scrapyard
cranes. Guns which the combined fleets of
the Third Reich and Imperial Japanese Navy failed
to muffle, are silent as hissing oxy-acetylene
cutters carve into their vitals.
Much of the valuable scrap goes to sea again in
the form of new ships, and thus fights in Britain's
export drive. Brass, copper and much needed alloys
are sent to Sheffield, while metal scrap goes to
Newcastle.

PHOTO SHOWS:- The as yet untouched forepart of
H.M.S. Royal Sovereign, showing her forward turrets,
at T. Ward's scrapyard.

"ROLL OUT THE BARREL"
A FULL-FLEDGED COOPER IS BORN DG/Tan

Among the last of the craftsmen to retain
their ancient customs and ceremonies is the
ancient trade of Cooperage, and at the
Guinness Brewery, Park Royal, Apprentice
G. E. H. BARNE was literally "put through
the hoop" when he came out of his time
and became a full fledged cooper. First
he was dumped into a new barrel of his own
making, then shavings, coloured dyes, and
all the most obnoxious brewery material his
comrades could find, tipped over him. During
the "pouring" an "orchestra " of tubes, pipes
and pieces of metal kept up a continuous
clamour. Apprentice BARNS was then rolled the
full length of the Brewery at Park Royal.
After the rolling, he was permitted to "come
up for air", given a drink, and then "tossed
up" by his workmates. Still smiling, he
cleans himself up and is "sacked" and re-
engaged by the Head Cooper in the status
of a fully qualified COOPER

PHOTO SHOWS: Looking more like a circus
clown than a qualified Cooper, G.E.H. BARNS
is still smiling as he is rolled the length of
the Guinness Brewery by his comrades.

VETERAN OF INDUSTRY.
CW/7262-29. Mrs. Baddow reads the day's news while husband,
John, aged 84, enjoys his pipe after a day's work at the
"Sons of Rest" workshop. John now earns about £4. a week.
When he was 14, he got 7/-d per week.

THE OLD FOLK OF INDUSTRY
GK/7262. Seeking to prove a man is "not too old at 70"
is the engineering firm of Rubery, Owen and Co, of Darlaston,
Staffs who have started an "Old Folks Workshop" which they
call "Sons of Rest". Situated about a mile away from the
noise and bustle of the main factory, twelve men, all over
the age of 70 work on their own with no young workers beside
them to give them an inferiority complex over their ages.
The veterans start an hour later than the main factory. They
do drilling and assembly work on office equipment and farm
implements for overseas markets. The experiment has been
going on for 10 months and has proved a great success. Doctors
who are urging more active employment for elderly people for
the benefit of their health support it. It is also a means
of saving for industry skilled hands vitally necessary these
days, which would otherwise be lying idle.

BANK CLERKS WORK BY CANDLELIGHT AS LONDON'S ELECTRICITY
IS CUT.
Work went on by candlelight in banks, offices, shops
and other business establishments when electricity
was switched off in London in accordance with the
Government's plan for dealing with Britain's fuel crisis.
With generating plants' coal stocks'desperately low,
there is no electricity at all for non-essential
industries in London, the Midlands and North-west
England. Other establishments are 'switched off'
between the hours of 9 in the morning and 12 noon,
and between 2 o'clock and 4 o'clock in the afternoon.
The Government say the 'switch off' - which comes at
a time when Britain is striving to increase exports -
will last until coal supplies, interrupted by the
severest winter weather for at least 25 years, are
restored.

Come September next and Mr. Henry Jackson will
celebrate his eightieth birthday, but perhaps
celebrate isn't quite the right word, for at
the back of his mind he will remember he's had

WILSON FAMILY BUILD THEIR OWN HOUSE AT GRAVESEND -
DAD SWITCHED FROM BEAUFIGHTING TO BRICKLAYING.

Convinced that the only way to get a house in these days
of building shortages is to built it oneself,
ex-Beaufighter radio operator W. Wilson of Parrock Street,
Gravesend, Kent, has set about erecting his own home
in Milton Hall Road, Gravesend.
Released from the Royal Air Force two years ago and now
a foreman bricklayer, Mr. Wilson has enrolled his wife
(a State Registered Nurse) and their two children,
Robin, 5, and Frances, 3, in the project.
Mrs.Wilson claims she can mix a heap of concrete as well
as any professional, while Robin and Frances make good use
of their wheelbarrow (carrying capacity: three bricks).
Construction work is carried on in the evenings and at
week-ends. In one week-end the Wilson family laid
a total of 1,750 bricks.

with his three-year-old daughter, Frances, while (on right)

and show
a high pressure hose is directed at the clay, and the

STANDSTILL AT 80 M.P.H.

The photograph shows for the first time the phenomenon
known as 'aquaplaning'. The Dunlop technician is touching a
smooth tyre which, although under an 800 lb. load, remains
stationary while the drum beneath revolves at 80 m.p.h. The
tyre remains stationary because a thin film of water has penetrated
between the drum and the tyre, giving the tyre no grip or contact
with the rough surface of the drum.

The amount of water sprayed on to the drum, 6 gallons
per minute, is considerably less than the 8 - 10 pints per second
that a tyre would have to cope with at 50 m.p.h. on a wet road.
At speeds below 45 m.p.h. the tyre revolved at the same speed as
the drum, but thereafter, as the drum speed increased and as the
grip became less and less, the tyre slowed down until at between
60 and 80 m.p.h. it stopped rotating and 'aquaplaned'.

Driving with smooth tyres on wet roads involves serious
and unwarranted risks to the driver and other road users alike.

REVIVAL OF VILLAGE CRAFT
Most of the children who live in the small Cotswold
villages of Laverton and Buckland, wear articles of
woollen clothing which they have made themselves from
the wool of their local sheep, which they have collected
and spun on spinning wheels, under the instruction of
Miss Mary Osburn, in her small thatched cottage at
Laverton. KKKKKK Even the dyes for the wools are made from
local hedgerow plants. Miss Osburn went to Laverton some
years ago from the Bow Settlement and began teaching the
village children the art of spinning wool and making it
into useful articles, with the result that many of the
homes in the district now have rugs, bedding and clothing
made of local wool, much of which is collected by the
children from the hedges and fences on which the sheep
have left tufts when rubbing themselves.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: MISS MARY OSBURN taking a spinning
class in her cottage at Laverton. At the spinning wheels
are VALERIE BRYANT (10) and CAROL CLARKE (10), while,
on the window seat HAZEL BRYANT (10) is carding wool. Miss
Osburn instructs about 20 children a week.

WAR ON THE COLORADO BEETLE.

Drastic measures are being taken to combat the threat of invasion
of the Colorado beetle,and war has been declared by the authorities
responsible for the protection of the crops in Great Britain.
The agricultural areas around the airports, where aircraft from
overseas land, where potatoes are grown, are being sprayed as a
precaution against this pest.
Members of the National Fire Service are rendering valuable
assistance by carrying the water used to make the spray.
A solution of lead arsenate, deadly to the beetle but not harmful
to the crops, is sprayed over the halms of the potatoes from multi
jets at the back of the tractors.
The beetles stow away in aircraft from the Continent, and, as they
live only on potatoes, make for the nearest field of them.
Those photographs were taken near Staines and Harmondsworth, to
the North and South of the London Airport at Heathrow.
PHOTO SHOWS:- National Fire Service men pouring water into the
special tanks of lead arsenate mounted on the spraying tractors,
in the Harmondsworth area.

TEN MILLION POUND CONTRACT

Taylor Woodrow (Building Exports) Ltd., in
conjunction with the Arcon Group, have concluded

exports company of Taylow Woodrow (Building
Exports) Ltd., who was accompanied by Mr.
EDRIC NEEL, of Arcon, and Mr. A.E. WALLIS, of
Steward and Lloyds.

Photograph taken this afternoon (Tues) shows

"THE THATCHED HOUSE"
GETS A NEW OLD LOOK. DS/PH

Replacing a thatched roof with one of less harmonious
slate or tile, is nothing new in rural architecture,
but at Humberstone, near Grimsby, Lincolnshire, the
reverse process is taking place-thanks to the thatching
skill of two of the youngest craftsmen in the country.
Working on the farmhouse of Fowler's Dairy farm,
Humberston, the brothers PETER and BERT MORLEY, of
Wimblington (Ely) and Brampton, respectively, have
not only changed the front of the house, but also the
roof, which now has its original type of thatch
instead of a brick ridge.
Both under 40, the MORLEYS are among the youngest
in the Thatchers Federation. Their family has been
following the craft since 1600.

PHOTO SHOWS: "Eave Expert", PETER MORLEY uses the
ancient eave knife for trimming. Many craftsmen have
turned over to the sheep trimmer for this work, but
PETER swears by his razor-sharp instrument.

DAILY HERALD Feb. 25 1955 7

Tenants get 'buy or rent rise' threat

A PROPOSAL has been made to four tenants of a tenement in Wellington-street, Dundee, that they buy their houses—or pay a 40 per cent. rent increase.
One tenant, Mr. John Macbeth, aged 60, was told on a postcard from the landlord's agent, Mr. George J. Lindsay, a Dundee pharmacist:—
"You will note we have not yet added the permitted increase of 40 per cent. to the rents—but we are considering doing so after May term. "Meantime, should you wish to purchase the house before May 28, the price will be £200.
"After May the price will be based on the increased rental. The increase in your case will be 25s. per quarter."
The three other tenants have been told verbally of the landlord's plan.

PROPER WAY
Dundee's chief sanitary inspector, Mr. W. M. Smith, said yesterday: "A rent increase under the Housing and Repairs Act must be submitted to the tenant on the prescribed form, giving details of the proposed increase, the work undertaken and the amount spent over a specified period.
"It is not legal to do it verbally."
Mr. Lindsay, of Castle-street, Dundee, said: "This is a private matter. There is an Act which allows increases.
"I have done nothing yet. If anything is to be done it will be done legally."

DAILY HERALD
25 FEB 1955

SAFETY MASKS HAVE GLAMOUR NOW

GLAMOUR goes hand in hand with safety in the new protective masks shown in these two pictures.
They are the latest type of protective wear for factory workers and they will be shown, along with other specially-designed protective clothing, at an out-of-the-ordinary fashion display in London at the end of the month.
The show, part of an exhibition of factory equipment at the Royal Horticultural Hall, aims to prove that girls who do a tough job can still look feminine and attractive.
Two mannequins will parade in overalls instead of the usual elegant gowns; on their feet will be flat-heeled, steel-capped shoes instead of spike-heeled sandals.
And in place of frivolous hats they’ll wear snoods and dust masks.
The idea is to convince factory girls that there can be charm in the kind of clothing that keeps them safe and healthy while they work.

THE BATTLE goes on non-stop. Throughout the day and long into the night.
For Britain's farm workers, like these at Space Farm in West Horsley, Surrey, it is a battle to gather the remnants of their storm-thrashed harvest.
Farmer Percy Yates, who has been working in the glare of arc lamps and tractor lights, cannot remember a more difficult harvest: "We have had to work hard in appalling conditions."
He added: "We have had to take advantage of every minute during the last few days of fine weather."
"But the fields are soggy from all the rain and the corn has been beaten down. It is very hard to combine and it is thick with weeds and grass."

Excellent

At the headquarters of the National Farmers' Union in Knightsbridge, cold statistics tell the story: Somerset, only 30 per cent. of the harvest in. Wiltshire, only 50 per cent.
Said an official: "Men are harvesting in paddy field conditions. The whole harvest is two to three weeks behind.
"Even in places like Cornwall, where they have got 85 per cent. of the harvest in, the grain is light and the yield is below average."
The long-range weather forecast is far from heartening: "Cool, disturbed and occasional stormy weather. Intervals of more settled weather are likely to be brief. Rainfall totals are likely to exceed the average."
Provisional estimates for the 1965 harvest are considerably lower than last year when the good summer yielded excellent crops.

NEW JOBS FOR THE RHONDDA.
(See Feature Set Intro. No. 251).

New jobs have come to the Rhondda as 23 new factories
have been opened in the valley. During the depression
of the 1930's there was one collier to every 2.7 of the
total population and four men out of ten suffered up to
15 years of unemployment. Now the ratio is one collier
to every 7.6 of the total population and there are
alternative jobs. Not only is the economic future of
the Rhondda on a broader and safer base, but jobs are
available to those who fall victim to the dreaded dust
diseases which can turn a man from the pits at any age
from 20 until he retires.

D. 48412. (16). Training of labour has always been the first trouble
in the valleys, where mining and domestic work are the

SCOTTISH ABADAN D/TAN

Erected on the same site as the old buildings dating from 1924, the new Grangemouth Oil Refinery was built on the Firth of Forth by Scottish Oils Ltd., a subsidiary of the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company. Started in 1949, it went into operation in 1951, with maximum annual crude oil capacity of 2,500,000 tons, helping to counteract the Abadan collapse. Its main objective is high-grade motor spirit, and it also supplies the raw material for the production of petroleum chemicals. To cope with its capacity of 30,000 barrels, or just over 1,000,000 gallons a day of imported crude oil, it was decided to establish an installation at Finnart, on Loch Long, and run a pipeline from there to the refinery, this being more convenient than using the old Grangemouth Docks exclusively. The approximate cost of the combined project was £15,000,000.

A NEW STAR appeared in London's West End yesterday — Fairy Bell, the Dairy Council's amazingly pretty cow.
A prize-winning Jersey of impeccable pedigree and manners, Fairy Bell, appeared in Oxford Circus to publicise next month's National Dairy Festival.
Afterwards, a Council spokesman had nothing but praise for her performance.
"She behaved beautifully. Everyone loved her. She hardly put a foot wrong," he said.
This year's Dairy Queen, 20-year-old Miss Joan Harland from Wetherby, Yorkshire, showed that she is more than just a pretty

VILLAGE POTTERY LIVES ON                      D/VAN

In June this year it looked as though the village
pottery at Compton, near Guildford, Surrey, would
have to close down owing to financial difficulties.
This news occasioned considerable regret since the
potteries, first built in 1902 and rebuilt in 1923,
had become part of the village life. Four local
people decided to join forces to try and keep it
going. They are: David Dunhill ("Dunhill" of the
"Take it From Here" radio programme), of Shalford,
near Guildford; his wife Barbara; Charles Bone, 1949
winner of the Federation of British Industries Prize
for Industrial Design, who lives at Puttenham; and
P.B. Smith a Guildford Solicitor. On December 5th the
kiln fires were once again lit, the ceremony being
performed by the grandson of Mr. George Aubertin, who
has worked with the pottery since it was founded, and
hope was rekindled for the survival of the crafts of
England.

PHOTO SHOWS: At the revived Compton Potteries, Peter
Cowell is seen handing vases into the kiln where they
are received by Harry Yalden, who has had 34 years at
the potteries.

SILAS leans out of a window, torch in hand, Bambi beside him, as a caller arrives.
Son, ordered out of house, stays with two dogs
THE SIEGE OF Chatsworth Road
Express Staff Reporter
SILAS ("Let 'em all come") Bentley is waiting for 10 o'clock this morning. For that is the hour at which he has been told by the local council to quit a house owned by his father.
West Ham Council wants to put in more tenants at 5, Chatsworth-road, Forest Gate, which it requisitioned in 1940. The last tenant moved out 10 weeks ago.
Last night 25-year-old Silas was at heavily bolted No. 5. Determined, he said, to stay. And with him were dogs Bambi, a Boxer, and Jack, a Manchester terrier.
Silas's father, Mr. Charles Bentley, made frequent requests for his son to be allowed to move into the house. To each the council said "No."
Yesterday Silas got on a bicycle at his father's shop in nearby Forest-street and pedalled with his bed on his shoulders to Chatsworth-road.
Bambi and Jack followed him yelping. The Bentley family—mother, father, sister, niece, and nephew—brought up the rear.
They carried Silas's provisions for a possible siege—five tins of meat, three tins of dog food, two tins of peaches ("I'm fond of peaches"), and four loaves of bread.
Silas came to a bedroom window to answer questions last night. The dogs began barking. It was two minutes before they stopped.
Who goes there?
Silas, a burly, curly-headed, 5ft. 8in. figure, called down, "Who goes there?"
I said I was a reporter. There was no answer. I did not have the password.
Silas's mother came to the rescue. She stumped round the corner crying "Cuckoo." This was the signal. I walked in behind Mrs. B. The dogs bounded forward. Silas shouted: "Stop." I breathed again.
"It is my father's house. I am his tenant, and here I am staying," said Silas.
"My wife Myrtle, for whom I had no home is coming up from Devon to join me."
"How long do you think you can last out?" I asked.
"A long, long time," replied Silas.

HOUSING DEVELOPMENT & CONSTRUCTION LTD.

PROTOTYPE HOUSES BUILT IN THREE WEEKS

The prototype of a new system of industrialised house building has just been completed by Housing Development & Construction Ltd., at Stratford-upon-Avon. It is a pair of semi-detached, three bedroomed houses, designed and built to the full Parker-Morris Committee Recommendations, and to the specification of the local authority Stratford-upon-Avon M.B. It only required three weeks of normal working with a very small team of men to complete this pair of houses for occupation. This is undoubtedly the fastest erection time of any system of truly permanent housing for local authorities yet developed.

The kitchen is separated from the dining area by a servery which provides useful storage space and allows room for a refrigerator or washing machine. The built-in larder is to the right of the sink. FROM COTTAGE TO PRE-FAB. AW/MA.

A contrast in country housing is shown in these two
pictures from Woodmancote, Gloucestershire. Mr. and
Mrs. W. A. Stewart and their family have moved from
their picturesque but ramshackle old cottage into a
nearby prefab of a type now being erected in many

By COLIN HART
FIVE hundred angry tenants whose rents are to be raised mobbed councillors leaving a housing committee meeting last night. And after a scuffle with police, two men were arrested.
The tenants live in council houses at St. Pancras. Before the monthly meeting of the housing committee, they presented Councillor Paul Prior, chairman, with a petition.
Then, while the 13 committee members talked business in St. Pancras Town Hall, a chanting, hostile crowd gathered outside.
Women with shopping bags cried: "Not a penny on the rents," "Down with the Tories," and "Prior must go." Extra police were called in.
Soon after nine o'clock, councillors began to leave. The crowd surged forward as they walked down Euston-road. Fists were waved, and two mounted police cleared the Town Hall steps.

BANKSIDE POWER STATION: PRODUCTION GETS UNDER WAY
24448

London: An industrial project which has aroused
much controversy from the time of its conception
has just gone into operation.
It is the Bankside Power Station, at which
the first 60,000-kilowatt turbo-alternator of about
80,000 horse-power, has started to supply electricity.
The project was allowed on condition that oil and not
coal was to be burned. Other conditions which had to
be observed were that the building must be set back
far enough from the Thames so as not to interfere with
the projected road and promenade.
Opposition to the power station was so strong that
in January, 1947, a public inquiry was held, with the
result that the scheme was given Government sanction.
On completion the Bankside Power Station will
comprise four 60,000-kilowatt generating sets, the
oil consumption at full load (16-hour day) being
67 tons an hour, consuming in one winter's day about
850 tons.

SIXTH GENERATION OF CORNISH FAMILY
CARRIES ON AN OLD CRAFT.

MJH/P.1.

Although with today's modern methods, not many people
work with the same materials and tools as did their
grand-fathers, the village carpenter is one man, who,
despite modern improvements, often has to use the same
materials and tools as generations before him have done.
One such man is Mr. James Jelbert of Gulval (Penzance Cornwall),
who is the fifth generation of his family to carry on the
old trade of village carpenter, which means that, at some
time of other, every beam in the village of Gulval, must have
been fashioned by one of his family.  The knowledge for this
craft is passed down from father to son and the skill is
inherent in the Jelberts.  The sixth generation of the family,
Mr. Jelbert's son Evan, is also following the family craft and
works alongside his father in their Gulval workshop.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS:  Mr. Evan Jelbert, making cart wheels, watched
by the expert eye of his father, Mr. James Jelbert (right)
in their workshop at Gulval, Penzance, Cornwall.

A NEW LONDON RISES FROM THE OLD

The West Ham Corporation's "master plan" for the rebuilding of
the Tidal Basin area, one of the worst blitzed districts in the
country, is the first implementation of the Greater London Plan
by a local authority. In what was one of the most sordid of
London's dock areas, 47 acresof land have been bought, on which
well-planned homes, parks, community centres and schools will
replace rowsof mean streets. Tenders amounting to £300,000
have been accepted for 230 of the 700 houses that are to be
built, and it is hoped that the Ministry of Health will
approve the building of a further 127 at a cost of £147,317.
The Tidal Basin area suffered severely in the Nazi raids on
London's Docks, as many as eighteen parachute mines having said
to have fallen in one night. The picture shows:
a panoramic view of the 47 acresof devastation with
transformation work in progress.

FROM COTTAGE TO BOND STREET

A cottage industry which produces
hand-made shoes for the world's

six years' apprenticeship with the

member of the family supervises
each process of manufacture.

engaged in the industry.

Mr Shinwell's pronouncement on the latest coal situation
will have been received nowhere with greater interest than at the
Beckton plant of the Gas Light and Coke Company of London, which
is the largest gas works in the world. The works are capable of
producing daily 120 million cubic feet of gas equalling 600,000
therms, but actual production is, of course, dependent upon the
amount of ocal available.
Beckton is situated upon the North Bank of the Thames just
East of the Royal Albert Dock, and has a river frontage of 2500 ft
for the handling of its coal, which comes by water mainly from
the coalfields of Durham. The works cover 280 acres (540 acres
including the adjoining chemical works) and there are over 70 miles
of full-guage railway tracks for internal transport. The

One of the biggest contracts for large diameter steel
pipes ever placed in Britain has just been secured by
South Durham Steel and Iron Company, an old established
Teeside firm. The order, from the Basrah Petroleum Co.
(an associate of the Iraq Petroleum Company) is for the

markets for the British steel industry, the £900,000
order will mean a saving of some 2½ million dollars, as
hitherto most large diameter oil piping has been obtained
from the United States.

USED - 4 MAY 1938

ON the stained glass windows of Mr. John Burdett's home at Alderman's Hill, Palmer's Green, N., there are 14 Devices.
One is a Union Jack, another a Red Cross flag, a third a part of the arms on the reverse side of a silver coin.
The rest, Mr. Burdett thinks, are sections from towns' arms.
* * *
THE Devices were there two years ago when Mr. Burdett took the house; have been there, in fact, for 30 years.
Well, about Coronation time the Middlesex County Council said: "What about paying the armorial bearings duty?"
Mr. Burdett refused to pay, and the Council twice hailed him before the court.
Once the case was dismissed under the Probation of Offenders Act; the second time he was fined.
Still he refused to pay, maintaining that his Devices were not, as the Bench said, armorial bearings.
* * *
SO now the Middlesex County Council has decided to press the County Councils' Association to ask for the abolition of the duty.

although he is now 75-years-old. He is now teaching his
13-years-old grandson, Edward Beck, his craft, hoping that
the boy will follow in his footsteps as the village blacksmith.

KENT PIONEERS BUILD THEIR OWN HOMES, MJH/RS,

On a housing estate in Hawes Lane, Beckenham, (Kent) a group
of 25 pioneers are building their own homes in their spare
time. Only a few of them are builders by trade, the others
include, cashiers, clerks, shopkeepers, a Post Office engineer,

and amicable manner and while each man works with a will on a
friends bungalow, he looks forward to the time when he will
be working on his own.

GLASS-FIBRE ROOF CAR MAKES IT'S APPEARANCE.   EH/RS.

A British car with a complete all glass roof with all the
modern windows fitted in the ordinary splintex glass, is
now being tested on the streets to see if it stands up to the
weather conditions. The roof is glass-fibre cloth moulded
together with resin and taking four hours to cure. The
hood and roof can be dismantled in two minutes, making the
car a complete sports model. The weight is 45 lbs, exactly
half the weight of an ordinary car roof. The glass-fibre
has already been tested with a 4 lb hammer, and although
only 1/8" thick, no impression was made on it at all.
The Vanden Plas (England) 1923 Ltd, a famous British car
builders, have completed this roof and, although the whole
thing is moulded at first on a gig, there is no join
whatsoever.

1983 - 5236/40539

AGRIC - MACHINERY .

237168               DE
'TROLLEYBUS' TRACTOR GETS FIRST TRY-OUT

Reading, Berkshire: Something new in farming machinery is
the 'trolley-bus' tractor, an electric device invented by
Russian scientists, and now being tried for the first time in
this country.
The miniature tractor, seen being operated by 17-year-old Yvonne
Shepheard, has no engine. It is driven instead by a simple
electric motor powered from the mains. A strong, thin cable
links the tractor with a wooden pylon in the middle of the
market garden. The cable is automatically paid out as the
girl drives away. Counterweights take up the slack as she returns.
The scientists at the Electrical Research Association Laboratory
near Reading, who are testing the garden 'trolley bus', claim it
has three outstanding advantages over an engine-powered tractor:-
It is much cheaper to run. It needs less attention and is almost
free from breakdowns. It is much more powerful for its size.

ESTEN . D.H. 1983-5236/910508 1.2.44.
NAT'S SCORE IS 25,000 not out.
In the tiny hamlet of Milford situated on the
outskirts of Salisbury lives 70 year old Nathaniel
Barber, Blacksmith for 53 years. Nat belongs to
a fast dying profession, for blacksmiths are now
becoming a rarity.
Motor Engineer is the new term for where Nat used
to shoe over 200 horses six times a year, now only
20 come to him to be reshod.
Nat's father was a blacksmith as were four of his
eight brothers of whom he is the only one left.
In spite of the lack of horses to shoe, Nat
persuaded his 40 year old son to learn the craft
and now when Nat passes on, Ronald will become the
fourth generation of Barber - Blacksmith.
Nat boasts of the time he shoed famous racehorses
in the district.
Nat estimates that he has made and forged 25,000
shoes in his 53 years and hopes to make a few more
thousand yet. He works from dawn till dusk six
days a week throughout the year.
There is another son, Horace, profession motor
engineer.
O.P.S.1 70 year old Nat. Barber at the forge
at Milford Mill.

1983-5236 / 53560 .

NEW CREPE & RAYON INDUSTRY IN NORTHERN IRELAND.
A new industry which has sprung up in Northern
Ireland is the preparation and weaving of
rayon crepe and other rayon fabrics.
Crepe Weavers Ltd., of Newtownards, Co. Down,
which commenced in 1948 occupies part of Newtownards
Airport which was originally built for the production
of aircraft.
It employs 125 people at present but will employ
200 people by the end of the year when the mill is
fully equipped.
Owing to the male unemployment situation in the
district it is the intention of the firm to employ
60 per cent men and 40 per cent women.
The production target for the end of the year is
30,000 yards of Rayon fabrics per week, of which
between 50 and 60% will be for export.
Most of the workers engaged are trainees formerly
agricultural labourers and laundry workers.
Care has been taken not to engage workers from linen
textile mills in the district which would have added
to the production of the new firm but would have
caused difficulties in the established firms.

LIFE AT THE BLUE COAT SCHOOL.

Christ's Hospital or "Blue Coat School", was founded by
Edward VI on the site of an old Greyfriars Monastery, and down
to a few years ago was one of London's best known scholastic
institutions. It was pulled down to make room for extensions
of St. Bartholomew's Hospital and the new General Post Office,
in Newgate Street. The School is now carried on at HORSHAM in
an imposing building. Besides the usual subjects included in
any school curriculum, the boys are taught intersting things,
such as clay modelling, carpentry, weaving, spinning etc., and
have taken advantage of their move into the country by acquiring
a farm, the work on which is done by the boys. The school has
a band complete with mace bearer and this is a familiar sight
once a year in London when the school marches through the City to
their annual church service. The boys still wear the picturesque
costume of knee breeches, yellow stockings and blue coats.

GOLD FOR PRINCESS ELIZABETH 'S FINGER ?
WELSH MINE MAY PROVIDE ROYAL RING
When. in that solemn moment on November 20th Lieutenant Philip
Mountbatten slips the ring on to the third finger of Princess
Elizabeth's left hand at Westminster Abbey, it is highly
probable that the golden band will be fashioned from
British gold, mined in the only gold mine working in
Wales.- Graigwen gold mine.
Owned by Mr. Thomas Michaeliones, Graigwen gold mine
near Barmouth , is producing very rich ore - both in gold and
silver - and with the arrival of modern concentrators
it is likely that 90% of the metals existent in the ore
willbe recovered. At present only 29% of the metals are
being recovered.
Gold is richest on the top reef of the field,where the
quartz is blue in colour. One assay from this field , was
as much as 19 ounces per ton of rock.

LONDON has seen noth-
ing quite like it since
the hungry Thirties.
South Wales miners, nearly a
thousand strong and backed by
railwaymen, marching to the
House of Commons demanding
work for the unemployed.
Their slogans and banners
protesting against pit and rail
closures cast a shadow from the
past, even in prosperous Oxford
Street.
'GETTING BAD'
One bowler-hatted umbrella-
carrying Londoner said: "I
don't know quite what it is all
about; but when Welsh miners
do this, things must be getting
bad."
A special train ran through
from West Wales picking up the
men for London — delegates
from 110 colliery lodges, repre-
senting over 80,000 miners.
It might have looked like a
Rugger special as they poured out
into Pad-
dington
Station.
Welsh
miners are
like that.
Never
gloomy
even in
their more
serious moments.
A Cockney porter shouted:
"Up the Welsh."
The Musicians' Union laid
on a 50-piece brass band to
greet them with Sospan
Fach and Land of My
Fathers. The roof of old
Paddington rang with the
voices of a mighty choir.

WHERE COLD WEATHER MEANS "BIG BUSINESS".      MJH/FM.

A man who looks forward to wintry weather is
53-years-old Mr. Stanley Russell of Croydon.
The reason for this unusual penchant is that
Mr. Russell owns one of the oldest and largest
firewood businesses in Croydon and naturally
cold weather to him means a "boom".  Mr. Russell
supplies firewood to houses, shops, hospitals,
schools, hostels etc., in an area 25 miles around
his yard and at this time of year, his staff is
extremely busy.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS:    Lending a hand to tie the
bundles of firewood at Mr. Russell's Croydon (Surrey)
wood yards is 78-years-old MRS. ROSE ("GRAN") NORMAN.
"Gran" usually works in the office, but at busy
time, such as at present, she helps out in the tying
and packing sheds.

THE QUEEN embarrassed safety experts yesterday
for the second time in a fortnight.

She drove an estate car with Princess Margaret's
three-year-old daughter, Lady Sarah Armstrong
Jones, perched on the front seat beside the
Queen Mother.

Safety experts say the front passenger seat is
the most vulnerable spot in a car. Less than
three weeks ago Mrs. Barbara Castle, then
Minister of Transport, announced plans to launch
a campaign persuading parents to put their
children in the back seat.

That is where Prince Andrew rode yesterday,
when his mother drove the royal party back to
Windsor Castle from a polo match in Windsor
Great Park. She used a private road, but it
crosses the main Staines road.

Only a fortnight ago when Princess Anne was
at the wheel, the Queen sat in the front passenger
seat with four-year-old Prince Edward on
her lap.

SUITCASE IS COT IN SQUATTERS' KENSINGTON LUXURY FLAT.

Nearly a thousand persons from overcrowded homes in the
Greater London area have seized two blocks of luxury flats
and seven houses and mansions in the wealthy West London boroughs
of Kensington and Marylebone. Formerly, squatters had mainly
operated at vacant Army camps.
Forty-six flats (usually rented at £10 10s. a week and upwards)
are occupied by squatters in Duchess of Bedford House,
Duchess of Bedford's Walk, Kensington
These flats, in which several hundred people are now accommodated,
had been empty for some months and had been in the hands of
the Ministry of Works, who were preparing to repair them and
hand them over for letting.
PHOTO SHOWS:- Mrs. M. Mullins feeding Christopher (centre) and
Maureen (right) as baby Patricia sleeps peacefully in a suitcase,
which until furniture arrives, serves as a cot in the Mullins'
flat at Duchess of Bedford House.
Mr. C.J. Mullins, husband of Mrs. Mullins, is a 32-year-old
ex soldier who had been waiting 12 months on a priority list
for accommodation.

“IT’S more than you dare do,
Garrett,” said the land-
lord’s agent.
“Is that so?” replied Mrs.
Esther Clara Garrett, of Irene
House, Flower and Dean-street,
Whitechapel, E.
She is the chairwoman of the
committee formed by 180 tenants of
tenements there, to demand rent re-
ductions and repairs.
With no schooling except that
which comes from going to work at
eight years of age and bringing up a
large family, Mrs. Garrett yesterday
made her first “public appearance.”
She left the two-room flat for
which she pays 13s. a week rent and
spoke to 250 men, women and
children.
They cheered as she told them,
“I’ll go to the landlord and whatever
there is to say, I’ll say it.”
The meeting followed a procession
from Flower and Dean-street, with
drums playing and banners flying.
Organised by the Stepney Tenants’
Defence League, the meeting decided
to send the landlord a suggested
scale of rents and repairs, with a rent
strike ultimatum if there is no satis-
faction or negotiation in seven days.

GLASS-FIBRE ROOFED CAR MAKES ITS APPEARANCE.      EH/RS

A British car with a complete all glass roof, with all the
modern windows fitted in the ordinary splintex glass, is now
being tested on the streets to see if it stands up to the
weather conditions.  The roof is glass-fibre cloth moulded
together with resin and taking four hours to cure.  The hood
and roof can be dismantled in two minutes, making the car a
complete sports model.  The weight is 45 lbs, exactly half the
weight of an ordinary car roof.   The glass-fibre has already
been tested with a 4 lb hammer, and although only 1/8" thick,
no impression was made on it at all.  The Vanden Plas (England)
1923 Ltd, a famous British car builders, have completed this
roof and although the whole thing is moulded at first on a
gig, there is no join whatsoever.

Photograph shows :-  Mr George Smith (left) and Mr J. Brooks,
both of Kingsbury, converting the sports model Austin Somerset
into a saloon. at Vanden Plas Ltd, Kingsbury works, London,
N.W. 9.

ONLY ENGLISH SILKWORM FARM PRODUCES SILK FOR
      DUCHESS' CORONATION GOWNS.
5,000-YEAR-OLD ART MASTERED AT KENT CASTLE

The only English silkworm farm, established at
Lullingstone Castle, Kent, by Lady Hart Dyke,
is producing the silk which will be used to
make the purple velvet Coronation gowns for
the Duchesses of Gloucester and Kent.
The 5,000-year-old art of cocoon reeling has
been mastered at the farm and five years after
its foundation millions of silkworms are bred.
The breeding and feeding rooms occupy the
entire west wing of the Castle and to feed the
worms 27,000 mulberry bushes are grown.
Sir Oliver Hart Dyke, distinguished engineer
husband of Lady Hart Dyke, has designed the
reeling machines on which the silk is wound.
The silkworms spin their cocoons on straw structures,
producing one thin thread up to half-a-mile long in
48 hours.
PHOTO SHOWS:  Gathering the cocoons from the straw
structures where they spin in 48 hours one thin
thread of silk up to half a mile in length.  The
cocoons remain on the straw for ten days to harden off.
      G January 3rd 1937  PN.g.

AGRICULTURAL RESEARCH LABORATORY. PC/FRES.

The Agricultural Research Council Radio-biological
Laboratories, near Wantage, Berkshire, is the organisation
that carries out regular tests on milk collected from
milk sampling zones and depots in Great Britain, that
determine the amount of iodine 131 content. The fear
that the quantity of radio active content in milk may
rise because of the recent Russian Nuclear tests is
officially over, and it has been announced in the House
of Lord's by the Minister of Science, Lord Hailsham, that
milk throughout the country is free from a dangerous
level of iodine 131 and is safe for young children.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS:- A plastic jar containing the protein
and iodine 131 into the counter. The thick lead walls
shield the detector from natural background radiation.

ERECTING KENT'S FR ST ALUMINIUM SCHOOL . . . .
Ods 12.4.49.
The first of the five schools to be built by the Kent County
Council in aluminium prefabricated sections, is now well
under way. The school will be the Grays Farm County Primary
School at St. Paul's Cray, and the walls and roofs are of
aluminium alloy supplied by the Bristol Aeroplane (Housing)
Company. The section are delivered to the site ready for
erection, thus saving much time and labour apart from materials.
The block illustrated in these pictures will accommodate five
classrooms and one general purpose room. There will be another
block housing two classrooms and one general purpose room, an
administrative wing, assembly hall, canteen kitchen, dining hall,
etc., and the whole school will accommodate 360 children. The
only brickwork in the buildings will be the external gable end
walls, and the boiler house, the foundations of which can be
seen in some of the pictures, which were taken during a visit
to the site today.

169652(CHI). NEW SHERVIK TRACTOR DEMONSTRATES EQUIPMENT
FOR USE IN EAST AFRICAN GROUNDNUTS SCHEME.

BAGSHOT(Surrey)ENG: A demonstration of the new Shervik
tractor, which has been specially designed for work on
the British Government's East African groundnuts scheme,
was held here. The new tractor, built by
Vickers-Armstrongs, Ltd, combines certain of the components
of the Sherman Mark V tank, including one of the two-stroke
Diesel engines.
All the tractors are fitted with a universal "U"frame
to which a variety of implements can be fitted. Stumper
blades are used for digging out tree stumps with their
roots, and trees can be quickly uprooted with the use of
the treedozer. After the root-cutter has been at work
collection of the roots is accomplished with a root-rake,
16 feet in width.

'AIRBORNE' ATTACK ON HOUSING PROBLEM -
HORSA GLIDER BECOMES A HOME.

The fuselage of a Horsa glider - the type used by
airborne troops in World War II - is being converted
into a home for a London businessman by Mr. Arthur Bedford,
a building contractor at Southbourn, Bournemouth, Hampshire.
The glider-home will have three rooms - a bedroom measuring
10 feet by 7 feet, a living room 15 feet by 7 feet,
and a kitchenette 8 feet by 7 feet.
If the experiment is successful, the builder will convert
more gliders. People baffled by the housing shortage
will be able to have these homes built quite cheaply on
their own sites.

MACE FOR BRITISH JEWELLERS' ASSOCIATION 26.1.55.

The British Jewellers' Association, which
represents nearly 2,000 manufacturing and
wholesale jewellers, has become a patron
of its own trade.The Central Council of the
Association recently decided that the ancient
art of silversmithing was in serious danger
of extinction without public support.It was
decided that the Association should commission
a special piece every year, thus building up its
own collection of fine silverware and, at the same
time, setting an example to similar organisations
who might become patrons to the trade.The first
piece, amodern silver mace for use upon ceremonial
occasions, has now been completed, designed by the

FOUR-SECTION PREFABRI CATED ALUMINIUM HOUSE ON VIEW TO LONDONERS

An Aluminum House, factory-made in four sections, has been put up
on a bombed site outside Selfridge's, the departmental store in
Oxford-street, London. The lightweight home, which may play an
important part in the solution of Britain's housing problem, was
designed by the Aircraft Industries Research Organisation on Housing,
and built by the Bristol Aeroplane Company, of Weston-super-Mare,
Somerset, and is called the Airoh House. Electrical fittings are
installed when the sections are constructed, being plugged in to the
mains after assembly, which can be completed in four hours. Production
of the Airoh House in aircraft factories ensures continuity of
employment for skilled workers in aluminium, hitherto employed on
making parts for aeroplanes, besides meeting a national demand for homes
to replace those destroyed in the war.

DISCS HELPED TO MAKE THE '90s GAY
May 9th 1964 PAR 109905-1 (M-R)
-------------------------------------
DISCS HELPED TO MAKE THE '90s GAY

If modern teenagers think they invented
the record boom, here's evidence that even
great-grandfather may have had his
Top Twenty.
Mr. A.W. ORD-HUME is pictured at the
Londoner Hotel, Welbeck Street, W., to-day
(Saturday) with discs from the 1890s, and
musical boxes they were played on.
The instruments are, left to right:
A Symphonion of 1897 (11 7/8 in. disc);
a Regina of 1898 (27-inch disc); and
an 1894 Regina (15 1/2 in. disc).
The musical boxes were on display
at the conference of the Musical Box Society
of Great Britain, whose members were able
to view a selection of instruments dating
from 1790 to 1912, all in working order.
The Society, which has a membership of
nearly 100, exists to raise funds to repair
and maintain musical boxes in museums and
collections throughout Britain and to keep
alive interest in this form of mechanical
reproduction of music.

CHARCOAL BURNERS SERVE THE MODERN WORLD

Equipment of the kind used for centuries
is still employed by the charcoal burners
of the New Forest, Hampshire, as they
carry on their traditional trade under
the jurisdiction of the Forestry Commission.
Though the technique of making charcoal
is old, there are new markets for the
product in modern industry.
Charcoal is used in the production of
drugs, chemicals (including nylons),
steel, fabrics and other commodities.
PICTURE SHOWS:- Smiling TOM WEST,
descendant of a long line of charcoal
burners, with a sack of charcoal
fresh from the kiln in King's Hat Wood,
near Beaulieu, Hampshire.
Though charcoal dust invades
hair, teeth and throat and lies thick
on the face, Mr. West never suffers
from respiratory or digestive troubles.
The life of a charcoal burner is
reputed to be healthy - and long.

MAINTAINING ENGLISH CRAFTSMANS IIP .
E.M./MAE.

Much has been done in recent years by the Gloucestershire
Guild of Craftsmen to revive old English handicrafts in
the County and as a result, many of the members have achieved
fame all over the world with handm de furniture, pottery,
basketwork, ironwork and fabric.  In wartime, many of the
members are engaged on war work, but a few areable to carry
on with their crafts.  Among these is Mr. F.F. Foster, of
Whiteway, near Stroud, whose furniture and articles made by
hand from locally grown wood have become well known.  Mr.

To few sailors falls the privilage of seeing

memories of Admiral Cunningham-then a Lieutenant,
now C.in C. Rosyth. In this recent war, Mr.

FISHING FOR COAL IN THE LEEDS-LIVERPOOL CANAL.
The Leeds-Liverpool canal at Chorley, Lancs,
is almost dry-just a little water in the middle
of masses of mud.
Seventy-three-years-old Jimmy Blundell, who sailed
that canal as captain of the barge for almost 50
years and his pal Bob Davis, aged 66, another ex-barge
skipper, remembered that coal fell out of the barges
into the canal.
So Jimmy and Bob made a metal dredge. It pulls up
broken bottles and stones but coal too.
The two ex-captains are working their way along the
canal and average two bags of coal every afternoon.

Transcribed_Text:
DAILY HER
30 DEC 1960
MRS. D. ANDERSON
"A car, holidays"

WIVES go out to work first and foremost because they want the money.
But they do not usually need it for basic necessities. Nor do they spend it as "pin-money" on themselves.
They want it so that their families can have a higher standard of living than is possible on one wage alone. And if a conflict arises between the claims of their jobs and the interests of their families, they put their families first.
This new evidence on the con-troversial subject of working wives and mothers is put for-ward today in a report published by the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research.
It is based on a study of mar-ried women workers, sponsored by the DSIR, and carried out by social scientists from the London School of Economics under Professor R. M. Titmuss, at the Peek Frean biscuit factory in Bermondsey, London.
At this factory, three-quarters of the 4,000 workers are women—most of them married, more than half of them with children. Few work the full 10-hour day. Most are part-timers on shifts of 4, 5 or 6½ hours.

NOT AN ESCAPE
The investigators found that for most wives "work was un-dertaken as a means of helping the family, not as an escape from it."
Two pay-packets in the family mean that more can be spent on refurnishing the home, on more varied food, on pocket-money and toys for the children, on a small, second-hand car or on a proper family holiday.
Though many wives said they would miss the social contacts if they did not work, their first loyalty was always to their families.
The biscuit factory—abandon-

By JOYCE CHESTERTON
ing its pre-war bar against married women because of the labour shortage — has done much to make it easier for wives to work.
The 9.30 a.m.-4 p.m. shift, for instance, consists mainly of mothers with school-age chil-dren. They can leave home and get back at the same time as their families.
Mothers with under-fives work mostly in the evening, when husbands are at home to take over and put the children to bed.
Without considerable help from husbands, in fact, most of the wives would find it very hard to cope with both job and home.

TERRY FINCHER

Transcribed_Text:
SAIDMAN (ILLUS)                               28.5.43.
A FORTRESS THAT DID NOT RETURN.1983-5236/91005
OPS.1. The Flying Fortresses are leaving on another
daylight bombing mission to Germany.  As the big
planes vault off the runway a ground crew watches
its ship leave. "There she goes!"...The bombers swim
slowly around the airdrome like trout in a pool until
the last plane is airborne.  They form a loose battle
formation.  The men on the ground count them one-by-
one as they cruise off.  At the rendezvous point
there is another giant ring-around-the-rosy as group
after group of Fortresses arrive from East Anglian
airdromes to complete the great armada.  Now the
Fortresses close in tight together so that no fighter
dare break through between the wingtips.  In each
B17 there are ten men.  These ten men, multiplied by
hundreds of great machines, and thousands of fifty
calibre guns, are moving in close-packed battle
formation into the sub-stratosphere over Europe.
The ground crew men will wait for their ship and their
ten combat men.

LUMBERJACKS OF BRITAIN'S WEST

Buzz of power saws, the roar of the
bulldozer and the ring of the big axe
echo through the shaded depths of
the Quantock Forest, which clothes
the hillsides to the west of Bridgwater,
Somerset.
For the forest, covering 2,750 acres,
supplies most of the pit props for the
Somerset coalfield, and also sends them
to the Forest of Dean and South Wales.
Ninety per cent of the timber produced
is used for this purpose.
Fifteen or more six-ton loads, with
500 props in a load, leave in a week.
Each prop costs two or three shillings.
Seedlings are planted to replace the
trees cut down.
The Quantock Forest, one of the
Forestry Commission's oldest stretches
of woodland, is worth £150 to £200
an acre. Its income target for the
coming year is £150,000.
PICTURE SHOWS:- Pit-props being cut
to length on a mobile electric
circular saw by Quantock Forest workers.

food shortage is being brought about by a revolutionary
agricultural machine, the Fergusson Tractor, which is now being

LAUNCHING OF THE "REGENT LIVERPOOL"   PC/

    A new oil tanker, "Regent Liverpool", was
launched today, Thursday, at the Belfast Ship-
yard of Harland and Wolff by Mrs. Charles C.
Dunn, wife of the managing director of Regent
Oil Company Limited.  With a dead weight of
47,600 tons, and an overall length of 746 feet,
"Regent Liverpool" is the biggest tanker ever
built in Belfast.  She is powered by Harland
and Wolff geared turbines developing 16,500
s.h.p. at a service speed of 16 knots. "Regent
Liverpool" is the 218th vessel in the Regent/
Texaco/Caltex Group fleet which links a world
wide network of more than 80 ocean terminals.
The tanker will also serve the new refinery
that Regent plans to build at Milford Haven.

LONDON SCHOOLS' CHRISTMAS FESTIVAL BEGINS. MJH/HA.

The first concert of the 1955 London Schools' Christmas Carol
Festival, is taking place today at the Central Hall, Westminster.
A massed choir of some 16,000 children from more than 550 schools
in all parts of London are taking part in this Festival, which
comprises a series of six concerts, on December 6th, 7th.
8th, 9th, 12th, and 13th., the first two being held at
the Central Hall and the last four at the Royal Festival Hall.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: Six young choristers seen taking part
in the first concert of the London Schools' Christmas Carol
Festival at the Central Hall, Westminster this morning.
They are (back row left to right): CHARLES PAGE (11) from
Burdett Coutts School; BABLU MUKHERJI of Colville School,
Kensington(11); PAMELA DUNCAN, COLVILLE School, (10);
Front row: MARY JANE MILNER (10) of Highgate; OWEN MASON (10)
Westbourne Park: ANN RUMALRES (11) of Eltham.
The concerts are all conducted by Dr. Leslie Russell, the L.C.C's

MR. BARNETT JANNER, LABOUR CANDIDATE FOR WEST

O.P.S.  Mr. Barnett Janner talking to Mrs, M.Ellmore,
Mrs Barwick and Mrs. Duddle in the communal yard

questions arising under the Rent Restrictions

problem and the Rent Restriction Problem a very
important place in his campaign.

ALL black and white poster showing the Queen in her now-famous miner's suit and safety helmet has been published without Palace permission.

And yesterday the British Safety Council, which has made the poster, said the Duke of Edinburgh had stopped it using a similar picture of himself in a miner's helmet.

CLYDESIDE BUSY ON THE "CORONIA"
14.5.47.

A masive hulk of rivet-studded rust-
stained steel is creeping up to the blitzed-
scarred roof tops of bustling Clydebank.
Alongside the John Brown's cradle which fostered
her big sisters, Queen Mary and Queen Elizabeth,
a new Cunarder is being born. The "CORONIA",
largest ship being built at present in the world,
is only 32,000 tons. But several hundred men
are determined that when she leaves the Clyde
this "little" liner will be no ordinary "baby"!
Already, four months before the scheduled launching,
her raw steel plates from bow to stern present
a streamlined grace which veterans say no other
ship possesses. When completed the new Cunarder
will have delicately coloured plastic instead of
hardwood planking on her decks. She will do the
6000 mile trip to the United States and back
without refuelling.

WEDGWOOD TEA SERVICE TO BE PRESENTED
TO THE QUEEN. MJH/HT.

Expert workers at the famous factory of Messrs. Josiah
Wedgwood & Sons, Ltd. at Barlaston, near Stoke-on-Trent,
are now busily working on a bone china tea service,
for 12 people, which will be presented to H.M. The Queen,
