They’re shining up partizans
and axes

GLITTERING swords . . . shining partizans and axes . . . they’ll all play their part in the grand pageantry of the Coronation next year.
And at the Acton, Middlesex, factory of the famous sword makers, Wilkinsons, 1,000 swords are being made for Guardsmen, Cavalrymen, Lord Lieutenants of Counties, diplomats, statesmen and officers of the three services.
Hundreds of other swords, handed down for generations, are being repaired and repolished.
Mrs. Mary Fry (in the picture below) is seen giving the final polish to some of the completed swords. In another small room, Charlie Webb, 39-year-old embosser, works on thep artizans—the broad spear-heads carried on tasseled poles by Yeomen of the Guard and Yeomen Wardens of the Tower.
He is cleaning off the late King’s arms and cypher and re-etching them with those of Queen Elizabeth. He is also regilding the axes carried by the Gentlemen at Arms.
★
SIX Prime Ministers will attend a meeting of the Coronation Commission at St. James’s Palace on Friday. The Duke of Edinburgh will preside.
In addition to Mr. Churchill they are the Prime Ministers of Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Pakistan, and Ceylon, who were all appointed members of the Commission when it was set up in April.
Friday’s meeting probably will discuss the part the Commonwealth forces will play at the Coronation and also the question of television.
It is likely to be the only meeting that the Prime Ministers can attend, although their High Commissioners are also members of the Commission.
★
WORKMEN yesterday moved into Westminster Abbey to begin preparing it for the Coronation. The nave and west door are now closed to the public.
The public will be allowed in for services up to and including Christmas, but the whole Abbey will be closed from January 1.
Five days after the Coronation the public will be able to visit the Abbey to see the Coronation trappings.

Transcribed_Text:
1983-5236/42672
Indus- Fuel & Power- Coal--Accidents- Cambrian Colliery, Rhonda,
May 1965
AN explosion tore through a colliery yesterday and blasted 31 men to pieces. Last night, as the Rhondda Valley lay silent and numbed with shock, the cause of the disaster was still a mystery.
Weeping wives and mothers stood at the pit-head of Cambrian Colliery in Clydach Vale, Glamorgan, as the remains of their men were brought out of the black hell 800ft. below.
It was lunchtime when the blast hit the mechanised plough face of the colliery’s No. 1 Pit.
The miners working there had no chance. Men 500 yards away were knocked off their feet and injured.
The doomed men were in a slender tunnel only 2ft. 8in. high.
A grey-faced, shaken rescue worker said: “The sight down there was terrible.
“Some men were decapitated, others without arms and legs. Their clothing was ripped to shreds.”
Among the dead were colliery manager Ernest Breeze and under-manager Les Williams.

5th May, 1964.

FORD CARS TAKE TO THE RAILS

First new 'Liner' Train to Scotland

A new British Railways service used exclusively to carry Ford
cars and commercial vehicles to Scotland began running this week.

This high speed 'conveyor belt' service will comprise three
trains a week from Dagenham to the Ford distribution centre at
Bathgate in Scotland, and two trains from the Ford Halewood plant
near Liverpool.

The first train, seen here, left Dagenham last night (Monday,
May 4) and arrived at mid-day today. Each train carries 65 to 70
cars which are then distributed throughout Scotland by road
transporter or delivery drivers.

The benefits of the new system are far reaching - it will
speed up deliveries, keep mileage to a minimum, substantially
reduce the risk of damage and ultimately reflect lower costs to
customers.

ISSUED BY PUBLIC AFFAIRS STAFF, FORD OF BRITAIN.

the war. There are now 136 members of the British Breeders

two hundred pelts for the large auction at Beaver House which
is to tave place shortly. Mr Bernard Hicks who runs this minv
farm at Strathearn Nursery and Fur Farm at his home at
Totteridge Green, North Finohley, started the fur farm in
April 1951 for his daughter Nancy, who is 20, and his son
David, age 17, also helps.

seen hanging out pelts to dry after the animals have been
villed. Some two hundred of these little minv animals have
been villed this veev, and the pelts will realise four to

HELP-YOURSELF SHOE-REPAIRERS                              D/HT

Appreciating that footwear repair costs are becoming
altogether too high for many people, Jim Clennell (60)
and Fred Smith (40) who run a repair shop at Seven Kings,
Essex, have begun a new service. They have installed
five lasts and sets of tools and invite customers to come
and do their own mending. They estimate what the full
cost of the job would be, and charge 2d in the shilling
for use of the equipment. They sell the customer the
leather at wholesale price and the result is that the job
costs one third less. Jim and Fred give their advice
free and charge 6d extra for professional finishing if
required. They remain open until 9 pm, and are planning
a special ladies night, since so many women do their
repairs at home.

as she trims the leather round the sole of her show which

ORANGES AND LEMONS GROWN IN ENGLAND.
When Oranges and Lemons were sold at Maidenhead
to aid the local War Prisoners Parcels' Fund
everyone was asking "where did they come from?".
78-year-old Alfred Bayley knew the answer.  He
grew them!    In his greenhouse at Burnham Buck's,
even now he has some still growing.
Formerly a diamond miner in South Africa and friend
of Wells who found the Cullinan diamond, they
both worked at the Premier Mine in the Transvaal.
Bayley had the orange trees sent from South Africa
23 years ago;  each year he grafts a bud to another
plant in order to form a further plant.  Now he has
over twenty miniature orange and lemon plants.
The original plant cost 2/3, including the freight
charges from South Africa.  Bayley thinks more of
his oranges and lemons that he does of the world's
largest diamond.  He can afford to smile!!!
      O.P.S.  Alfred Bayley with his orange and
      lemon plants in his greenhouse.

DURHAM PRODUCES DOLLAR-SAVING PIPELINE D/ TAN

One of the biggest contracts for large diameter steel
pipes ever placed in Britain has just been secured by
South Durham Steel and Iron Company, an old established
Teeside firm. The order, from the Basrah Petroleum Co.
(an associate of the Iraq Petroleum Company) is for the
manufacture of 80 miles of 24-inch pipe, weighing 17,000
tons, to be laid next year from the Zubair oilfields in
Southern Iraq to the port of Fao on the Persian Gulf,
near Basrah. In addition to opening new and increasing
markets for the British steel industry, the £900,000
order will mean a saving of some 2 1/2 million dollars, as
hitherto most large diameter oil piping has been obtained
from the United States.

seen stacked at the South Durham Steel and Iron Company's

BRITAIN' S BIGGEST LAND PLANE.

The BRISTOL TYPE 167 low wing cantilever monoplane, 
sometimes unofficially referred to as the BRABAZON I, 
is the biggest land plane yet to be built by the 
British aircraft industry and is now taking shape in the 
Bristol Aeroplane Company's factory at Filton, Bristol. 
Estimated to cost £4,000,000 the 167 is being 
built solely for flight development work and is expected 
to fly in the early summer of 1947. 
The aircraft with an all up weight of 285,000 lbs, 
- approximately 126 tons - will have a maximum level 
speed of more than 300 m.p.h. at 25,000 feet, a cruising 
speed of 250 m.p.h., at 25,000 feet, and a still air 
range of 5,000 miles.

THE BRISTOL TYPE 167 LW-WING CANTILEVER MONOPLANE -

process. Its object is to produce the concave
front, and the convex back and hinge.

LIFE AT THE BLUECOAT SCHOOL.
...........................

Christ's Hospital, or "Blue Coat School", was founded by
Edward VI on the site of an old Greyfriars Monastery, and down
to a few years ago was one of London's best known scholastic
institutions. It was pulled down to make room for extensions
of St. Bartholomews Hospital and the new General Post Office,
in Newgate Street. The School is now carried on at HORSHAM
in an imposing building. Besides the usual subjects included in
any school curriculum, the boys are taught interesting things,
such as clay modelling, carpentry, weaving, spinning etc., and
have taken advantage of their move into the country by acquiring
a farm, the work on which is done by the boys. The school has
a band complete with mace bearer and this is a familiar sight
once a year in London when the school marches through the City to
their annual church service. The boys still wear the picturesque
costume of knee breeches, yellow stockings...

EMBRASURES FOR SANDBAGGED BUILT BLOCKHOUSES.
The weak feature in all rapidly constructed blockhouses
is the wooden framing used to form the opening.  The
opening does not protect the rifleman because the rim
can be penetrated by a bullet, also the splintered wood
carried away by the bullet can produce nasty wounds.
The present suggestion is to pre-cast the embrasure
opening of the desired aperture and angle, the outer
extremity having a light sheet steel framing embedded
in the face to prevent the concrete edges shattered by
a bullet from being detached and forming missiles.
The embrasure weighs less than 1½ cwt. and can easily
be lifted into place by two men.     Manufacture can be made
in quite simple wooden moulds by any local building
contractor, breeze block manufacturer, in Corporation
yards, and so on;   using the quick setting concrete
and be produced ready for installation within 24 hours.

DURHAM PRODUCES DOLLAR-SAVING PIPELINE          D/ TAN

One of the biggest contracts for large diameter steel
pipes ever placed in Britain has just been secured by
South Durham Steel and Iron Company, an old established
Teeside firm.  The order, from the Basrah Petroleum Co.

order will mean a saving of some 2 1/2 million dollars, as
hitherto most large diameter oil piping has been obtained
from the United States.

FOOTPRINTS ON THE MOON
SUN USED 31 JUL 1969
MOON
THEY stand out sharply. Like some weird footprints in the snow on a holiday beach — the footprints of the First Men on the Moon. In the centre, the American flag "flutters" in the airless atmosphere, with the help of a wire device attached to its golden standard.
And the shadow of the moonbug Eagle, which took astronauts Neil Armstrong and Edwin Aldrin on man's most historic journey casts its shadow across the surface at Tranquillity Base.
The picture, taken from Eagle, is one of hundreds brought back by the astronauts and one of four released last night after being "cleared" in an elaborate decontamination process at the Houston Lunar Receiving Laboratory where Armstrong, Aldrin and Michael Collins are living in isolation.
The astronauts sat up until midnight to see the pictures—and colour film released to world television last night—at a special preview on Monday. Their verdict: spectacular.
July 29

The thought of jig-
sawing an old Vic-
torian house into the
shape of 1965 is enough to
give many a modern
architect the shudders.
Yet the fact that such a
conversion can be done with
a minimum of space wastage
is superbly illustrated by this
house overlooking the Rugby
football ground at Twicken-
ham.
This modernisation is one of
the most impressive pieces of
building surgery I've seen.
It began when the owner,
Mr. Smith, was faced with the
need to take his parents in
with the family. He and his
wife had often complained
about the shortcomings and
inconveniences of living in a
house planned and built in
Queen Victoria's day.
Now, with more room
needed, they determined to
alter and extend the house,
at the same time wiping out
all the irritating features in-
herited from the past—narrow
kitchen, shortage of power
points, aged electric wiring,

21 XII 58

AND while at the Central Library
the young actors, laughing
and talking, were making up for their
parts, in another part of Bermondsey
there was tragedy.
At the corner of Dockley-road and
Rouel-road, I came upon a house where
the upper windows had been boarded up.
A charred settee, a burnt and smashed
door, had been flung in the front garden.
Small groups of people were gathered
around, talking in low tones.

SOME of them told me the story of
tragedy and heroism which ex-
plained the scene.
Bill West, aged 81, a retired railway
porter, went downstairs early yesterday
morning to make a cup of tea for his
schoolteacher daughter. He had a
seizure, collapsed across a settee—that
charred settee. It was set afire by the
candle he was carrying.
Bill's daughter, trying to save him from
the blaze, was dragged away by neigh-
bours only just in time to prevent her
being badly burned.
And Bill himself died in the hospital.

IN the stained glass windows of Mr. John
Burdett's home at Alderman's Hill,
Palmer's Green, N., there are 14 Devices.
One is a Union Jack, another a Red Cross
flag, a third a part of the arms on the
reverse side of a silver coin.
The rest, Mr. Burdett thinks, are
sections from towns' arms.
* * *
THE Devices were there two years ago
when Mr. Burdett took the house;
have been there, in fact, for 30 years.
Well, about Coronation time the
Middlesex County Council said: "What
about paying the armorial bearings
duty?"
Mr. Burdett refused to pay, and the
Council twice hailed him before the
court.
Once the case was dismissed under
the Probation of Offenders Act; the
second time he was fined.
Still he refused to pay, maintaining
that his Devices were not, as the Bench
said, armorial bearings.
* * *
SO now the Middlesex County Council
has decided to press the County
Councils' Association to ask for the
abolition of the duty.

OLDEST SWORD MAKER IN ENGLAND NOW MAKES
BAYONETS AND COMMANDO KNIVES.
HAS MADE SWORDS FOR FIVE SOVEREIGNS.

1983-5236/57860

The oldest sword maker in England
is Tom Beasley, aged 82, who has been
working with the same firm for 56 years.
He started in a forge at the age of 8
years. The craft of sword making has
been handed down in the Beasley family
from father to son for generations
for more than 250 years.
Tom Beasley has made swords for five
Sovereigns. In the last war he made
bayonets. During the years of peace
he returned to his swords. Now he has
gone back to bayonets - and commando
knives. His two daughters have joined
him in the business and are now busily
employed helping war production.
He has no sons to carry on the family
tradition.

SCHOOL FOR STOCKMEN (AND WOMEN). MUM/HT.

Arranged experimentally for the first time last year, a residential school for stockmen is being repeated at the Kent Farm Institute, Sittingbourne. This course is for working cowmen, shepherds and pigmen from all parts of Kent, who wish to bring themselves up to date in the technique of their work. Women employed on the care of stock can also enrol. The course is organised as a series of self-contained sections sections, dealing in turn with dairy cattle, pigs, sheep and beef cattle and each section covers management, feeding and prevention and control of diseases of stock.

A WALL TO LAST. EH/ ME.

Oxfordshire County Council stone masons - John Williams and S. Townsend are busy at present building a long length of Cotswold dry wall, traditional to the district, skirting a widened stretch of the A.40 London-Wales road between Witney and Burford. A feature of the new wall is that the outer faces are uncemented, but the centre is filled with concrete instead of loose rubble, as is customary with these walls. The concrete will prevent stones becoming dislodged and also enables the wall to be built of less thickness than the completely "dry" type. One advantage farmers get when they lose land for road widening is often a new wall,

producing pottery as well which has found its way over-
seas to export markets and to the windows of fashionable
London shops. Recently, the brickmakers discovered a
strong seam of clay. It proved suitable for making
pottery of high quality which they were able to fire in
the kiln alongside the bricks. An old outhouse of the
brickworks is being used by two potters, and a girl
models figures from the same clay. Using only their
skill, and without the aid of modern machinery, the
potters are producing works of individual stamp which
bear the hallmark of the English craftsman.

Mr

HERALD
1 FEB 1956
DAILY

Pl 1 col x 2 1/4

SUBST

ONE moment Mrs. Phyllis Faithfull, aged 32 (above), was emptying a dustpan in the scullery yesterday. The next moment she had vanished.
Where the scullery had been there was a crater 20ft. wide and 130ft. deep. Unknowingly, the scullery extension of the Royal Oak Hotel, Yattendon, Berks, had been built over an ancient well.
With bricks and masonry falling all round him, Fire Officer Leslie Evans was lowered by rope down the hole (arrowed).
Sixty feet of rope had been paid out when his muffled voice was heard: "I'm afraid there's no hope." He could go no farther; the well was blocked by the debris that had fallen.
As he spoke a burly, fair-haired man at the crater's edge sobbed and turned away. He was Percy Faithfull, husband of Phyllis. They lived in a cottage nearby with their 12-year-old daughter Betty.
At nightfall rescue work was halted.

Britain's carpet industry is to aim at an export target of 60%
as against 27%, in the new drive to close the gap between imports
and exports.

factories of Carpet Trades Limited, the extent of whose trade can be

New Zealand, USA, Canada, Canary, South America, Central America,

which are popular in each country. For instance, the preference in

There's nothing like doing it yourself providing you can.

AN explosion tore through a colliery yesterday and blasted 31 men to pieces. Last night, as the Rhondda Valley lay silent and numbed with shock, the cause of the disaster was still a mystery.
Weeping wives and mothers stood at the pit-
head of ambrian Col-
liery in Clydach Vale, 
Glamorgan, as the 
remains of their men 
were brought out of 
the black hell 800ft. 
below.
It was lunchtime 
when the blast hit the 
mechanised plough face 
of the colliery’s No. 1 
Pit.
The miners working 
there had no chance. Men 
500 yards away were 
knocked off their feet and 
injured.
The doomed men were in 
a slender tunnel only 2ft. 8in. 
high.
A grey-faced, shaken 
rescue worker said: “The 
sight down there was 
terrible.
“Some men were decapi-
tated, others without arms 
and legs. Their clothing was 
ripped to shreds.”
Among the dead were 
colliery manager Ernest 
Breeze and under-manager 
Les Williams.

A HERTFORDSHIRE STEEL WORKS.                                AW/O

Steel works are usually associated with South Wales or the industrial North, but it is a surprising fact that the steel foundry with the largest output of carbon or plain steel castings in the country is situated at Letchworth, Herts, only 30 miles from London. It provides employment for 1,500 work-people, many hundreds of whom have migrated from the North and distress areas. The work on hand is for a variety of industries ranging from ship building and locomotives to Power stations and cigarette machinery. The flow of steel means a flow of prosperity to thousands of homes in Hertfordshire and it is hoped to find employment for several hundred more by the end of 1937.

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION FIRDAY'S EVENINGS DECEMBER 19th.

SPINNING THE ARTERIES OF OUR CIVILISATION
19.12.41.
This is one of a remarkable series of photographs
taken mainly by the natural light of the processes
by which a British ironworks produces mile upon mile
of cast iron pipes for public services of gas
and water which are a prime necissity of civilised life.
A large percentage of these pipes are spun by a
centrifugal process which eliminates defects and gives
a close-grained metal, easily worked and with
a high degree of resilience and resistance to impact.
In addition to its own requirements, the plant also
produces pig-iron for steel manufacture, contributing
largely therefore to the country's output of armaments.
After tapping the blast furnace the molten iron
begins to run down the "sow" (main channel)
into the "pigs" (sand casts). Hence the ingots
are known as "pig iron".

SCOTTISH ABADAN                                  D/ TAN

Erected on the same site as the old buildings dating from
1924, the new Grangemouth Oil Refinery was built on the
Firth of Forth by Scottish Oils Ltd., a subsidiary of the
Anglo-Iranian Oil Company. Started in 1949, it went into
operation in 1951 with maximum annual crude oil capacity
of 2,500,000 tons, helping to counteract the Abadan collapse.
Its main objective is high-grade motor spirit, and it also
supplies the raw material for the production of petroleum
chemicals. To cope with its capacity of 30,000 barrels, or
just over 1,000,000 gallons a day of imported crude oil, it
was decided to establish an installation at Finnart on Loch
Long, and run a pipeline from there to the refinery, this
being more convenient than using the old Grangemouth Docks
exclusively. The approximate cost of the combined project
was £15,000,000.

PHOTO SHOWS: The mass of gigantic pipes which for the
boiler feed pumps and steam receivers at the Grangemouth
Oil Refinery.

QUEEN OPENS BRITAIN'S BIGGEST DAM.

Rhayader, Radnorshire: Queen Elizabeth and the Duke
of Edinburgh pictured when the Queen officially
opened the Claerwen dam - newest and largest dam
in the British Isles - in the Elan Valley here
today.

ITALIAN MARBLE SUNK IN 1881 BEING RAISED BY SANCTIONS.
The shore of Bowcombe Creek, near Kingsbridge, Devon rings
with the sound of chain and tackle and sledge hammers. Large
seaweed-covered blocks are lying in the mud and on the shore.
scrubbed and polished to a glistening whiteness there are
more of these squares. This seashore Stonehenge is worth
thousands of pounds. The great stones are pure Italian marble
which have lain at the bottom of the creek defying all efforts
of salvage since 1881. 55 years ago a small Italian sailing
vessels was wrecked there. On board were over 200 tons of
Italian marble. Sanctions affecting the price and supply of
marble have now caused Mr. Partridge, of Salcombe, owner of
the wreck to salvage the marble.
Photo shows- One of the huge blocks of Italian marble
weighing over 100 tons ready for shipment to London.

"WHEN IT'S NIGHT TIME IN NIPPON"
PUZZLING JAPANESE CLOCK                      DG/HT

Mr CHARLES WEIR,clockmaker of Motcomb street,
Belgravia, London, is thinking of taking a trip
to Japan, to solve the mystery of his puzzling
Japanese Seasonal clock. He easily mastered the
mechanics of the timepiece, but the system (based
on a six hour day) is still baffling.
   Whatever the time of year, the Jap clock cuts the
daylight up into exactly six hours. Moreover the
hours are marked in signs of the Zodiac Mr Weir
breakfasts at "hare-hour", is sound asleep by
"rat hour" (midnight), and stops for lunch at
"horse hour. Clock strikes in a 1.2.9.1.8
sequence which has Mr Weir's head "ringing".

PHOTO SHOWS:- "Honourable Clock is puzzle". MR
CHARLES WEIR is perplexed by the Japanese
Seasonal clock . He may present it to the Government.

THIS COULD WRECK THE RADIO SHOW.

This unusual looking electronic device appears to be harmless but if it were set at the suitable frequency resonance it could cause the stand to disintegrate completely and all other stands within a radias of 100 yards at the Radio Show.

The machine is the V.1000 Vibrator. It is used for fatigue and vibration testing which has come very much into the fore recently with high speed supersonic planes and guided missiles and rockets, and electronic vibrating has become the accepted form of fatigues testing in these industries.

The machine was used to test the Comet II.

Today USA delegates from Shafe visited the Radio Show and had a close inspection of this machine which could be a 'secret weapon' of a future war. Tomorro Russian visitors are expected to see the V.1000.

CHRISTMAS CUSTOM REVIVED AT GLASS FACTORY. MJH/HT.

An old custom, to celebrate Christmas, was revived today
at the Whitefriars Glassworks, Wealdstone (Mddx). In olden
days, glassblowers working in the intense heat of the furnaces
were in the habit of drinking beer to quench their thirst, but in
recent years water has been substituted. This Christmas, however,
thanks to the generosity of a brewers (Charringtons), it is
possible for the glassblower to revert temporarily to the happy
customs of the past and today they are quenching their thirst
with ale from a variety of drinking vessels of their own making.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: Enjoying his Yard of Ale is MR. BEN SMART
78-years-old, who has been in the glass industry for 64 years,
33 years of which have been in the service of the Whitefriars
Glassworks. Scottish by birth, Mr. Smart lives in Wealdstone.

1983 - 5236 / 45743

P70 - 378 - ROLL A

Industry.. Agriculture.. Pigs

by Kingsley 20 May 70 Lulu 1

Cartoonist Gabriel Barlow thinks pigs are misunderstood. Most people think they are dirty, smelly, stupid and useless for anything other than pork chops and bacon rashers.

But that's all wrong. Take Lulu here. Six months old and 200 lbs of sheer charm, says Gabriel, 57, who keeps her in a made-to-measure stye in the garden of his cottage in Boughton, Kent.

Like the family's collie Shep, her good pal, Lulu comes when she is called , loves an affectionate stroke on the ear and follows her master around the garden obeying orders not to trample the flower and herb beds.

She works for her pig meal too, digging parts of the garden ready for planting. And when the Barlows move into their new home and develop herb-growing as a business, her strong trough of a nose will be even more useful.

"If you treat a pig as an animal as intelligent as a dog you find they respond," said Gabriel, a vegetarian and a life-long campaigner for animal rights.

"Lulu is very sensitive and she's only one generation removed from a factory pig who has never had any real contact with human beings. Lulu's piglets - and we plan to let her have a few litters - are sure to be really domesticated and lovable."

Watching Lulu gnawing a bone side by side with Shep, He added: "In a way she's more like a dog than a pig as people know them. But I'm not interfering with nature. Pigs have as much right to be part of a family as any other animal."

The Agricultural Research Council Radio-biological
Laboratories, near Wantage, Berkshire, is the organisation
that carries out regular tests on milk collected from
milk sampling zones and depots in Great Britain, that
determine the amount of iodine 131 content, The fear
that the quantity of radio active content in milk may
rise because of the recent Russian Nuclear tests is
officially over, and it has been announced in the House
of Lord's by the Minister of Science, Lord Hailsham, that
milk throughout the country is free from a dangerous

By FRANK FEARON
VISCOUNT NEWPORT, 44-year-old Londoner and heir to 20,000 acres, claimed a tiny tied cottage yesterday with a battering ram.
It splintered the back door of Griffith Jones' home where he, his wife Alma and six children have lived for five years. Last night they were homeless and separated.
Lord Newport won an eviction order a year ago against 35-year-old Mr. Jones, who rented the cottage from him but does not work for him. But yesterday the tall, sturdy farmer barricaded his family in the three-bedroomed cottage at Crossroad Farm, Weston-under-Lizard, Staffs.
Just before 3 p.m., Mr. Stuart Timmins, the sheriff's officer, and Mr. Evans, welfare officer from Cannock, persuaded him to leave the house to parley.
They told him their plans to find homes for his children. He rejected them.
“I love my children,” he said. “How could I see them if you scatter them round the country? I will never agree. You must take them by force if you want them.”

Of the "Comets" under construction 14 are for the BOAC, 2

January 22nd 1962 PAR 94107-1 (PNR-R)

THE 'PEACOCK' IS HIS PRIDE

Mr. DENNIS STEBBINGS of Dallinghoo, Suffolk,
who claims to be one of the last blacksmiths
to use drawn steel for ornamental work,
is pictured here with his just-completed
masterpiece - a firescreen in the form of
a peacock with tail outspread.
Eighty-nine separate pieces of steel have
gone into the making of the magnificent tail,
and the job took 72 hours' work.
Mr. Stebbings - a blacksmith for 42 years -
estimates that he spent £30 on the raw
materials.
He made the firescreen as a gift for his wife,
and he has refused all offers for it from
would-be buyers.
Now he is getting many inquiries from people
who want him to make replicas of it.

BEHIND the bright curtains of a little suburban bungalow a spy ring was busy transmitting top secret military information to Russia, it was alleged yesterday.
In an underground compartment under a trapdoor in the bungalow in Cranley-drive, Ruislip, Middlesex, was a high-frequency radio geared to transmit to a place near Moscow, said the Attorney-General, Sir Reginald Manningham-Buller.
He was asking at Bow-street that five people should be sent for trial accused of an offence under the Official Secrets Act.
Sir Reginald alleged that one of them - Gordon Lonsdale - was a Russian spy masquerad-ing as a Canadian businessman. His wife sent him letters in Russian on microfilm reduced to the size of a speck of dust.
Peter Kroger and his wife, Helen, acted as bankers to the ring and ran the headquarters with top security efficiency, he said. All their doors and windows were fitted with special locks and bolts.
Harry Houghton and his fiancee, Elizabeth Gee, both Civil Servants at a secret Naval establishment, provided the in-formation, he added.
The five sat side by side in the dock in the hushed No. 1 Court, which was filled to capacity. There was room for only 10 members of the public

FIFTEEN engineering workers will be fast asleep on their factory floor to-morrow, helping to narrow the nation's trade gap.
There are export orders to be met, and the men do not intend to be caught napping.
At least, not at home.
They had sleeping bags and camp beds with them yesterday when they turned up for work at the Cimex factory in Orping-ton, Kent.
Industrial cleaning gear worth £15,000 had to be com-pleted for firms in Germany, Sweden, Denmark and Canada, and the deadline was getting close.

'For love'
One of the workers, Mr. Joe Wright, aged 49, explained: "An order from Russia put us be-hind, so I suggested kipping on the factory floor to save time going home.
"The lads thought it was a marvellous idea."
When the workshop sleep-in ends at midnight on Sunday "the lads" will have done about 64 hours work with eight to 12 hours rest.
Tea in bed will be served by colleagues after the snatches of sleep.
Of course, there will be over-time pay. The basic rate is £14 10s. a week.
But managing director Frank Elvy said: "These men work for love."

81090

SIX men and a woman waited in a closely guarded side-room at London’s Bow - street Court yesterday — the Nameless Ones in the sensational secrets case.

No clue must be given to the identity of these seven. Strict orders were given by the court that they must not be photographed or described in print.

When it was their turn to give evidence they were escorted to the witness box by a police officer. Afterwards they were escorted back to their waiting room.

These men and women are MI 5 agents — Britain’s spy-catchers. Part of their job is being completely unknown.

By letters

In the witness box they passed their names to the magistrate written on a small piece of paper. No-one else in court was allowed to see it. 
at

They were identified by letters of the alphabet “Mr. A,” “Mr. B,” and so on. The woman was known as “Miss K”.
ey
el

They gave their evidence in quiet voices, keeping their backs to the public and Press galleries.

When the court closed for the day the seven were taken to a side door which is normally kept locked. Cars were waiting to drive them away.

Today more of the Nameless Ones will be at Bow-street to give evidence. They will arrive and leave in the same way—in a cloak of secrecy.

Yesterday three men and two women accused of an offence under the Official Secrets Act glanced at each other occasionally and smiled as the MI5 agents gave evidence.

The bankers

The five—described as a company director, a bookseller and his wife and two Civil Servants—were in fact a Russian spy ring and their two main sources of information, alleged the Attorney-General, Sir Reginald Manningham-Buller.

Gordon Lonsdale, 37, Canadian company director, of the White House, St. Pancras, is a Russian with a Russian wife and three children, said Sir Reginald.

Peter Kroger, 50, and his 47-year-old wife Helen, ran the headquarters of the espionage ring at their home in Cranley-drive, Ruislip, he said.

Elizabeth Gee, 46, and Harry Houghton, 55, both Civil Servants, supplied them with Naval secrets, he added.

TWO RIGS FOR B. P. 'S NORTH SEA OIL
DRILLING.
B. P. r G. 10589 22.10.64.

By RONALD BEDFORD, Science Editor

A £2MILLION order for a giant drilling platform to probe for "black gold" gas and oil deposits beneath the North Sea has been placed in Britain.
Harland and Wolff, of Belfast, have got the contract, the British Petroleum Company announced yesterday. Delivery will be early in 1966.
The new platform, with the drilling rig erected, will stand 320ft. tall. It will have a triangular deck. Each side will be more than 100yds. long.

Stable

A BP spokesman said yesterday: "The platform will provide air-conditioned accomodation for 60 people.
"It will have a helicopter landing deck, plant to turn sea water into fresh water, and a complex telecommunications and navigational warning system.
"The platform will operate anywhere in the North Sea, and be one of the biggest installations of its kind in the world."
It will be able to drill down to 20,000ft., and can operate either resting on the seabed or as a floating rig, stable in all seas.
Next year, a smaller drilling platform, now being converted, will start drilling operations about 40 miles east of the Humber.

A SLATE-GREY, smoky mining village whose 2,000 people take pride in the fact that they are "one big, happy family," is setting a big problem for the planners.

AT last, after all these years, I have
tracked my old friends, the
Bottle Makers, to their lair (writes
Spike Hughes).
Way down in
Clapham, S.W.,
there is a work-
shop in a mews—
Cape's Glass
Works, one of five
firms left in Lon-
don where they
still blow glass
bottles.
It was medicine
bottle day yester-
day; three men
on a bottle.
James, who dip-
ped his tube in
the burning fiery
furnace and
blew; Harry,
who made the
necks; and John,
the manager, who
picked up the bottles in a shovel and
them in a cooling oven.
them they make 1,728 little
Between them and me,

however, we managed to produce some
very strange glassware.
"Just blow," said James, handing me
a gas pipe with some red stuff on
the end.
I blew, giving a perfect imitation of
"Bubbles." The largest bottle in the
world swelled at the end of the pipe.
One gallon it held; two; four; ten—
then, somehow, I was left picking the
splinters out of my hair.
The next bottle I blew didn't hold so
much as a dram. It was solid from the
neck down (see picture);
James was patient. He held the tube
while I blew, guided my hand as I put
the glowing end in the mould. Between
us we produced a lovely blue bottle,
octagonal and eminently useful except
that I had forgotten to leave an opening
at the top. This, it appears, it rather
important.
The bottle was a sight for sore eyes.
How did I suspect James of diplo-
macy? After the Birth of the Blue
Bottle he told me that glass-blowing
cannot be taught.
"It suddenly comes to you—after ten
or twelve years."

THE GREATEST FUR SALES IN THE WORLD.
The greatest fur sales in the world are held in London and the
winter sale is now on. Most of these sales are held in the great
amphitheatre of the Hudson Bay Company, Garlick Hill, E.G, and
buyers from all parts of the world attend. At the sale not a
fur can be seen for they are inspected at the warehouses days
before. Bådding is like machine gun fire and as much as
220,000 worth of furs have been sold in about twenty minutes.
The fur business is a romantic one for many of the furs are
collected from distant posts in Northern Canada and reach the
cities by slow and arduous routes.
Photo shows Foreign buyers inspecting White Fox furs at the
Hudson Bay warehouse today. They wear white coats as a
protection against the natural oil in the skins.

BOY FARMER PLOUGHS LAND AT NIGHT AFTER
GREAT BLIZZARD.
BERKSHIRE, ENG: Derek Isaac, aged 19, and his father,
run the hundred-acre West Enf Farm, at Midgham, near
Newbury, Berkshire, which includes attending to 20
milking cows, and 60 head of other cattle.
Heavy snowfalls during the recent great blizzard
in Britain donsiderably delayed work on the farm -
so Derek, with the aid of his tractor headlights
and a floodlight for the plough works each night
till nearly midnight while there is ploughing to
be done, in an effort to catch up with the valuable
lost time.

A vast new lake is being created at Staines, Middlesex,
to provide London with a new reservoir, 350 acres in extent,

OXFORD HAVE A NEW BOAT

JS 3.3.54.
Contrary to expectations in view of the ever growing costs
of organising the Boat Race, the OXFORD crew have ordered
a new boat for the 100th race against Cambridge on the
Tideway on April 3rd. It is being built by George Sims
of Hammersmith, who have made the boats for this event for
many years. It will be 61ft 6 ins long, 23 and seven-
eighths inches at the widest part and 9 and 7-eighths
inches deep. It will weigh 280 pounds and cost £320.
All Empire materials have been used in the construction -
Canadian silver spruce for the keel unwhale and seat
bearers, English sycamore for the ribs, and British
Honduras cedar for the skin.
In this picture Mr GEORGE SIMS is seen supervising
the construction of the boat.

IN SOME WAYS Beaconsfield
Buildings, just a short bus ride
from the glitter of Piccadilly
Circus, could be considered a
showplace.
For to film producers at least, the
grey-bricked, five-storey blocks of flats
seem to have an irresistable fascina-
tion.
There was Max Bygraves in Cry From
the Streets, and Spare the Rod and
Spoil the Child. There was Joe Brown
in What a Crazy World. And Jess
Conrad in The Boys.
Each finding in the rows of miserable
flats—known without affection as The
Crumbles—the perfect setting for a film
about slums.
For today Beaconsfield Buildings has
about as much in common with the
affluent gadget world of 1964 as it did
when Prime Minister Disraeli laid the
foundation stone in 1875.
The plumbing is still Victorian. There
are few separate kitchens, few bath-
rooms, and landing lavatories shared by
between five and eight families.

YESTERDAY morning was
a good time for hop
stringing. It was warm
but there was a breeze,
although not too strong a
breeze to make it
uncomfortable at the top
of 18ft. stilts. And the
ground was firm so that
the stilts did not sink and
become unstable. Bertram
Bishop was out in the hop
fields stringing the poles
ready for the hop plants
as he has done on April
days for more than 40
years. Mr. Bishop works
on a hop farm at Paddock
Wood in Kent. He is 65,
has nine children and a
wife called Nellie. Today
there aren't many
hop stringers who still use
stilts. Mr. Bishop is the
only stilt man on his farm.
The job is usually done
now by men working on
little towers fitted to
tractors. We thought
you would like to see a
farming craft before it
became history. We were
just in time to catch Mr.
Bishop. He retires next
month.

TO HANDLE 70,000 GALLONS DAILY.

milk depot will be brought into use at
Wood Lane, Shepherds Bush, London, with
the arrival of a special milk train at
midnight on Wednesday, January 2nd.

on the verges of arterial roads in Britain has
proved a success.

THE ELVER FISHERS.      EM/MA.

At this time of the year shoals of Elvers or small eels come
up the River Severn, and hundreds of workers who live near the
river are now busy in their spare time catching them with home
made net scoops of a type which ahs been used for this purpose
from the Roman days. The Elvers are regarded as a great delicacy
in the district, and there is a ready sale for them over a wide
area. With the much higher prices now prevailing the Elver fisher
can collect about 100 lbs in a night, which becomes a profitable
side line. Before the war Germans collected large quantities from
the Severn and shipped them to Germany for restocking rivers
there.

GOLIATH CRANE COMMISSIONED AT ATOMIC POWER PLANT AT
BRADWELL, ESSEX.........................19.3.58.

Bradwell-On-Sea, Essex, England.
For the first time, pressmen were to-day allowed to visit
the nuclear power station being constructed at Bradwell-on-
Sea, Essex, where the giant Goliath Crane has just been
commissioned. The crane is as high as Nelson's Column in
Trafalgar Square (177 ft), 226 ft in width and is able to

as the twelve 200-ton boiler shells and the heavy steel rings

impressive example of modern British Engineering designed and
constructed by Clarke, Chapman & Company Ltd., of Gateshead.

Laboratories, near Wantage, Berkshire, is the organisation

milk sampling zones and depots in Great Britain, that
determine the amount of iodine 131 content. The fear

DAILY HERALD Copyright Photograph

NEG IN REJECTS 16.9.60
ANTHONY CLIFTON BROWN, 58-year-old ex-banker, had a heart attack yesterday after a court had given him four weeks to pay the £18,000 balance of a £20,000 fine. Last night he was seriously ill at his home in Cheyne-walk, Chelsea. And his wife Bridget said: "It is almost impossible for us to find this money."
She added: "We desperately need six months to rebuild our lives. I think it was all this worry and the court's decision that resulted in the attack."

MEDWAY PIPELINE CROSSING
2,000 Yards of 18" steel main across bed of river

Today the South Eastern Gas Board began laying the first section
of tl e 2,000 yard long 18" diameter steel gas main across the bed of

A CORNISH TIN MINE.

The tin-mining industry in Cornwall, so ancient that most
people had forgotten about it, takes on a new important
with the loss of our supplies from Malaya; however, before
it can be exploited to the full a Government grant would be
necessary. Water has to be pumped away from the mine at
the rate of 1,000 gallons per minute, the mine being 2,000
feet deep. The miners descend in a cage to the bottom of
the mine; they drill holes five or six feet deep and
charge them with explosives - the next shift on duty clears
up the ore and inserts fresh charges.

Photo shows:- Tipping tin ore down a shute to the
bottom of the mine; the ore is then hoisted up to
ground level, a distance of 2,000 feet. 269186.

MANCHESTER
A CORNISH TIN MINE. E.M./RS.
The tin-mining industry in Cornwall, so ancient that most
people had forgotten about it, takes on a new importance
with the loss of our supplies from Malaya; however, before
it can be exploited to the full a Government grant would be
necessary. Water has to be pumped away from the mine at the
rate of 1,000 gallons perminute, the mine being 2,000 feet
deep. The miners descend in a cage to the bottom of the
mine; they drill holes five or six feet deep and charge
them with explosives - the next shift on duty clears up the
ore and inserts fresh charges.
Photo shows:- A tin-miner boring a hole in the rock
into which an explosive is inserted.

PLASTIC CONTAINERS FOR MOTOR OIL

Employing an entirely new process, British Petroleum is to introduce on May 15th 1962, plastic containers for motor oil. The containers are manufactured from high density polyethylene, a product of BP's associated petroleum chemical companies. BP will be the first major oil company to make available to the motorist on an international scale lubricating oil packed and sealed in containers manufactured from its own product.

The plastic containers are automatically filled with BP Visco-static motor oil at BP's blending installation at Ghent of Anglo-Belge des Petroles S.A. Exact measurement of the correct quantity of oil in each container is obtained by volumetric displacement.

(5PERSON - 3 BEDROOM)

The very latest in 'industrialised housing' can
be seen on a council estate at Woodhouse near Sheffield.
The 'Hallamshire' house is built mainly of factory-
made components.   The house is designed to the Parker
Morris scale of recomendations and has a total area of

through lounge, large kitchen and a separate ground
floor cloaks and W.C.   The house has a minimum number
of component parts which eliminate site work by reducing
the number of joints - all external wall panels have
insulation built in at the factory.   Great attention
has been paid to the design of internal fittings -

MEN of the 8th Hussars, just home from Korea, watch with
interest as a 20-pounder Centurion tank gun is mounted on a
tressle and tested at a Cardiff factory.

Precision job a triumph
of British workmanship

CREWS of the Centurion—the tank that has done eve-
thing but fly in Korea—walked around a Cardiff C-
nce factory yesterday to meet workers who make the
20-pounder guns.
They were men of the 8th Hus-
sars, who made the 50-ton Cen-
turions the envy of the United
Nations Forces and the dread of
the Communists.
The party was led by their com-
manding officer, Lieut.-Colonel Sir
Guy Lowther—“Buster” to his
troops. Patting a 17-foot gun bar-
rel, he said:
“We have heard much of the
decline in British workmanship,
but here we have the answer. Pre-
cision work has made this tank
gun the most accurate in the
world. It could only have been
made by people with real pride in
their job. It is so good we even
picked off snipers with it.”

HOME COMFORTS
Trooper John Harty, of Taun-
ton, added: “The tank has all the
home comforts, too. If things are
too hot to get out, we boil water
for a cup of tea in an electric
kettle.”
The Hussars have just finished
month’s leave on their return
from Korea.

Another great battleship - HMS "NELSON", once the pride of the British Navy, is being reduced to a shapeless shell at the hands of the shipbreakers in Messrs Thos. Ward's Yard at INVERKEITHING, on the Forth. Completed in 1927, HMS "NELSON" performed great service during the war. Sold for scrap to provide valuable steel, she has gone to the same yard as her sister ship HMS "RODNEY" and HMS "REVENGE". The picture shows part of the control tower falling to the dismantled decks after the steel had been cut through with oxy-acetylene cutters and the final break-away effected by crane hauling with steel cables.

BRITISH MINT WORKS OVERTIME -
TO PROVIDE MORE CHANGE FOR WORKERS.

London  Because of a scarcity of change, workers at
the Royal Mint here are being increased from 800 to
1,000 - working day and night in twelve-hour shifts.
With over £127,000,000 worth of coins in circulation -
double the amount in 1939 - firms often find difficulty
in filling pay packets with the correct amount.  The
momentary shortage is an apparent mystery - but hoarding
is blamed for some of it.
The Royal Mint, Government office on Tower Hill where
British money is coined, was erected in 1810.
PHOTO SHOWS: A truck-load of coins in canvas bags,
labelled and sealed, ready for issue to the banks.

ARMY'S 650 ACRE SECRET EH/CRE
SOMEWHERE-IN-THE-MIDLANDS.

In a place which must be kept secret for fear of war-time
bombs, is a 650 acre depot, which is helping to put the Army
on wheels. Two years ago the Army had 4,000 motor vehicles,
today it has more than 22,000, a triumph of behind scenes
organisation. Freed of red tape and run by the Royal Army
Ordinance Corps, this one depot keeps 1,3000 civilians
and 300 soldiers busy. Every day andnight there are 200 motor
drivers on the roads of England collecting and delivering
vehicles from this Midland station.

Industry... Building and Construction... Bad Weather measures

1965 3328. RevA

(Warner 26th Dec 65)
Building houses under plastic 'Balloons' at Colchester (see story)

3

New houses in winter...
THIS is a picture of one of the busiest building sites in Britain. Slap in the middle of that inches-deep sea of mud, five smart new houses are going up in record-breaking time.
And yet there is not a soul in sight. Just like every other building site just now.
What makes this site different is that gigantic object lying there like a stranded whale.
The makers prefer to call it the Barracuda. But, no matter what it looks like, it is the key to a new technique which could revolutionise the building industry.
For it is really an enormous, inflatable tent. So big, in fact,
that it can cover a terrace of five houses.
So while the rest of Britain shivers and other builders have to stop work, the men on this site at Colchester, Essex, can work on in almost summery conditions.
So much time is normally lost during winter, that the building industry and the Government decided to study cold weather techniques abroad.
The Ministry of Public Building and Works asked the contractors handling the Colchester project if they would help test the Barracuda.
So far, the experiment looks like being a success. For the terrace should be completed to roof-level in three weeks—the normal summer building rate.
Of course, the Barracuda will no longer be needed when winter is over. We hope.

that defiant challenge
was flung down from a
block of flats last night

has enough provisions for a

out. If the bailiffs arrive, it
will shoot skywards and
bring 2,000 other rebellious
tenants to his aid.
The deadline was midnight
last night, when a court order
expired. It says Don must quit
his council flat—No. 39—in Ken-
nistoun House, Kentish Town,

THREATEN'D WITH EXTINCTION.

The old industry of making earthenware teapots in Scotland is
threatened with extinction. Its last stronghold is in the old
East Lothian village of Prestonpans, where one pottery only
remains out of four .Years ago the demand for these teapots was
greater than the supply. Tea-tasters agree that earthenware is
the best container for the flavours of tea.

CH/RS
The oyster beds of the Colne Fishery at Brightlingsea are guarded

attached to the Colchester Police, patrol the vicinity to protect

YOGI BEAR LEADS THE PROTEST MARCH :

LONDON : A smiling Yogi Bear - hero of a
TV cartoon - was pushed at theh head of a protest march
through London's West End today. But the people in the
procession were not smiling - for they were tenants from
Bethnal Green protesting over their high rents. Their
destination was the Eton Square, Belgravia, home of
Lord Broughshane, president of the National Federation
of Property Owners and chairman of the Greencoat Properties,
the 2million pound firm which is threatening to evict
200 families unless they pay rent rises. The tenants,

peer's home after the Greencoats Tenants Association received
no reply from Lord Broughshane to meet the Association.

THE QUEEN looked at 18-year-old
James MacKay’s painting yes-
terday and gasped: “It’s horrible!”
She hastily checked her art criticism
and became the tactful sovereign again
with the words: “I mean it must have
been very difficult. The perspective is
very tricky.”
It happened yesterday during the Royal
visit to Loretto public school, near Edin-
burgh.
The Queen and the Duke during their tour
of the grounds and schoolrooms paused in
the art class to see the boys’ handwork.
James had been painting a still-life of fruit
around a bottle when the Queen stopped—
and spoke.
Said James later: “I was in such a flap
I couldn’t say anything in answer. It was
only later that it struck me how funny it
was.”

WARNING TO AIRCRAFT
-----
Although these red and white discs have been
placed on electric pylons at Eynsford and Shoreham (Kent)
Valley now for some time, few people realise their meaning.
When the Central Electricity Board erected them,
the various air liner companies approached them and asked
them to make the pylons visible from the air.
As the pylons were in direct route of the continent,
and as the liners used the valley as a guide during
bad weather, the C.E.B agreed.
So now, if the pilot of a low flying machine sees
these red and white discs he knows a line of pylons
are in front of him, and steers higher and to safety.

title: Photograph of baby rhinocerous Rupert playing with David and Diana Condy
description:
Photograph titled 'The Orphan of the Zambesi'. Caption on back reads: "Water in Lake Kariba, which already contains 1500 square miles of water, continues to rise behind one of the largest dams in the world, and as it rises it very often traps wild-life on small newly made islands. It is the function of 'Operation Noah' -- as it has become known to the wold -- to rescue from drowning, animals which have become trapped on these new islands. The service of these rescue operations continues and the latest story of survival is that of a young rhinocerous called Rupert, who at six-weeks-old was trapped on one such island with his mother. 

Though his mother died in the rescue baby Rupert -- all 150 pounds of him -- survived and was taken in hand by government vetrinary surgeon, Mr J.B. Condy, who eventually took him home for his family to look ater at their home near Salisbury, southern Rhodesia, where he now lives in a specially heated garage and is fed milk from a bottle.

The Condy children, Michael, Katherine, David and Diana all hope that he will not become too tame during during his stay with them, as one day he will have to be transferred to the Great Wankie Game Reserve, where he willhave to fend for himself'

Daily Herald photograph by Capa, Zimbabwe, 5 June 1962.

Transcribed_Text:
By DAVID NATHAN

MR. HENRY BROOKE, the Housing Minister, fled from the platform when rioting broke out in Holborn Hall, London, last night during a Rent Act meeting.

The whole platform party, including TV star Mr. Geoffrey Johnson Smith, turned and ran when the microphone was torn from its socket and a table was overturned.

Tumblers were smashed and chairs hurled at the platform from the body of the hall.

Half an hour after the rioting, a police squad escorted Mr. Brooke out of the hall—from a side entrance.

Before Mr. Brooke arrived at the meeting balloons floated down from the ceiling bearing the slogans like “Evict Henry,” “Repeal the Rent Act.”

BOOS AND SHOUTS

When Mr. Brooke walked on to the platform the audience booed for ten minutes. There were continuous shouts of “Resign.”

When the chairman said that those who did not want to listen could go home, there was more jeering and a shout “You’re putting us out of our homes.”

Mr. Brooke tried to speak. “The Rent Act has two purposes,” he said. But his words were lost in the uproar. After eight minutes he ended a speech which hardly anyone heard and asked for questions.

Suddenly there was a rush towards the platform. Men jumped on to it, and fighting broke out between stewards and groups of men.

Mr. Brooke, Mr. Johnson Smith and Mr. Ronald Gilbey, a member of the London County Council and chairman of the local Tory Association, and Miss Clare Mansel, another member of the LCC, fled to a back room.

The fighting became general. I saw a swinging chair hit a man.

A bottle flew through the air and hit a demonstrator struggling on the platform. The microphone fell on a demonstrator’s head.

The Union Jack on the table was ripped away as members of the Union Movement, rival demonstrators, and Tory stewards had a “free-for-all.”

Police were caught in the struggle.

THEY WERE IN A "DEVILISH MOOD".
Imperial Airways overcome menace of
mosquitoes in tropical countries.

Imperial Airways invited a number of Pressmen
to their laboratores in Battersea, to see a device
similar to that now employed by many London
Hospitals for disinfecting their wards.  It
consists of a portable vaporising machine which
permeates the atmosphere with a pyrethrum
insecticide which kills the mosquitoes which are
liable to carry disease within a few minutes.

Richie Calder, takes a devilish delight
in seeing his 25 mosquitoes "Go West" at the
demonstration.

LAST OF DYING RURAL INDUSTRY.

Mr. Robert Punt, age 76, of South Weald, Essex, still works

work .

AS the building industry faces disorganisation through official strikes, a Herald team visit a big London building site.
They meet some of the men who may be called out to back up the unions' claim for higher basic wages and a shorter basic week.
None of the men interviewed worked the basic week of 42 hours; all did a minimum of ten hours overtime. Skilled and un-skilled men on this site are paid more than a shilling above the minimum rates—between 5s. 3d. and 5s. 10 1/2d. an hour.
Work on 250 selected sites will stop on Monday.
What the men in the picture say
By ERIC GORDON
WHAT do they think about the strike, the men who will be asked to down tools? Do they believe that their unions are right to press for higher wages and a shorter week?
This is what the men on the site in Victoria Street had to say:
THE FLOOR LAYER
Frank Swan, aged 21, a concrete floor layer, of Larkhall Rise, Clapham North, works an average of 57 hours a week. Average weekly wage: £22.
" I have to work hard in the summer to make up for the winter when there's hardly any overtime," said Frank. " Then I pick up about £14 a week.
" But last winter was terrible. I was laid off for seven weeks because of the weather. I had to draw National Assistance of £8 a week. That didn't go far with a wife and baby to support. I back the unions all the way."
THE PLASTERER
Thomas Turnbull, aged 26, a plasterer, of Ansdell Road, Peckham, works an average of 53 hours a week. Average weekly wage about £20.
" Building workers earn every penny they make," said Thomas. " Conditions on some of the sites are shocking. Thick mud, dirt everywhere. Many of the canteens are filthy.
" I too was laid off for seven weeks last winter.
" There's no security in this job. We can be fired at a few hours' notice. Or lose money because of the weather.
" Why shouldn't we ask for more money? "
THE BRICKLAYER
Andrew McEwan, aged 27, a skilled bricklayer of Stepney, works an average of 72 hours a week. Hourly pay: 8s. Average weekly wage: about £28.
" I have to work long hours to earn a decent wage," said Andrew. " The unions' claim is definitely justified. Our basic working week should be cut."
THE SCAFFOLDER
Edward Barrett, aged 29, a scaffolder, of Romford Road, Forest Gate, works an average of 60 hours a week. Average weekly wage: £16.
" My basic wage is about £12 a week," said Edward. " What's the good of that? You've just go to work all the hours possible in this job to make a living.
" The unions are dead right to ask for more. Lucky I'm single. If I had a wife and family I'd never see them. Except in winter, when I'm normally laid off..."
THE CRANE DRIVER
Jim Flynn, aged 24, a crane driver, of Port Road, Barking, works an average of 70 hours a week during the year. Average weekly wage: £20.
This is his first week on the site. He worked 60 hours and drew £18.
" I think I should get more money for the job," said Jim. " It's a big responsibility—one mistake can cost a man's life.
" But I have to work a lot of overtime to make up my wage packet. It's not right. We must have a better basic wage."
THE LABOURER
Eddie Boggans, aged 29, a carpenter's labourer of Blackstock Road, Finsbury Park, London, works an average 65 hour week, including Saturdays. Hourly pay: 7s. Average weekly wage: £23.
" Sure I earn good money," said Eddie, " but I have to work for it. Sometimes, I put in 100 hours a week. I hardly see my wife and kids."

PROGRESS ON BRITAIN'S AERIAL GIANT
25.6.47.
At the Bristol Aeroplane Works at FILTON, progress is being
made on the huge 125-ton "Brabazon I" landplane - the largest
ever to be built in Britain - which when completed will carry
100 people direct from London to New York. A special runway,
for which a complete village had to be demolished and which
will cost £2,000,000, and an assembly hall, are being con-
structed to get this giant into the air. She will have a wing-
span of 230ft (30ft longer than between the main structures
of Tower Bridge), and will be powered by eight Centaurus gas-
turbines of 2500 h.p. each. The picture shows
Another picture which gives a good impression of the

underway in King Arthur's Vale of Avalon. In the district

flood annually and here four giant diesel pumps are in
operation disposing of tons of water per minute converting

drag-line excavators are at work and six giant scrapers draw

task with the grace-
ful body movements of a
Nureyev and the delicacy
of a country lady taking
tea with the vicar.
But, caught for a fleeting

Not even time for the

NORFOLK' S " MAGINOT LINE " AGAINST SEA AT HORSEY.

Norfolk has its own " Maginot Line" in the form of sea
defence work at Horsey, scene of the devastating flood last
February.  Work commenced on April 8th and has not ceased
since.  A vast concrete wall is being constructed  and in
four years time it is anticipated that a wall containing
50,000 tons of concrete and 4,000 tons of steel will give
permanent protection to eight miles of coast between
Winterton and Happisburgh. Behind the wall Marram grass is
being planted on sandhills to hold sand together.

The first British flying-wing monoplane, Burnelli-designed,
is nearing completion in the Cunliffe-Owen aircraft works
at Southampton airport, and will shortly be taken on Test

638) FOOT AND MOUTH PRECAUTIONS IN HAMPSHIRE

As the result of an outbreak of foot and mouth disease 
at Netherhill Farm, Durley, Hampshire, confirmed 
yesterday, it is feared that annual farmers cattle 
shows at Fareham, Alresford and Romsey, to be held at 
the end of the month, may have to be cancelled. One 
hundred and thirty head of cattle had to be destroyed 
to check the spread of the scourge.

Photo shows:- All roads leading to the farm were 
under police supervision. Here is a motor-cycle being 
sprayed with a powerful disinfectant as a precautionary 
measure. All passing vehicles were similarly treated.

Transcribed_Text:
1983-5236/46746

NO FREEZE-UP AT JACKBLOCK

In the Arctic weather which has hampered work on building sites,
normal working has continued on Costain's Jackblock site in
Coventry. No men have been laid off, there has been no short
time working, and building progress has been maintained to
schedule. This has been achieved by surrounding the three lower
floors with a large plastic tent and installing blower heaters
thus bringing factory conditions to a building site.

Picture shows concreting being poured inside the "factory".

HOP PICKING IN KENT.
Some Hop picking is still done in the old fashioned way
O.P.S. Three generations of the Fitzpatrick family
gather round their bin harvesting the Hops on the
itbread Hop Farm, near Tonbridge, Kent.

Down on the farm—three generations of the hop-picking Fitzpatrick family

Exclusive these hop-pickers

By DENNIS CRAIG

ROLLS-ROYCE OWNERS TURNED AWAY
—UNLESS THEY'VE GOT A 'REFERENCE'

THEY roll up in their expensive American cars, Jaguars and even the odd Rolls-Royce, begging for work which pays about 5s. an hour.

But they don't stand a chance. For to become a hop picker in Kent these days the first recommendation you can have is an address in London's East End and a 90-year-old great-grandmother who has been hop-picking for years.

People are rushing to volunteer to work at Whitbread's hop farm in Paddock Wood, Kent.

But now more than 90 per cent. of the hops are picked by machines, and there is no room for the inexperienced who want to work on the farm just because it's a novel kind of holiday.

DESCENDANTS

Farm manager Michael Pelley told me: "Before mechanisation we had more than 5,000 people in the fields during the three picking weeks.

"Now, apart from a student force of 65, the 1,500 pickers are either old hands from the East End or descendants of people who have picked hops with us over the last 50 years or so."

Of course the East End has changed, too. Most pickers from the area travel to and from the field in their own cars.

When I called at the farm three generations of the Fitzpatrick family, including five children, were working there.

John Fitzpatrick, a 39-year-old truck driver from Bermondsey, told me:

"The happiest days of my childhood were spent in the hop fields, but I thought I'd do something better for my kids.

FIVE YEARS

"We tried the Costa Brava, holiday camps and the rest. But on those holidays we are forever telling them 'Don't do this, don't do that.'

John's mother, a 62-year-old widow, chimed in: "I suppose hop-picking won't last many more years. You can't stop progress, but it's a damned pity."

Manager Mr. Pelley agreed.

"I give hand-pickers another five years," he said.

"No doubt about it, mechanisation is quicker and more reliable because—unlike humans—machines are consistent.

"But it's going to be a sad business when all these hand-pickers go. They're wonderful people."

And the East End doffs an affectionate cap at Mr. Pelley. One of the farm-workers said: "This place is better than a home-from-home."

FROM today it is an offence to sell flammable nightdresses for girls up to the age of 12. But will this remove all danger of death and injury by fire for small children?
The Consumer Council do not think so. "This new ruling means that to begin with there will be fewer nightdresses on the market," they say, "and mothers will start making them themselves."
PATTERNS
And so far there is no ban on selling flammable materials.
The Council came up with these suggestions to protect the customer and help to save hundreds of young lives:
Childish patterns should not be used on flammable materials; nightwear for all ages should carry a compulsory warning label if flammable; and particularly flammable articles such as full-skirted party dresses should also bear warning labels.
Flare-proof children's material costs 5s. 11d. a yard; the same material non-flare-proof costs 3s. 11d.
An extra two shillings which could mean the difference between a child's life—and death.

FOR PUBLICATION MONDAY'S EVENINGS, March 18th
THE WORLD'S OUR MARKET FOR CARPETS
18.3.46.
The famous Royal Wilton Carpet Factory was founded in the
17th century near Salisbury in a district noted for its
weaving since Elizabethan days. The factory received its
Royal Charter from William of Orange in 1701 and shortly
after, two Frenchmen, Anthony Dufesey and Peter Jemavle,
were said to have been smug led over from France in
barrels to take charge of the factory. These Continental
weavers were masters of their trade, and the s uggling of
them was necessary owing to the strict laws of France
against craftsmen taking away the secrets of their trades
to foreign countries.
Hand-made carpets have been made at Wilton for many
important buildings in this country and throughout the
world, and now that the factory is released from war work,
it is busy on order from the United States, Canada and
South America etc. This picture taken recently at the
factory shows
Hand loom carpet weavers at work. The short lengths of
coloured wool used for the "knots" are seen in the box.
Millions of these "knots" go to form the pile of a
single carpet.

SMITHFIELD SHOW.
"Everest Perthshire Queen", or "Fluffy" to her friends,
stole the xxxx honours as the prettiest Bovine Beauty in
the show. Fluffy is a 12 month old off-white Heifer
owned by Frank Speak of School Farm, Lockerley, Hants.
She also won 1st prize in her class.
O.P.S. "Fluffy" is congratulated by Shelley Hunt,
daughter of the stock man.

1963-2723-5

Prettiest in the show—
Fluffy, with stockman's
daughter Shelley Hunt.

The wonders
SMITHFIELD Show is not
down on the farm any
more. You can spend the
whole day there and come
away with your boots clean.
There may have been 1,627
animals on show at the open-
ing at London's Earls Court
yesterday, but you could hardly
see them for automation.
The factory, the university
and the stock exchange have
taken over.

Judging rings where white-
coated stockmen and carefully
brushed cattle kicked up the
sawdust were forsaken for the
wonders of the trade stands.
There was a tractor with a
coupe hood to protect the
ploughman; a machine that
picks and tops carrots at the
same time; a potato lifter
which, say the makers, "really
pampers your crop."
It was a relief to meet
veteran stockman Edgar Hunt,
from Romsey, Hants, who was
anxiously grooming a white
shorthorn heifer named
Everest Perthshire Queen and
telling admirers that the beast
was insured for £1,500.
"There's nothing that any

other country can tell us about
breeding," he said confidently
as he led his charge—he calls
her Fluffy—to the ring for her
prize as the prettiest beef in
the show.
Scientists have even devised
a mechanical sow, which rears
five-day-old piglets while their
mother gets on with producing
some more.
Certainly, down on the farm
automation is spreading faster
than muck.

CARRERAS' NEW FACTORY.

SOMETHING FRESH IN LONDON ARCHITECTURE.

It is designed on the basis of the Temple of Bast, the
Egyptian Goddess of the Cats, conventionalised to meet
modern commercial demands.      Two huge bronze cats of
ancient Bubastis flank the main entrance.   Behind them
rise twelve tall pillars against the face of the building.
The colours with which they are decorated were ground
from glass.    Over all is set the winged solar disc,
emblem of Ra the Sun God, the mellower of tobacco.

WORLD'S BIGGEST, FASTEST TRAWLER

PORTIA IS FISHING INDUSTRY'S NEW "QUEEN" AND FIRST DIESEL-ELECTRIC

The diesel-electric trawler "Portia" - 883 tons, 210 feet in length -
left Middlesbrough today (Friday, Oct. 26) on her acceptance trials
before being handed over to her owners, Hellyer Bros Ltd., of Hull.

"Portia", built for safety-first, is nearly 100 tons bigger than the
largest trawlers now operating.  Her speed of 15 knots will help to
get her catch back more quickly to market.  She has cost over
£250,000.

title: Photograph of Helen and Peter Kroger boarding a plane to Warsaw
description: A photograph taken from the Daily Herald Archive showing Helen and Peter Kroger, members of the Portland Spy Ring boarding a plane for Warsaw, 23 October 1969.  Photograph by Steel for The Sun.
Transcribed_Text:
THE Krogers had been waiting for eight
minutes in the aircraft which was to take them
to Poland when Mrs. Helen Kroger suddenly
walked out on to the gangway to wave to
photographers. A moment later Mr. Peter
Kroger joined her and for a few seconds
there they were: two Russian spies, two
professional wreckers of Britain's defences,
displaying themselves like a film couple.
Was it a belated surge of sentiment for the
country they tried to damage that impelled
Mrs. Kroger to make a smiling exit? Or was
it a last gesture of defiance?

The Krogers leaving London Airport.

FEBRUARY 2nd 1969
RENT REBELS FIGHT WITH POLICE DURING MARCH TO THE
HOME OF THE HOUSING MINISTER
    Rent Rebels from every estate in and around London
converged on the Hampstead Heath home of the Housing Minister
MR ANTHONY GREENWOOD this afternoon, after holding a mass meeting
in Parliament Hill Fields, Highgate. When they arrived at the top
of Downshire Hill, the road in which the Housing Minister lives,
fighting broke out between the members of G.L.C. Tenants action
association and the police. The march was planned by the Action
Committee as part of a campaign against the GLC rent increases
imposed last October and which were approved by Mr Greenwood.
Tenants have been withholding the increases and they say "Not
a penny on the Rents" will be paid by them. The GLC has written
to these tenants warning them that if the increases were not
paid they could find themselves in a lot of trouble.
PHOTO SHOWS  Police trying to hold back Rent Rebels as they try
            to brake through the police cordon at the top of
            Downshire Hill - the road in which the Housing
            Minister has his home.
AM/KEYSTONE         IS/816033

Housing.. Rents.. Demonstratio ns.

TWO POLICEMEN were hurt
and four people arrested
yesterday in fights outside
Housing Minister Anthony
Greenwood's home.
  A crowd of 6,000 marched on
the house to protest at Greater
London Council rent rises, and
scuffles broke out when they
were confronted with a police
cordon.
  The injured officers, both in
their 20s, received leg and face
wounds.
  Two girls were also hurt and were
carried away after being crushed.
  The arrested marchers were later
charged with assaulting policemen
and obstruction. The demonstrators

1983-5236/55226
MAK ING THE CORONATION CARPET ON THE LARGEST
LOOMS IN SCOTLAND. 10.3.37.

The carpet that is to be laid in Westminster Abbey for
the Coronation ceremony is now being carefully made in a
Glasgow Mill. The carpet has several special features. Itis
one of the biggest ever made, the pieces of which there are many,
measure 40ft. x 33ft. and the surface is getting extra special
treatment to give it a surface nearly as smooth as glass, this
being necessary to allow the floawing trains of the royal ladies
and peeresses who will walk on it,an easy passage, as any minute
obstruction would catch in the frail material they will wear.
The carpet, owing to its gigantic size, is being made on the
largest looms in Scotland of Messrs. TEMPLETON of GLASGOW who
also made the Coronation carpet for King George V ceremony in 1912.
The Scots girls now working on the carpet feel delighted to be
sharing in the work for this historic ceremony and are taking
extra special care at all stages of progress to produce the finest
example of carpet making.

O.P.S. Putting a surface as smooth as glass on one section of
the carpet. HHS/B. KEYSTONE.

RAILWAYMEN and their families in the concrete bungalow settlement at Rogiet, near the Severn Tunnel, will soon have their worst housing troubles settled.
As reported in yesterday's "Daily Herald" the tenants have been on a month's rent strike to induce the authorities to get a move on in making their homes more habitable.

By LESLIE DOWD

FIVE THOUSAND people marched on London’s County Hall last night—singing songs from the Blitz era.

Men, women and children linked arms and sang “Roll Out The Barrel” and “Side By Side” on the two-mile march from Lincoln’s Inn Fields to the South Bank.

As they trooped across Waterloo Bridge, chanting, singing and waving banners, traffic was brought to a halt.

The marchers were protesting against rent increases of up to 10s. introduced by the Greater London Council.

Their leaders claimed that 10,000 had already refused to pay the rises—and threatened that unless the increases are withdrawn, London will have the biggest rent strike in its history.

At County Hall, the marchers were met by 100 policemen but there were no incidents.

After 20 minutes, a deputation were allowed to meet Mr. Horace Cutler, the GLC’s housing chairman.

Then about 50 of the demonstrators, many of them irate housewives, were allowed to see their own councillors.

But Mr. Cutler told the marchers: “The rent increases stay.”

He promised, however, that he would hear tenants’ views in January when the GLC will be planning more increases which have been approved by the Prices and Incomes Board.

‘Iniquitous’

The tenants’ leaders remained angry. They warned the council against taking court proceedings over non-payers.

Said Councillor Jim Kelly, chairman of the Tenants’ Joint Co-ordinating Committee: “We’re giving the GLC full warning that if there is any victimisation we will immediately call for a rent strike throughout London.”

“These increases are iniquitous,” he added. “Many cannot afford them and this is all building up to trouble the like of which makes me shudder to think of.”

Dockers’ leader Jack Dash, there as chairman of an East End tenants’ association, said: “We’re going to win this fight.”

“I am advising all trade unionists to press their unions for industrial action in support of this protest if the GLC tries to victimise people refusing to pay the increase.”

RENT RIOT
clerical
Police escort a council creical worker to a Tube station.
The clerk, Mr. Thomas, was leaving at the end of his day's
work, when the crowd, mistakenly assuming he had some
connection with council's rents policy, pursued him,
jeering. So a strong band of police were detached to make
sure he got home unmolested.
1959-1710-1
DAILY
15 SEP 1959
HERALD
RENT
Police escort
councillor
crowd had jeered him
FIVE hundred angry tenants whose rents are to be raised mobbed councillors leaving a housing committee meeting last night. And after a scuffle with police, two men were arrested.
The tenants live in council houses at St. Pancras. Before the monthly meeting of the housing committee, they presented Councillor Paul Prior, chairman, with a petition.
Then, while the 13 committee members talked business in St. Pancras Town Hall, a chanting, hostile crowd gathered outside.
Women with shopping bags cried: "Not a penny on the rents," "Down with the Tories," and "Prior must go." Extra police were called in.
Soon after nine o'clock, councillors began to leave. The crowd surged forward as they walked down Euston-road. Fists were waved, and two mounted police cleared the Town Hall steps.

Transcribed_Text:
DO you dream of living
in a luxurious cen-
trally-heated house with
picture windows, three
bedrooms, two bathrooms
and a super kitchen?
Then don't all rush, but
I can put you on to a bar-
gain and here's a picture
of it.
A builder dreamed of
just such a house and
what's more he built it,
on a choice terraced site
at Scarborough. It cost
him £17,500
But it's so dream-like
and modern that nobody
in Yorkshire will consider
it and today it can be
bought for £5,000.
Even the heating sys-
tem is so remarkable that
Lord Robens has paid a
visit to see it. It fills itself
with fuel automatically
and ash has to be emptied
only once a week.
HOW THEY KNOW
And there is a magic-
eye device fitted to the
three-car garage so that
the doors open as a car
approaches.
Is it conceivable that
Yorkshiremen can pass by
such a bargain?
The answer is yes—his
idea of a dream home is
still a semi-detached of
the 1930 period.
And—you've guessed it—
the builders of this 1965
dream house were a Lon-
don firm who wanted to
show Northerners “the
latest ideas in house-
building.”
Well, this experience
should teach those
Southerners a lesson.
When it comes to house
building it looks as though
what Manchester thinks
today London forgot 30
years ago!

Poles Coming—So 40
Families Move In
"HERALD" REPORTER, CHALFONT ST. GILES, Sunday
ALL today in the mile-long lane from this village to Vache Hill Camp families have struggled along on foot, carrying mattresses, beds in sections, rolls of lino and tables.
By tonight 40 families had moved into quarters at the camp.
This "squatters" trek was started by a remark by a Polish staff captain in a public-house.
"We have been given the empty Vache Hill camp for housing our Polish men and their Italian wives who are landing in England in three weeks' time," he said. He added that the garrison engineer was having the camp done up for them.
The news went swiftly round the village and soon the first "prospectors" were making their way to Vache Hill to get there first and occupy the huts.
600 Waiting
The camp has stood empty since it was used for soldiers on

Marshall. 10.8.46.
Thirty Ex-Servicemen and their families take possession of 250 Hut Vache Camp, near Chalfont St Giles, when they hear that it was being made ready for 500 Italian wives of Polish soldiers.

Transcribed_Text:
