STEPHENS. CARDIFF. 30/6/55
More than thirty National Coal Board pit
ponies and horses will be on exhibition at
the Royal Show at Nottingham next week,
including six horses from South Wales.
One of these will be 'Ponty', a 13 year
old horse that has been working underground
at Pochin Colliery, Tredegar, Mon, since
1947.
Ponty is the last horse left at Pochin
Colliery, so when he was brought to the
surface ready for this show, 'Ginger' the
stable cat came up too.
Ginger has been going underground for
fourteen years, and is very friendly with Ponty.
OPS. The Colliery Manager, Mr. Bill Evans
(in overalls) and the Area Veterinary Surgeon
Mr. D.R.T. Davies, take a look at Ponty at the
Pit-head.

A COUPLE and their four children will have to move their beds twice a week and three times on Sundays—so that church services can go on.
For 34-year-old Paddy Doyle and his family are living in a mission hall.
They were thrown out of their own cottage home at Denham, Bucks, when Paddy lost his job as an electrician.
Mr. Gordon Green, pastor of the mission at Tatling End, Bucks, saw them sitting in despair at the roadside.
Weeping
Mr. Doyle's 35-year-old wife, Evelyn, was weeping as she held her youngest child, five-year-old Philomena, who is just recovering from flu. The other children gathered round, cold and hungry.
Mr. Green told them: "The mission hall is yours till you find a house . . ." and the family moved in.
They have set up four beds under a large text which says: "Only believe, only believe, all things are possible . . . only believe."
The beds have to be moved during the services.
And Paddy himself has to step out whenever he wants a smoke.
Mrs. Doyle, boiling eggs in an electric kettle in a room behind the pulpit, said last night: "The children think life in a church is some kind of picnic."

Transcribed_Text:
1983-5236/46141

A DAY IN THE LIFE OF A GIRL WITH AN
UNUSUAL OCCUPATION.

AT 21-YEARS-OLD AGE, MISS MYRTLE. TOPE IS BELIEVED TO BE THE
ONLY GIRL PIG FARMER IN ENGLAND. FROM SEVEN EVERY MORNING UNTIL
DUSK EVERY EVENING THIS VIVACIOUS RED-HAIRED GIRL MANAGES HER
FATHER'S PIGGERY AT YELLAND, NEAR TOTNES, DEVON WHERE SHE HAS
650 PIGS UNDER HER CARE. ALTHOUGH THE NATURE OF HER OCCUPATION
ENTAILS OF THE WEARING OF BREECHES ALL DAY, MISS TOPE IS A VERY
FEMININE PERSON, AND AT THE END OF HER LONG DAY DONS MORE
FEMININE ATTIRE. CLEANING OUT THE PIGGERIES, CARRYING HALF A
HUNDREDWEIGHT OF PIG MEAL ON HER BACK FROM THE STORE ROOM TO THE
FEEDING BARROWS AND THEN PUSHING THE BARROWS ROUND THE FARM TO
FEED 650 HUNGRY PORKERS IS HARD WORK FOR A YOUNG GIRL, BUT MISS
TOPE IS ENTHUSIASTIC ABOUT HER WORK. GROOMING THE PIGS FOR SHOW
PURPOSES IS ONE OF HER MANY TASKS, WHILE THE PIGLETS HAVE TO HAVE
SEED OIL RUBBED INTO THEIR SKINS TO PREVENT SUNBURN AND PAINFUL
CRACKING THROUGH DRYNESS. BREEDING PEDIGREE PIGS IS NO EASY JOB,
BUT MISS TOPE KNOWS ALL THE SECRETS OF HER TRADE.

PLS. THERE IS A GREAT RUSH FOR THE FEEDING TROUGH WHEN MISS
TOPE ARRIVES WITH THE DAY'S RATIONS. 365/B. KEYSTONE.

This was one of the moments of hatred and
violence . . . police battle with an angry mob . . .
a torn banner flutters down . . . women scream and
men are dragged away.

LONE MAN FACES MOB IN
BID TO END RIOTS

ONE man faced 2,000
angry people last night
in a dramatic bid to end the
worst day of hatred and mob
violence that Londoners
could remember.
The man: Councillor Charles
Ratchford, leader of the Labour
Group in St. Pancras council.
He stood in the yellow glow
of street lamps and announced
that the council's Housing Com-
mittee chairman had agreed to
meet a deputation of tenants to
discuss the cause of the violence
-the council's rent increases.
The crowds, packed into a cor-
doned-off street, cheered. And
suddenly the whole mood
changed. Gone was the bitter-
ness, the abuse, the hatred.
Councillor Ratchford advised
the crowd to go home to sleep
the sleep of the just, "and allow
the police to return from where
they came."

New threat

And not one dissenting voice
was raised among the crowd,
gathered outside Kennistoun
House, the block of council flats
where barricaded-in tenant Don
Cook was evicted earlier in the
day.
But, as he spoke, a new threat
was building up. A thousand
people who had gathered out-
side another "rebel" block of
flats—Silverdale House—were
marching to join the Kennis-
toun House crowds for a joint
meeting.
At their head was Arthur
Rowe, the barricaded-in tenant
who was also evicted by bailiffs
from his flat in the Silverdale
block.
Police feared that when the
two groups met, the would join
in a new outbreak of violence.
Reinforcements moved into
the area. Councillors at the
town hall hurriedly broke up a
meeting when it was reported
that an angry mob was march-
ing on them. Forty policemen
ringed the building.
Eight people were arrested
during the hours of violence
earlier in the day.
Thousands of screaming
tenants, some of them swinging
bottles, fought with hundreds of
police.

Bottles

Four hundred men from the
Shell building site on the South
Bank, and 200 railmen who
stopped work at Camden Town
depot, marched to join the
demonstrators.
The objective: To re-take Don
Cook's flat.
Women screamed as policemen
and strikers fell and were
trampled by the yelling mob.
After a ferocious five-minute
battle, when truncheon-wielding
policemen had their helmets
hurled into the air and coats
torn from their backs, the mob
broke through to the Kennis-
toun House gates.
There another posse of police-
men barred the way.
A boy was injured when he
was trampled on by the milling
demonstrators. He was taken to
hospital.

The performance remains unaltered - complete with powerful
vacuum brakes permitting express speeds. When the flaps are lowered
cars may be driven from one end of the train to the other for rapid
loading and unloading.
So far British Railways have built 24 of the new car
transporters. They take full advantage of the railways' ability
to move commodities in bulk at speed over long distances and also to
achieve unrivalled economy.
Hundreds of cars will now be transported weekly by the
new service. A second car transporter train will be introduced
shortly with others to follow.  The capacity of the service is
increased to 3,600 cars per month, nearly one third - 800 cars a week -
are already being carried by "Tier-Cartics". Each train journey
between Glasgow and the south is completed overnight. When the
trains arrive at destination they are distributed to points, often in
the south, they then load up with cars destined for the
north. Thus achieving efficient and economical two-way haulage.
The success of this transporter project is being
hailed as an example of the results which can be achieved when
British Railways, private industry and forwarding agents get together.
In addition, it is an example of how the railways are using expensive
capital equipment to maximum advantage.

By DENNIS CRAIG
Picture by CHRIS SMITH
THE whisper of surf on a beach, a tarred country road melting in the sun . . .
For each of us there will be a different memory of high summer 1964.
For 13-year-old Linda Stidson, of Wheathampstead, Herts — pictured above — the memory may be one of a golden sea of heavy-headed, waist-high wheat . . .
And for the farmer it will be a memory of bumper crops — the harvest of the century.
For the farmers have been fortunate in getting just the right amount of spring rains before the hot, dry summer.
In some parts of Britain combine-harvesters and their teams have been at work three weeks earlier than usual.
The field in which Linda is standing is only 18 miles from London—on Bowman's Green Farm, London Colney—and will be harvested today.
Says the owner, 27-year-old Mr. Samuel Legerton: "A little too much sun for gravel lands—but the barley crop should be a record one."
A survey by the National Farmers' Union shows that the best harvests to date are in the Cotswolds and in Somerset, where yields of between 35 and 40 hundredweights an acre are reported.
In the south-east, Oxfordshire and Buckinghamshire, farmers say it is one of the cheapest harvests they can remember, with little drying and fast harvesting.
For harvesting in the machine age is easy. Four men, three £2,200 combines and a tractor now do the work of teams of 36 horses and 20 labourers in about half the time.
The men can earn up to £30 a week. But to do so they have to work from sunrise to sunset.

title: Photograph of Peter Kroger visiting his wife Helen in prison
description: A photograph taken from the Daily Herald Archive showing Peter Kroger being taken to Ford Open Prison, Sussex to meet with his wife Helen, an inmate there, 5 August 1969.  Photograph by Markeson for The Sun.
Transcribed_Text:

PETER KROGER IS TAKEN INTO A
BUILDING (LEFT) WHEN HE ARRIVED AT
FORD PRISON TO-DAY TO MEET
HIS WIFE. HE DROVE THROUGH
THE DOUBLE GATES (IN FOREGROUND)
IN A CLOSED PRISON VAN IN

HE HAS A MEAL
WITH HIS WIFE
MASTER SPY Peter
Kroger, handcuffed to a
police officer on the left
of the picture, hurries
into Ford open prison,
Sussex, yesterday for a
meeting with his wife,
Helen.
It was the first time the
two spies had met since
they learned that they
are to be freed in October
following the Gerald
Brooke "swop deal" with
Russia.
White-haired, 58-year-
old Peter Kroger, serving
his 20-year sentence at
the top-security Park-
hurst prison, Isle of
Wight, was first to arrive
for the meeting.
K r o g e r and three
prison officers, in a green
van, drove aboard the
Fishbourne - Portsmouth
ferry early yesterday and
were escorted to the open
prison by two police cars.
Helen Kroger, jailed
with her husband in 1961
for her part in the Port-
land spy ring, was driven
from Holloway prison in
London.
The couple met in a
small room at the prison.
They had a meal together
and discussed plans for
their future.
Their meeting was
officially described as "a
routine quarterly visit
between husband and
wife, permitted by Home
Office regulations."
THEIR FUTURE
It is believed, however,
that the couple wanted
the meeting to discuss
their future after release
and Poland's offer to
give them a home.
They were told they
must speak in English—
and their conversation
was recorded by prison
officers.
Polish-born Peter
Kroger and his 55-year-
old wife talked together
for more than two hours.
Then they were taken
back to their prisons to
serve the last months of
their sentences.

RONNIE BRODY, star of stage, screen and poster is leaving the hoardings next month. Ronnie is the hero of those Pinta Man ads, by which I mean he is not the hand-some giant who drinks milk, but the worried little fellow who doesn't.
For the curious effect of this summer's National Dairy Council campaign to get us all hooked on cow-juice has been to turn ad-fanciers into Little Man fans.
When Pinta Man performed some feat of strength, Little Man looked on in an agony of weak ineffectiveness. When Pinta Man looked cool in a white suit and a fresh carna-tion, Little Man sweltered.
Naturally most of us chose to identify with the underdog, which must have hurt the feelings of the National Dairy Council no end. They wanted us to admire the big guy and to lap up milk by the gallon. Like him.
Next month Brody bows out and new posters go up featur-ing the Pinta family. No Little Man.

A COUPLE and their four children will have to move their beds twice a week and three times on Sundays —so that church services can go on.
For 34-year-old Paddy Doyle and his family are living in a mission hall.
They were thrown out of their own cottage home at Denham, Bucks, when Paddy lost his job as an electrician.
Mr. Gordon Green, pastor of the mission at Tatling End, Bucks, saw them sitting in despair at the roadside.

Weeping

Mr. Doyle’s 35-year-old wife, Evelyn, was weeping as she held her youngest child, five-year-old Philomena, who is just recovering from flu. The other children gathered round, cold and hungry.
Mr. Green told them: “The mission hall is yours till you find a house . . .” and the family moved in.
They have set up four beds under a large text which says: “Only believe, only believe, all things are possible . . . only believe.” The beds have to be moved during the services.
And Paddy himself has to step out whenever he wants a smoke.
Mrs. Doyle, boiling eggs in an electric kettle in a room behind the pulpit, said last night: “The children think life in a church is some kind of picnic.”

Today, as machines take over,

The system in operation at
Ormonde is called ROLF —
Remotely Operated Longwall Face
—a mining miracle consisting of a
coal cutting machine, an elaborate
system of hydraulic roof supports,
and control gear.
At Ormonde the seam of coal is
some 44 inches thick and ranges up
to 200 yards in width. To get the
coal out, parallel tunnels are driven
down the " flanks " of the seam so
that the coal is sandwiched between
them.
A coal cutting machine then
works across the edge of the seam
depositing the coal in the side tun-
nels where conveyor belts and lifts
carry it to the surface.
With ROLF the whole operation
of running the machines along the
face can be controlled from the
panel which David Baird operates
in the space and comfort of one of
the tunnels.
SUCCESSFUL
Ultimately it will almost certainly
be possible to run the whole opera-
tion from the pit head, with only
an inspection staff underground.
ROLF has proved so successful
in its experimental stages at Or-
monde, that the Coal Board is in-
stalling nine more ROLF systems,
one in each coal area except Kent.
At Ormonde the miners are all
happy about the coming of the
machine age. They think that the
day rate pay scheme should have
been made universal years ago.
None of them looks forward to
going back to the old orthodox

SURVEY OF PIPELINE ROUTE THROUGH TURKEY

In response to inquiries about reports that an Iraq Petroleum Company
survey party is engaged in surveying a pipeline route through Turkey, the
I.P.C. (in which B.P. is a partner) confirmed last week that a preliminary
reconnaissance is being carried out.

Long before the Suez crisis the possibility of a pipeline route
through Turkey was under serious consideration by the I.P.C. The
Turkish Government was therefore approached and its permission was obtained
for the making of a preliminary survey of a possible pipeline route. A
technical survey party, the I.P.C. spokesman explained, is now conducting
this reconnaissance as a basis for further consideration of the project,
which is part of a plan for the long-term development of Iraq oil production.

BOTTLED GAS FOR AUSTRALIAN HOMES

Bottled gas will be available this month from B.P.'s Kwinana
refinery, Western Australia. Gas will be marketed by the
Commonwealth Oil Refineries Ltd., B.P.'s distributing subsidiary.
The gas, which has a much higher calorific value than coal gas, is used extensively
in Europe and the U.S.A. where supplies of town gas are not available.
The gas will be offered to Australian users in 100 lb. and 25 lb.
cylinders, the latter being particularly useful for holiday-makers in
boats and caravans.

PHOTOGRAPHS

Photographs for press or other publication,
of all aspects of the B.P. Company's operations are
obtainable on application to Photographic Section,
General Department, The British Petroleum Company Limited,
Britannic House, Finsbury Circus, London, E.C.2.
(Telephone: NATional 1200, Ext. 344).

title: A photographic print of Industry, Motor, Factories - Exteriors
description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Industry ÃƒÆ’Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â» Motor ÃƒÆ’Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â» Factories - Exteriors.
Transcribed_Text:
ball match, a seaside carnival or a race meet-ing. Five days a week.
Fords employ 39,000 people there, and half arrive in their own car or somebody else's.
Eleven thousand cars pour into the plant daily and 8,000 may be parked at one time.
Getting there — then finding somewhere to park. It is ironic that the two great problems of the motor age are crystallised in the giant factory where the new age began.
I stood at the main entrance at 7 a.m. to see this problem, which is so complex that Fords have handed it to a professor to solve. He reports that it can be solved—at a cost of £1,250,000.
HEMMED IN
wwwwwwwwwwww
Fords' trouble is that they are hemmed in. They have the Thames behind them, marshland on their right, other factories on the left. Traffic can approach only from the North. And it is some spectacle.
The two private roads into the factory both lead off the deaf-ingly busy A13. This carries not only traffic bound for Fords, but heavy vehicles growling to Til-bury docks and Southend. Get-ting on and off this main artery is the headache.
A smash, a breakdown, the misjudgment of one driver causes chaos.
Says Mr. Norman Patmore, Fords central traffic manager: "You only have to blow your nose on the A13 and everything stops. If there is fog the situation is acute."
Once the Ford traffic has turned into the two avenues, it takes 60 works policemen at peak times to direct it into the 25 car parks.
LONG HUNT
wwwwwwwwwwww
Fords cover 562 acres, and 36 acres are car parks. Late-comers may have a long hunt for space and a long walk to office or workshop.
Trouble comes when shifts clash. Sometimes, 4,000 cars will arrive just as 1,750 are leaving. An hour's overtime can cause chaos, because it throws an extra shift into the rush-hour.
On a really bad night, it can take two hours to clear all the home-bound cars.
One worker, red-haired Leslie Finch, climbed from his elderly Standard and told me that he allowed one hour for the eight-mile trip from his home in South Ockendon. The
his home at Upminster, told me: "There is no more park-ing space. Really we need 50 acres. And in 10 years we would need 75 acres, because we expect the number of em-ployees' cars to rise by half."
So Fords called in Professor Janusz Kolbuszewski, the bril-liant traffic engineer from Birmingham University. He spent six months on surveys and censuses, and produced some fascinating data.
FLY-OVER
wwwwwwww
There are 19,623 Ford workers arriving by motor vehicle, 11,097 by public trans-port, 2,816 by cycle, 1,341 on foot and 509 by ferry across the Thames.
Some travel 50 miles, many live on the doorstep in Dagen-ham.
Mr. Marples would wring his hands over cars carrying only one or two people, but Fords can hardly be expected to discourage workers from using cars. After all, they make them.
The Ford newspaper lists people offering and wanting lifts, however, and Fords have suggested alternative routes when road works made con-gestion even worse.
When Henry Ford chose the site, perhaps he did not fore-see the full effect of the motoring revolution. Arthur Lee, of the works police, re-calls that in 1939 there were only 200 cars a day, though there were 12,000 employees.
Prof. Kolbuszewski's answer to the snarl-up is to build fly-overs over the A13. These would lead into multi-storey car parks, which could be moved about. He also suggests more slip-roads and bridges.
The scheme has only just reached the top Ford desks and is still being con-sidered. Mean-while Fords are appointing a traffic engineer.
One interesting point is who pays if the scheme is adopted?
When one slip-road was built nearby, benefitting both Fords and another factory, they shared the cost with the Ministry of Transport. Fords could argue that the fly-overs would benefit all the A13 traffic.
Fords dilemma is one which must make all large factories apprehensive. Vauxhall's (20,000 workers at Luton) and BMC (24,000 at Long-bridge, Birmingham) have similar problems, though their geography is more helpful. Entries and exits are not so hard to create.
SHIPPED
wwwwwww
Looking at the Thames, lap-ping so close to the factory doors, I asked Mr. Patmore why workers could not arrive by boat.
"They would also have a journey from their homes to the river," he said. "It would not be practicable."
The Thames brings raw material right to the factory, however, and new cars are shipped off the same way.
Ford's have a marvellous tradesmen's entrance—but a bottle-neck for a front door.

SUN USED 4 AUG 1969

Port Talbot, the town where a 7s. dispute can halt a large section of British industry

From JON AKASS: Port Talbot, Sunday

THERE ARE NOT, as far as I can discover, any wildcats in Port Talbot. The steel workers here are cool cats; the whole town hums with sweet reason.
There are no agitators and nobody is especially agitated. And yet, at 2 pm. tomorrow, a hugely unreasonable event will occur here. The Abbey Margam steel plant, the biggest in Britain, will close down.
Ostensibly, the strike is all about 7s. An increase of 7s. out of a national wage rise of £1 0s. 1d., which is not, for complex reasons, being paid to 140 furnacemen here.
These furnacemen have already been on strike for five weeks. The whole plant stops tomorrow, and eventually a sizeable slice of British industry could be forced to a halt as well.
From a distance, it all sounds remarkably silly. Listening to the steelworkers here, an uncommonly articulate and reasonable body of men, it sounds perfectly sensible.
Listen, for example, to Russell Bond, himself a furnaceman, a married man of 43, father of three children:
"They say labour relations have always been bad at Port Talbot. Speaking for the furnacemen I can say that it is not true. If anything, we have been too bloody soft."

CASUAL

"You should try working in the furnaces. Or just see it. And then try to tell me a man working there is worth £13 a week. There's something wrong."
Though not officially classed as skilled workers, furnacemen have an elaborated system of grading and promotion that can span a working lifetime.
He starts as a casual labourer—the men the strike is about—and moves upwards through the ranks of shift labourers, helpers, slaggers and, finally, keepers. It can take 25 years to become a keeper, who gets up to £35 a week.
In July the furnacemen at Port Talbot stopped paying their union dues on the grounds that the top union executive have become too remote and ineffective.
There is, too, the green book, a notorious document in this town. This is the Steel Corporation's productivity deal which threatens to cut through the complex system of skills, pride and status which sustains the closed world of the 16,000 men working at the plant.
"There is so much politics tied up with this," said Mr. Bond, "and I regret it. The last thing we want to do is put the TUC on the spot.
"But I tell you, they think we're peasants down here, peasants."
A lot of the objections to the green book, though, are specific and real. With thousands of tons of molten metal flowing about the place every moment of the day and night, a high degree of specialisation is, in their view, both safe and more efficient.
Crane driver Ken Thomas, aged 35, is qualified to operate 17 separate types of crane. He said: "Supposing you had to work beneath a man lifting tons of molten steel over your head. Who would you want working a crane—a man who has been at it 16 years, like me, or a man who has been at it five minutes?"
But behind these technical grievances there is a wider and deeper dissatisfaction that will not be easily resolved by the TUC, Barbara Castle or even Harold Wilson.
This is a one-industry town, though here and there you can still find the Edwardian bay windows of what was once a fashionable seaside resort. Where most factories are measured in acres, the Abbey and Margam is measured in miles.
When a boy leaves school here he either goes to the steel works or he leaves home. There are few alternatives.
So naturally, they feel a shade vulnerable, trapped.
And after a hard and disagreeable week's work they bitterly resent the fact that their pay is usually rather less than a London typist's.
Russell Bond spoke of all this at the Bayview Working Men's Club—the most elegant building in Port Talbot.
"There is something wrong," he said. "Something damned wrong."

DAILY HERALD

IT'S a workhouse. And nothing the LCC can do can alter that fact. There's a workhouse look about the outside, and a workhouse look about the inside.
The kind of place which everyone hoped would disappear when the Poor Law was abol-ished. Everyone included the LCC.
But the problem of

London's homeless is so big that 98-year-old Newington Lodge has still to be used-not as a workhouse but as shelter for those with nowhere else to go.
Here live three hun-dred women and child-ren. They are free, of course, from all the old indignities which went with the Poor Law.
There is bright red and

yellow paint on the walls of the corridors and the old stone stairways. There are scores of child-ren and their laughter echoes through the oh-so-clean (and warm) rooms.
With the determina-tion of incorrigible home-makers mothers have added their own family photographs and cher-

ished ornaments to the mantelpieces.
But dad's missing. Not even the limitations on privacy, the merely ele-mentary furnishings, the lack of real comfort—none of these hurts so much as the rule that fathers can't be accom-modated.
All the families deserve pity, some admiration for their courage and irre-pressible good spirits.
The big headache is get-

ting the families out of Newington Lodge as quickly as possible. Gener-ally Dad does his best, tramping London for a home he can afford. And the LCC does its best, too, to give them a start in a place they can make into a real home.

AGENT
1949

THIS wing-collared cadet, chosen from 550 to take charge of the Guard of Honour, had the best view of Princess Elizabeth when she inspected Dartmouth College yesterday.
But the 551st cadet had no view of her. Trees blocked his view as he sat on a deck-chair 100 yards away.
He was 16-year-old Colin Cape, who "borrowed" a 30-ft. Naval launch to visit Alderney three days ago when the Princess was there—but didn't see her.
Now he is detained while the Admiralty studies his case. During yesterday's inspection he was guarded by a woman in civilian clothes.

IN one picture: a perfect

schoolboys to ponder
upon.
As they bend to take
their punishment they
can, loosely speaking, hold
their heads high.
With justification. Be-
cause they alone create
demand for Britain's
wackiest export.
Canes (schoolmasters,
for the use of) leave this
factory at Hayward's
Heath, Sussex, at the rate
of between 15,000 and

They are tested first by
Mrs. Edith Hook (centre
in the picture) and Miss
Jackie Stonestreet.
Then they are sent to
schools in Africa (the
biggest customers for some
reason), America, New
Zealand, Canada, Ireland
and Britain.
But the firm have per-
sonal customers, too. Like
the woman who called for
a cane, accompanied by a
small boy obviously due for
a hiding.
Said a spokesman: "As
she turned to leave with a
cane, the boy gave our
salesman a hard hack on
the shins."
Or, as military men
would put it, a swift, suc-
cessful act of reprisal.

INTRODUCING pioneers ..
some of the 300 miners
and their families who
moved from dying pits in
Durham to the coal mines of
South Wales.
Ninety-six of the miners live
in £1,000 caravans which they
rent from the Coal Board at
Groves End, near Swansea.
Rent is 25s. a week. And the pit,
at Brynlliw, is just 500 yards
from the caravan site.
An inquiry by the Coal Board
has shown that these families
from the north enjoy life in
Wales.
So another 3,000 miners will
be invited to move next year
from Durham to the huge new
anthracite collieries, such as
Cymheidre and Abernant, in
West Wales, and Cym in the
east.

SINGING
The advance guard and their
families like the friendliness of
the Welsh people. They like
the thought of soon moving
into new Coal Board houses.
And they like the pay—about
£20 a week at Brynlliw. This
is slightly more than the aver-
age in Durham.
But there are things they do
not like in their new surround-
ings.
Chief among their dislikes

THEY LOVE WALES—BUT NOT
THE BEER OR THE SINGING
are the beer, the fish and chips,
and Welsh concert singing.
Said Mrs. Annie Eagle, wife
of 51-year-old Eli Eagle, yester-
day: "Welsh people are very
musical, but we prefer the kind
of sing-songs we used to get in
our own clubs.
"We like the people because
they are so kind. But there is a
lot we miss in this village, enter-
tainment mostly.
"Our clubs up north were big
and we had top-class entertain-
ment parties."
These views are shared by the
men who are raising money to
start their own club
But in the main these things
are not so important as the
reassuring economics of the
situation. There is enough rich
coal in the seams to keep the
Brynlliw pit paying handsome
profits for at least 80 years.

description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Industry ÃƒÆ’Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â» Textiles - Cloth ÃƒÆ’Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â» Fire-Proof, Non Shrink, Waterproof ÃƒÆ’Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â» (including Inflammable).
Transcribed_Text:
Tricia

Just 39 seconds after a lighted match was applied the pyjamas from Store No. 1.

STORY : MICHAEL RHIND
PICTURES : RON BURTON

THREE YEARS after a Home Office regulation ban- ned the sale of inflammable children's nightdresses in Britain, much of children's nightwear remains, basically, as dangerous.
This is the conclusion of a SUN survey which established two points:
● Children's safe nightdresses are now almost impossible to buy in popular price ranges.
● Two pairs of toddlers' pyjamas that were lit went up in flames in little more than half a minute.
The Home Office regulation was brought into use in 1964. It forbade the selling of child- ren's nightdresses which were not treated to make them flame and flare-proof.
Our inquiry began after a

reader complained that she was unable to buy a treated nightdress.
Woman's Editor Amy Land- reth visited several chain com- pany branches and found the com- plaint justified. Few night- dresses were available — but there were ample supplies of pyjamas, which are not affected by the regulation.
She bought two typical pairs —one from Store No. 1, for 9s. 11d., the other from Store No. 2 for 10s. 6d. Both were described on their labels as Empire Made. They contained

no fireproof tabs. With photo- grapher Ron Burton and with the aid of a stopwatch, I experimented on the two pairs, hung side by side on coat hangers.
A lighted match was applied to the Store No. 2 pair which caught fire immediately and after 14 seconds was well alight. The pyjamas had vir- tually disintegrated in 35 seconds.
It took four seconds longer for the Store No. 1 pair to reach a similar stage but they had the advantage of a thick cuff on the trouser bottoms.
One potential fire hazard attached to some pyjamas on sale. With changing fashions, many jackets now take a loose, smock shape, creating the effect of a mini-nightdress.
A spokesman of Store No. 1 said: "There has been some resistance to night- dresses treated for fire- proofing. It costs 30 to 50 per cent. more to treat the material and they have to be carefully washed to retain resistance."

description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Industry ÃƒÆ’Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â» Textiles - Cloth ÃƒÆ’Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â» Lace.
Transcribed_Text:
INDUS...... TEXTILES....CLOTH....LACE 1983-5286/53456.
Quality—the way to win in Europe
EXPORTS
TERENCE FOSTER was not looking for just another safe job when he became sales manager of Guy Birkin Ltd., the Nottingham lace manufacturers.
He knew that anybody wanting to survive in the 'rag trade,' where fashions change overnight and clothes worth millions go into the bargain-basement sales, had to get out and sell.
'I found the answer at Guy Birkin,' Mr. Foster told me at the company's offices in Sherwood, Nottingham. 'I joined a group of men who were already planning for the future.'
When he went to the firm three years ago, the directors had already realised that a possible trade recession was on the way.
With the livelihood of 250 employees at stake, they set up an export committee to look for new markets.
The result of this is that while dozens of companies in the textile field have stagnated, Guy Birkin have broken through into international markets to keep their machinery busy.
Exports have risen in three years from £100,000 to more than £250,000 annually.
There is always someone abroad finding new markets. Sales director Mr. David Attenborough is now in Japan having settled a deal worth £30,000.
Mr. Foster, married with a wife and two children, ran his hand through dozens of lace samples as he told me the story of the company's exports. 'This is a young man's com-
pany, full of young ideas,' he said. 'When I came here the directors launched me straight into selling abroad.
'We realised that Common Market tariffs might force our prices high above those of our competitors, particularly in France.
'It meant finding something new—and we have developed a superb quality elastic lace, better than any made anywhere else in the world. We are selling in the Common Market on quality alone, with our prices forced up by tariffs way above our competitors.'
'A German clothing manufacturer who buys our lace to trim his high-quality garments, says quite frankly that he would sooner buy his lace elsewhere.
'He has seven or eight factories nearby who can supply him with lace. Deliveries would be quicker. And the lace would be cheaper. He could even get lace from America, flown in quickly, on extended credit.
'But he has to buy British for the quality at prices at least one-third higher than he would have to pay at home.'
Mr. Foster sees a market worth at least £60,000 a year for the company in Germany alone if we enter the Common Market and tariffs drop.

1983-5236/58641

DAILY
30 JUN 1961
HERALD

STRIKE-BOUND Dagen-ham looked like a holi-day town yesterday—with temperatures in the 80's and 20,000 Ford strikers with a week's pay in their pockets.
The sunshine strikers queued for hours in the morning to collect money due to them up to the time of Monday's mass walk-out.
The "pay office" was in a bus shelter outside the gates of the giant Ford factory.
Afterwards hundreds of men joined their families at a swimming pool near the fac-tory. Many planned ways of telling the children that their real holidays may have to be cancelled.
Thirty-nine-year-old Mr. Jones added: "This would never have happened if the management hadn't pinned up that notice. They're treating us like schoolboys."
"That notice," pinned up in every department, said Fords would consider wage increases in September if there were no more unofficial strikes. It has caused unprecedented bitter-ness among the Ford workers.
Union leaders and Ford chiefs will meet today to try to find a way to end the strike.
And there will be a mass meet-ing of the strikers at noon.
About 1,000 workers at the Girling brake factory at Cwm-bran, Monmouthshire, were put on a three-day week yesterday because of the Ford strike.

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION MONDAY, Oct 21st.
ENGLISH VILLAGE MAKES WAY FOR GIANT PLANE
20.10.46.
Sacrificed to the cause of progress, the village of CHARLTON,
near Bristol, England, has been demolished to make room for
a runway spacious enough to allow the first take-off of the
giant Bristol "Brabazon" air liner prototype now under con-
struction at the famous works. A vast assembly hall hall is
also being built because she cannot be put together in any
existing building.
Features of the great aircraft are - wing span 230ft, height
50ft at rudder, and length 177ft. All-up weight 126 tons,
and sleeping berths for 80 passengers for night travel. It is
designed to fly direct between London and New York or
Montreal, and gas turbines in the wings accessible during
flight will give her a speed of 350 mph at 25,000 ft and her
range will be 5,000 miles. The picture shows an impression of
the dimensions and spaciousness of the interior of the giant
air liner. Ribs, spars and the forward bulkhead are seen.

title: Photograph Reuben the mountain gorilla at London Zoo
description: Photograph titled 'New Gorilla at London Zoo', shows Ugandan baby mountain gorilla called Reuben at his new home, the London Zoo. Daily Herald photograph by Terry Fincher.
Transcribed_Text:
1983-5 236/19940

BUT HE'S HAPPY JUST THE SAME
A BABY male gorilla gave his first Press conference yesterday. And he couldn't have received more top-level treatment if he had been a film star or a head of State.
The photographers (right) even wore face masks because gorillas can catch human diseases.
SO RARE
In fact, the gorilla is a much rarer personality than any Pressman is likely to encounter among people.
He is one of the few mountain gorillas left in the world and only the second to come to London Zoo.
Game wardens in the Birunga Mountains in the Central African State of Uganda found the baby.
DESERTED
He had been deserted by his mother and was sitting on the chest of a dead male gorilla he had adopted as protector.
The orphan was too small to defend himself against mountain leopards. So he was captured and flown to London.
A female chimpanzee flew with him in case he got frightened.
But the Zoo expert needn't have worried. He apparently enjoyed his 4,405 - mile journey so much that he ate a gorilla-sized meal as soon as he landed.
The Zoo now faces the problem of a name.
Back in Uganda they suggested Reuben, which may be all right for a baby gorilla, but will seem a little silly when he grows to 6ft. and weighs 450lbs.
The Zoo will be glad to have any ideas — BIG

20.5.60
FINCHER DH

The Batman cape flares up within fractions of a second after Sun
fireman Arthur Webb put a cigarette lighter to the cape.

BATMAN CAPES sold in shops throughout London as Christmas presents were shown to be highly inflammable in a test conducted by the SUN yesterday.
In 35 seconds, a cape—a part of a 12s. 11d. kit which includes trunks and a mask—was reduced

LIKE A TORCH
It comes from Accessory Novelties (Ware) Ltd., a small firm in Hatton Garden, London, run by Hungarian-born Peter Vitmayer.
I bought the kit at a toyshop in Hartfield Road, Wimbledon. The shop is run by Mr. John Johnson, who contacted the SUN after reading the “killer” toys probe in yesterday’s paper.
Mr. Johnson told me: “I bought 36 kits from Accessory Novelties after my supply of official Batman kits ran out.
“When I read of potential dangers from toys, I tested one of the black plastic capes with a match and it went up like a torch.
“I immediately started to contact customers who had bought the kits. I have traced all but five.

“Something like 1,500 of these kits have been sent out mainly to small shops in the London area and in Bournemouth, but I am discontinuing the line because I don’t think it sold very well, and in any case it is too late in the season.”

THREE FIRMS
Mr. Vitmayer added: “I do not know why the Batman kits were sent back to Mr. Johnson. It must have been a mistake. I had already agreed by telephone to accept them.”
I told Mr. Vitmayer of the SUN test and asked if he planned to withdraw kits still in the shops.
He replied: “I don’t see why I should, unless I am ordered to by the Home Office.”

ALL THE FUSS
“I sent the unsold ones back to Novelty Supplies, but after a few days they were returned in the post stamped ‘Consignee Unknown.’”
Before conducting the test in the Sun office, I phoned Mr. Vitmayer and invited him to be present. He told me: “I am far too busy to come along. Anyway, what is all the fuss about?”
Later I saw Mr. Vitmayer at his office in Greville Street, Hatton Garden, where he identified the trunks from the kit as manufactured by his firm.
Mr. Vitmayer, aged 51, who came to Britain from Hungary in 1938, told me: “I have been in business for 20 years and this is the

Mr. Vitmayer agreed to hand over a Batman kit still left in his office to Mr. Hill for further tests.
A spokesman for Mervyn Brodie Associates Ltd., and Walter Tuckwell Associates Ltd.—who hold the world rights for Batman products outside the U.S. —commented later:
“There are three firms in Britain who hold licences from us to manufacture the Batman kits, and the material they use conforms to British Standards Institute regulations. It will not support a flame.
“Mr. Vitmayer has no right to manufacture them. We shall have to investigate the matter, and decide whether we should take any action.”

LEVEN brass bands marched
big parade-the gayest concer
tion of oompah-oompah for many
year.
The occasion: the Nottinghamshire
Miners' rally at Mansfield on Saturday.
Tableaux and bands joined in a mile-long
parade through the town. Rows and rows
of pitland's finest virtuosos.

ON TAPE
Said miner Wilf Harper, of Howard Street,
Sutton-in-Ashfield: "This sort of music is
part of our way of life round here."
That is why 62-year-old Wilf, once a mem-
ber of Teversal colliery band, was busy with
his tape-recorder on the bandstand at
Mansfield's Berry Hill.
He said: "Some of my mates, disabled
and crippled in the pits, can't leave their
homes to listen to the bands.
"When I play these tapes to them it will
be just as though they were here today."

COAL QUEEN
The National Union of Mineworkers, who
organised this 14th annual rally, laid on a
packed programme of entertainment for
20,000 miners and their families.
High spot was the crowning of 17-year-old
Monica Smith as Nottinghamshire's Coal
Queen.
Monica's father, 38-year-old
Ron Smith, a face-worker at
Bolsover Colliery, Chesterfield,
declared: "I'm the proudest dad
here today."
Monica and her two attend-
ants - Mrs. Margaret Smith,
aged 21, of Calverton, and Miss
Pamela Woodcock, 18, of Mans-
field Woodhouse - were chosen
from 36 finalists.
The fair-haired Coal Queen, a
grammar-school sixth-former,
plans to train as a maths
teacher when she leaves school.

FASHIONS
While wives watched a fashion
show and children enjoyed
donkey rides, the mine-workers
listened to speeches from Mr.
George Brown, Deputy Leader of
the Labour Party, and Mr. Will
Paynter, NUM secretary.
The prize for the best band of
the march went to the Black
Diamonds of Bestwood Colliery.
Harworth Colliery gained four
awards in the tableaux competi-
tion.
For the rest there were
whippet races, physical culture
displays, boxing and wrestling
- and plenty of sunshine which,
like almost everything else at
the rally, was free.

O.P.S.
Women pickets and banner bearers outside the flats where they are on a Rent stBrike in Russia Lane.
Photograph
Number
ISSUED - 3 AUG 1938
WOMEN acted as pickets when hundreds of tenants in Quinn-square, Bethnal Green, E., one of the most densely populated areas of London, came out on a rent "strike" yesterday. Women in colourer paper caps with "Picket" across the front stood at the entrances to houses. Tenants allege that in some cases of controlled tenancies they are paying too much, that decontrolled pre-mises are too dear, and that there is undue delay in making repairs.

"DON'T BID"
CRY BY WOMEN
Feb 22 1934

From Our Special Correspondent
MACCLESFIELD, Tuesday.

BY singing and jeering and re-
fusing to allow bids, 400 farmers
and their womenfolk stopped a
forced sale of stock today at Big
Tidnock Farm, Gawsworth, near
here, where bailiffs are in pos-
session.

The auction was ordered by the
High Sheriff of Cheshire to satisfy
a £50 fine imposed on the farmer,
Mr. W. Nixon, by the Milk Marketing
Board.

"If I can get nobody to bid, I shall
have to postpone the sale for a day or
two, but I don't know whether it will
help things," said the auctioneer, who
represented a Manchester firm.

The auctioneer remained impassive
while the crowd sang, and then stepped
from the low wall where he had been
standing, and after a talk with Mr.
Nixon left the farm escorted by police.

OWES £83

Mr. Nixon was fined for selling milk
at less than the regional price fixed by
the Milk Marketing Board. He now owes
£83 13s. in fines and costs, which are
still mounting.

When the sale was postponed five
head of cattle had been sold, but not
one left the farm.

All had been knocked down to Mr.
Nixon's brother-in-law for £36.

Afterwards the farmers, many of
whom had travelled long distances to
attend the sale, made a collection for
Mr. Nixon which realised £27 17s. 10½d.

FRAYED TEMPERS

Uniformed police, specially drafted
into the area to prevent trouble, mingled
with the crowd and occupied farm
buildings.

Soon it was seen that one man was
starting the bidding and tempers became
frayed.

Women shouted "Behave like an
Englishman and don't bid," and violent
words were exchanged.

An ugly scene was developing, but
tact by the police and an appeal from
Mr. Nixon restored order.

When no more bidders could be fou
Mr. Nixon was cheered and there
loud cries of "Down with the
Marketing Board," accompa
booing.

Mr. Nixon told me he wo
to defy the Board even if
he would lose all.

Other farmers addr
declared that they

COUPLE FORCED TO LIVE IN A BARN
TWO old age pensioners, 75-year-old Mr. Henry Lee-Burgess and his wife Sarah, aged 72, are living in a farm barn without heat, light or water.
Over the week-end they survived 20 degrees of frost inside the barn at Clymping, Sussex.
During the recent blizzard they were cut off for two days before a farm worker got through 15ft. snowdrifts to bring them warm food and blankets.
Yesterday the couple huddled together under blankets with their dog Susie. They sleep in a makeshift tent inside the barn, covering themselves with straw, sacking and blankets.
Mr. Lee-Burgess, a naval veteran of both world wars, explained: "We had rooms in London, but had to leave because the owner wanted the rooms.
"We tried sleeping in a tent, then a farmer said I could have this barn. God bless him."
Welfare officers will visit the couple today. A county council spokesman said: "We shall certainly look into this and do whatever we can."

Transcribed_Text:
1983-5236/55559

THE SALESMAN
standing outside the
headquarters of Rolls
Razor in Cricklewood,
London, was full of
convincing optimism.
He strode the pave-
ment, rallying the
doubters, with the per-
suasive air matured on
a thousand doorsteps.
"Bloom," he said, "is
one of the lads. A real
goer. He'll think of some-
thing to pull us through."
The men about him, the
salesmen who had
crusaded the country with
low - price washing
machines, nodded agree-
ment. If not in faith, in
hope.
Somehow, to them, it
seemed impossible that all
would not be well. That
the meeting of directors
inside the building would
not produce a miracle
solution.

Transcribed_Text:
1983-5236/51716

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION FRIDAY'S DAILIES, Sept 26th.

ANOTHER REFINERY TAKES SHAPE ON THE THAMES
25.9.52.
Mac
After some two years of hard work and endeavour on a site
at first largely given over to sea birds and salt water, the
CORYTON OIL REFINERY of the Vacuum Oil Company has now
reached a stage where the final outline is taking shape.
Coryton is an Anglo-American enterprise, and it is hoped to
commence distilling the crude oil - 28,000 tons of which has
already arrived in the storage tanks - before the end of this
year. The project is costing £12 millions, and it will have
a 272feet high thermofor catalytic cracking plant - the first
of its kind in the United Kingdom - for the production of
high grade fuel. This is expected to be in operation by next
June. This is one of a new series of pictures taken at the
site. It shows

PHOTO

Enormous quantities of water are neede in a refinery which
will produce some 900,000 tons of oil annually. Apart from
about 1,000,000 gallons daily of fresh water - most of it
to be used in the boilers - a very large flow of cooling
water will be needed in the power plant and in the process
units. xxxxxxx For this purpose water drawn from the Thames
will be used. It will be drawn off by pumping equipment
circulated through the refinery, thoroughly clarified and
returned to the river. The pumps will supply about 45
millions gallons of water a day, and this picture shows some
of the intake pipes in position.

YOUNG SUN. 31.7.69. story Dodd.
Tin prospecting in Cornwall.

MR
TELFER
MITCHELL

1969-1584-Lou A IZA

8 x 5

TELFER MITCHELL is a pros-
pector. He has a shovel, a
hammer, even a stiff leg.
He moves slowly, does Telfer
Mitchell, scrutinising the piles of
earth, the clusters of soil and the
humps that lie around the old
desolate Cornish mines.
Telfer Mitchell prospects for tin,
just 20 hours a week, enough to
supplement his pension.
Tin is once again important to
Cornwall. The Germans, the
Canadians, the South Africans, the
British, all are investing millions
of pounds in sinking new shafts
and opening up old ones through-
out Cornwall.
But all over the county that is
so rich in minerals are the chim-
neys of old mimes and the clutter
of lost generations of tin workings.

Tin saver

Mr. Mitchell now works for
Tolgus Tin Company, Redruth,
which produce tin from the waste
in a rather traditional way.
They take the waste, crush it
and separate it, wash it and then
send it off for smelting.
The public can pay 2s. 6d. a head
to see the operation in motion.
Mr. Mitchell is the man who goes
out to a new site with his "van-
ning" shovel, flicks up a cup full
of soil and water and shakes it up
until the tin begins to separate
from the rest.
"Look," he says, "that's tin. That
yellow stuff. That's why this shovel
is shaped like this. Tin always runs
uphill and tries to get away from
the other stuff."
Business for Mr. Mitchell is
improving. Tin can now cost £1,450
per ton and there are millions of
tons of waste to be investigated.

Time saver

Mr. Mitchell can tell with eyes in a
second what a chemist may take an
hour to do.
"He's never more than one half
per cent out," says his employer, Mr.
Phillip Welch.
Says Mr. Mitchell, shaking the soil
around: "Anything up to one per
cent of tin you can make a profit
on these days."
"That's 22lb. of tin to the ton of
waste. If I tell the company it is
good waste they will buy the area
around it and get the digger in."
Mr. Mitchell believes he is the last
of a long line of tin waste prospec-
tors. "One time," he says, "there
were dozens about. Perhaps with
tin coming back a bit some more
people might start doing it."

title: A document of Industry, Metals, Aluminium & Light Alloys
description: A document from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Industry ÃƒÆ’Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â» Metals ÃƒÆ’Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â» Aluminium + Light Alloys.
Transcribed_Text:
RECEIVED
DAILY HERALD
EDITORIAL DEPT.
16 JUN 1938
12, WILSON STREET, W.C.2
1983-5236/56225

What is probably the
Glasgow Empire Exhibition will be on view to the public next week. The
news of its appearance announces one of the greatest technical achievements
shown at this exhibition.
It is an aluminium wire so fine that 10,000 yards laid side by
side would measure only one inch in width... 20 ounces of it --
aluminium wire would cost over £10,000,000 but it would encircle the World
at the Equator (24,000 miles).
This phenomenal exhibit weighs .00000000342 pounds per foot and
has a diameter of 1/10,000th of an inch. 200 of these aluminium wires will
be equivalent to the thickness of one human hair... visualize it if you
can, dividing a human hair into 200 parts, then in quarters and continuing until you
have divided it 100 times (! really?). When you have done so the small section
you have is the thickness of this aluminium wire. Incredible as it may seem, this
exhibit can be seen through a high-power microscope as our eyes are fixed in the
Gassiot Section.
The aluminium films are used in scientific research. A modern
method of finding oil by means of sound detection, or similar films as records.
detector is used by the Navy to establish the presence of submarines. The
difference in vibration caused by an explosion in the sea is recorded by these
fine aluminium wires in a galvanometer.

LONDON MODELS SHOW SWIMWEAR
FASHIONS TO THE GIRLS WHO MAKE
THEM AT SHREWSBURY

INDUS .WORKERS . . . WOMEN . . . . NOT FACTORY SCENES

USUALLY the models in
the picture stalk graci-
ously down red - carpeted
platforms at London's top
hotels.
Yesterday they went " on
tour " — and discovered that
their stage was an ordinary ,
four-legged wooden table in
a factory canteen.
But the audience who
watched the parade of
swimwear were just as
critical as fashion writers or
buyers.
' MARVELLOUS '
They were the 800 girls
who make the swimwear at
the factory in Shrewsbury ,
Salop.
An official of the firm
explained : " Fashion
experts saw the same
parade in London two days
ago.
" But we wanted our girls
to see their own work on
show. "
The girls ' verdict on the
models? " Marvellous. They
show off our work very
well. "

HERALD

Port the only drink
WHEN the Royal Visit to London docks was
entered in the Queen's engagement book on
a raw, damp day last October, no-one dreamed the
mid-May temperature would be in the 80's. But
that's the way it was yesterday—and all the Queen
and Prince Philip had to drink was a glass of
PORT. They got that when they looked round a
vault to see wines in bond. Elsewhere, it was busi-
ness as usual. These meat workers were among the
lucky ones in dockland yesterday. They had a
breather in the freezer every now and again.

ARTHUR STEEL SUN
200 plane-makers from Coventry and the Rev. Simon Phipps stormed into
the Houses of Parliament today. (STORY V. CHAPPLE)

Indus . Aircraft Workers .

3 7/8" deep

IN the midst of a mass of British planemakers on a mission to Westminster yesterday is an odd man out-a man in a clerical collar.
The planemakers came from Coventry to argue against a proposal to scrap the Hawker-Siddeley 681 four-jet freighter. And the Rev. Simon Phipps believes that what concerns the men on the shop-floors of his parish, concerns him.
Here they are outside the House of Commons. There were 200 in the deputation altogether - many of them shop stewards.
They talked to MPs and then Mr. Phipps, old friend of Princess Margaret and now industrial chaplain in Coventry, adjourned to a nearby pub.
He said: "Discarding this plane could mean the loss of 5,000 jobs in our diocese alone.
"One reason I came today was because I want to identify the concern of the Church with the concern felt by people working in the industry."
Mr. Maurice Edelman, Labour MP for Coventry North, met the delegation and said: "To supersede the 681 with the American C130-already an obsolete plane-would be a big blow to the British aircraft industry.
Resolution
"Apart from the 5,000 jobs at Coventry it could put another 10,000 at Manchester and Belfast out of work."
The shop stewards passed a resolution to Aviation Minister Mr. Roy Jenkins calling for him to proceed with the project.
Mr. Phipps explained: "All these men suddenly without work would create a tremendous problem. I wan't to see the project kept going."
He speaks with a certain authority. He was a plane-maker himself once-trying the job so that he would know what he was talking about.

AN AMERICAN LOOK AT SOUTH AUSTRALIA

Adelaide, the capital city of South Australia, is one of the most
attractive and well-planned cities in the world. It was named after
Queen Adelaide, wife of King William IV, and was founded in 1836. The
city was planned by Colonel William Light, who chose its site on a fertile
plain between the sea and the hills. Colonel Light's plan was a simple
one - a square mile of city surrounded by a belt of parklands.

Today, Adelaide is a modern, bustling city with a population of over
600,000. It is a city of wide streets, beautiful parks and gardens, and
modern buildings. It is also a city of culture and education, with a
university, a museum, an art gallery, and a public library. At one end
of North Terrace, the city's cultural center, is Government House, the
official residence of the Governor of South Australia. At the other
end are the Parliament Houses.

The city's climate is mild and sunny, and its people are friendly and
welcoming. There are many things to see and do in and around Adelaide.
For those who like the outdoors, there are many beautiful parks and
gardens, as well as many fine beaches within easy reach of the city.
The nearby Adelaide Hills offer spectacular views of the city and the
surrounding countryside.

South Australia is a land of contrasts. To the north are the vast, arid
regions of the outback. To the south are the fertile valleys and plains
of the agricultural regions. South Australia is a major producer of
wheat, wine, and wool. It is also an important industrial center, with
many large factories and plants.

In the past few years, South Australia has experienced a period of rapid
growth and development. New industries are being established, and existing
ones are expanding. The population is also growing rapidly, as more and
more people from all over the world are attracted to this land of oppor-
tunity.
